articles.title: COP31 failed, does it matter?
articles.standfirst: Blog COP31 failed, does it matter? The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP)—the annual climate change gathering aiming to steer the world toward lower emissions and increase its resilience to climate change—ended without an overarching political agreement. Does it matter? Thankfully, ever less so. To the trained observer, COPs follow a well-known script. Countries make ... Read more
paragraphs: The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP)—the annual climate change gathering aiming to steer the world toward lower emissions and increase its resilience to climate change—ended without an overarching political agreement. Does it matter? Thankfully, ever less so.

To the trained observer, COPs follow a well-known script. Countries make their positions and red lines known, raising seemingly unreconcilable demands before the COP. They then meet for two weeks to agree on pending decisions on technical workstreams as well as high-level political texts. Along the way, they raise more demands which makes them appear even further apart than before their meeting. And then ultimately the political posturing crumbles under the stroke of smart diplomatic language.

Except, not this time. Not even in the age of all-capable large language models could delegates muster enough literary ingenuity to produce a text bridging differences between large producers of fossil fuels (e.g., Saudi Arabia, Russia) on the one side, and large fossil fuel importers such as the EU, on the other. The EU, represented by Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’Brien, refused to endorse a text that had been stripped from any reference of the role of fossil fuels in driving climate change and instead had emphasised the potential of carbon capture and storage. The EU was followed by the UK, Norway and, in the end, around 130 other countries. The Presidency gave up on presenting another cover decision text, and the curtain came down on Antalya’s COP.

Although a political deal wasn’t reached, several negotiated items, with mostly procedural outcomes, were adopted. For instance, parties approved a three-year extension of the Just Transition Work Programme. These are not affected by the failure to adopt the cover decision. Countries also announced or reaffirmed their commitments under several international partnerships like the Global Methane Pledge.
The disagreements over the cover decision were broad, including the divisions around the 35% by 2035 electrification target, announced by the COP President in Bonn last June.

This announcement confirmed that electrification had reached the top of climate diplomacy, driven by recent technological and political momentum. The focus on electrification was a significant shift from the early days of the energy transition, when almost all attention went to decarbonising power generation. It was also an acknowledgment that, although electrification has progressed, further and faster progress was needed. Although the absence of a cover decision means that no global political endorsement of the electrification objective exists, around 90 countries and 180 business and civil society organizations have taken the voluntary 35 by 35 electrification pledge regardless of a final agreement.

A COP agreement is several steps removed from decisions that will turn electrification from a political objective to an operational one, such as building a grid line or setting an EV sales target. Still, political signals matter and this one would have provided momentum to coordinate decisions needed to speed up electrification.

Despite the failure of COP31, the transformation of energy systems will continue. Economics will drive the deployment of renewables in power generation around the world as well as, with some support in the early stages, the electrification of end uses. In that sense, a failure of COP is less consequential than it might once have been. Indeed, this process has failed before–think 2006 (Nairobi) and 2009 (Copenhagen), but the wheels of decarbonisation kept turning. COP21 brought the Paris Agreement, and policy-supported technological development led to a very substantial fall in the price of the components of the so-called electricity tech stack.

Still, we should guard against dismissing the value of the UN process wholesale. It’s a key gauge of the global community’s commitment to cooperation and an anchor to countries’ national decarbonisation plans as well as the private sector’s investment decisions. Flagging global momentum weakens the signal sent downstream.

Given the urgency of reducing global emissions and adapting to a rapidly changing climate, there is great value in preserving the signalling effect of climate commitments and windows of climate action opportunity. This should be led by proponents of stronger climate action such as the EU, together with willing partners such as China.

Several fora including these parties, such as the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets, have emerged in the last few years for coalition building. Carbon markets combined with CBAMs offer the possibility of a globally significant race to the top on climate action.

But building successful and effective coalitions requires standardised data and procedures; efforts in that direction are therefore incredibly valuable to the success of the energy transition in an increasingly fragmented world.

articles.title: COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya
articles.standfirst:
The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, have failed to reach agreement on a “pact” that lacked clear references to…
The post COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya  appeared first on Carbon Brief.
paragraphs: The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, have failed to reach agreement on a “pact” that lacked clear references to curbing fossil fuels or scaling up climate finance.
The “Antalya pact”, proposed by the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, was rejected in the final hours by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable nations.
Meanwhile, many developing countries criticised the lack of progress on climate finance and indecision on a proposed $120bn target for funding climate adaptation.

With stark divisions preventing agreement on the presidency-led pact, UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell expressed “deep disappointment”, speaking of “scope to improve, modernise and reform” the UN climate process.
Despite a chaotic endgame that saw the overrunning COP become the longest in history, it did not end in complete failure, with many items adopted in the closing plenary.
These included fairly limited or procedural outcomes on a new “mechanism” for global “just transitions”, plus support for countries struck by climate disasters.
There was some progress beyond the negotiations, though, with growing coalitions of nations championing “roadmaps” for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels.
With the presidency promoting “electrification” as a key theme, around 80 nations also signed up to a global target of securing 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035.
Here, Carbon Brief provides in-depth analysis of all the key outcomes from Antalya, both inside and outside the COP31 negotiations.
(See Carbon Brief’s coverage of COP30, COP29, COP28, COP27, COP26, COP25, COP24, COP23, COP22, COP21 and COP20.)

Turkey and Australia presided over the longest COP in history – and failed to find consensus on their proposed “cover decision”, exposing deep fractures between countries on key issues such as fossil fuels and the need for developed nations to meet climate-finance pledges.
Experts told Carbon Brief that, strictly, the talks did not “collapse” as several negotiated items were still adopted.

Rather, the rejection of the cover decision represented, for the first time, “those who want a higher level of ambition actively reject[ing] the lowest common denominator on offer”, said one veteran observer.
Dispute over who would host COP31 – representing the “western Europe and other states” region – had gone on for three years.
In the end, the two main rivals, Turkey and Australia, agreed to a deal last year at COP30 that the summit would take place in Antalya, Turkey, with Australia acting as “president of negotiations”.
Critics questioned whether either country was well-placed to host, given their ongoing fossil-fuel expansion.

Turkey faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields on the eve of the summit, while recent Carbon Brief analysis found that Australia is the third-largest CO2 exporter in history because of its fossil-fuel production.
Ahead of the summit, the presidency released four official letters outlining a vision for COP31.

The first letter, written by COP31 president Murat Kurum in April 2026, confirmed the appointment of Australian climate minister Chris Bowen as “president of the negotiations” and announced that a pre-COP would be held in Fiji in October.

The second letter, authored by both Kurum and Bowen from the Copenhagen climate ministerial in May, said that “COP31 presents a vital opportunity to further accelerate…in the areas of clean energy, electrification and resilient infrastructure”.

The third letter, published in August 2026, gave more details on the presidency’s plans for the “action agenda” – the part of the UN process that mobilises coalitions of nations and non-state actors to push climate action further.

This letter also introduced a key aim from the presidency to get countries to agree to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 (often referred to as “35 by 35”). (See: Electrification.)

The final letter, published in October ahead of the pre-COP in Fiji, said that the presidency would centre on “delivering a COP focused on accelerating implementation, electrification and resilience in an uncertain world”.

It added that “many parties have emphasised the importance of reviewing and continuously improving UNFCCC processes, to ensure it remains fit for purpose, sustainable and focused as negotiations evolve over time”, adding:
“At COP31, we will hold presidency consultations to hear parties’ views on how to strengthen UNFCCC processes, to ensure growing demands are met and to effectively deploy resources.”
The pre-COP in Fiji was held from 5-8 October and was attended by 3,000 people.
In this somewhat intimate setting, Bowen announced that Turkey and Australia had agreed to negotiate a “presidency-led” cover decision at COP31.
He added that revealing this before COP was part of the presidency’s “upfront, transparent and consultative approach”.

Later that month, the presidency named the five ministerial pairs from developed and developing countries that would take key negotiation issues forward at COP31. These issues were mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and oceans.

COP31 kicked off on 9 November, with climate negotiations scholar (and Carbon Brief contributing editor) Dr Joanna Depledge noting that it was clear from the summit’s opening ceremony that “Australia [was] the junior partner” in the presidency.
COP’s opening day ran late into the night as the presidency worked to avert a fight over proposed changes to the summit’s negotiations agenda.

Simon Evans 9 November 2026, 10:40 GMT COP31: Agenda adopted! Agenda adopted! Moments ago in Antalya, Turkey, COP31 president Murat Kurum outlined how an “agenda fight” has been averted, despite various proposals for additions to proceedings. This came after a short delay, while a series of huddles took place on…
The next day, in plenary, Kurum announced that a resolution had been found.

He said that calls for new agenda items on adaptation finance and trade were rejected, whereas an item on a new climate finance “work programme” had been added. (The EU expressed “deep concern” about the addition.)

Kurum added that two extra proposed items on mountains and climate change – made more poignant by recent catastrophic floods in Nepal – were also not added to the agenda. However, he said that the presidency would instead hold consultations on the topic.
Though an early scrap over the agenda was avoided, the summit’s opening days were plagued with logistical problems.
Attendees were forced to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to get into the venue – sparking serious access concerns.

The problems persisted into the first day of the world leaders’ summit on 11 November, when delegates were informed that they should travel between the hours of 5-7am to secure access to the venue. Ire only grew when security staff still let people in after this time.

On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This was an “informal note” with a bullet-pointed list of topics that might be included.
On Saturday evening, Kurum told a press conference that “around 30 countries” had indicated support for the 35 by 35 pledge.
However, he had little to share on progress in the negotiations and eluded questions on how he planned to include “fossil fuels” in the cover decision.
In the small hours of Sunday morning, half-way through the summit, Kurum announced presidency and ministerial consultations on “outstanding political issues”.
He also invited ministers to a “divan” – a group meeting, not a daybed – to discuss cross-cutting issues.

On Monday afternoon, the presidency dropped an 18-page first draft of its proposed cover decision – along with a short “presidency note” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text. (See: Cover decision.)

At a press conference, Bowen told journalists that the presidency decided to release the text “early” to allow parties to debate on it for as long as possible and acknowledged that it would need to be “refined” down.
On Wednesday evening, the presidency held its divan, where delegation heads sat in a circle and were asked to share their priorities for finding consensus in the negotiations.
Speaking at the divan, Kurum told parties that the second draft cover decision would be published that evening.
In the end, the second draft cover decision was published on Thursday.
Later that day, Kurum and Bowen spoke at a press conference, talking up their latest draft with lofty claims that it could “achieve [the] covenant of 1.5C and nothing more”.
However, the second draft was rejected by countries and civil society alike. (See: Cover decision.)
On Friday – the summit’s last scheduled day – the mood at COP soured. With few official updates, delegates relied on ever-changing rumours about when a new text might emerge.
Negotiations on other key issues also remained stuck, as civil society dubbed it the “worst COP in history” at a press conference attended by Carbon Brief.
In the evening, the presidency opened the closing plenary to gavel through non-contentious items – and announced that a new text would not be released until Saturday morning.
They were interrupted by a protester wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” and with a red noose around their neck.
As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update failed to arrive.
An open letter signed by 100 civil society organisations told the presidency it was “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UNFCCC has ever had”.
As Turkish support staff started packing down the party pavilions, behind-the-scenes disputes between country ministers intensified.

Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UK, the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the Independent Association of Latin America and the Caribbean (AILAC), the Umbrella Group (UG) and least-developed countries (LDCs) – approached the presidency as a united front to demand changes to the cover decision.
These changes included on how it referenced transitioning away from fossil fuels, adaptation finance and carbon capture and storage. (See: Cover decision.)
A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.
With official updates still few and far between, rumours swirled that many countries were still not happy with this iteration of the text and planned to reject it.
Later that day, another version of the text arrived – but it contained only minor changes.

In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, several countries rejected the cover decision – citing reasons including its failure to respond to humanity’s overshoot of 1.5C of global warming, its failure to clearly mention fossil fuels and its lack of clear figures for adaptation finance. (See: Cover decision.)

While countries rejected the cover decision, they did find consensus on other texts, including for the just transition work programme, the global goal on adaptation, the climate finance work programme, carbon markets, long-term finance and “Article 2.1c”.
The final gavel came down at 7:33pm local time – nearly 50 hours after the summit’s scheduled end. This makes COP31 the longest in history.
The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 countries during a chaotic – and, at times, acrimonious – closing plenary in Antalya.

Towards the end of the summit, Kurum had told a press conference attended by Carbon Brief that he wanted the cover decision to be known as the “Antalya accord”. (This was later amended in the last formal draft to be the “Antalya pact”.)
But, in the closing plenary, the EU told the assembled delegates:
“We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.”
According to Carbon Brief’s tally during the closing plenary, the agreement was also explicitly rejected by Panama, the Marshall Islands, Belize, Norway and Vanuatu.

After it was clear that the pact would not be adopted, the 44-member LDCs, the UK, South Korea and Japan all said that consensus had not been reached, a softer form of indicating dissent. The six-member environmental integrity group (EIG) also registered its “concerns” with the text.
For months ahead of the summit, the Turkish and Australian presidencies had been talking up the idea of a COP31 cover decision – an overarching political statement.
Indeed, Bowen had publicly raised the idea of a COP31 cover decision at last year’s COP30 in Brazil, even before the agreement to act as joint president with Turkey had been finalised.
In his opening speech in Antalya, Bowen said that he had agreed with Kurum to take forward a “presidency-initiated, party-driven [cover] decision for COP31”. He had said at a pre-COP in Fiji:

“There is a clear expectation that COP31 must respond to the global moment – to send a clear message to accelerate implementation…And to demonstrate our continued commitment to multilateralism, to international cooperation and to the Paris Agreement.”

Bowen stressed that this should not lead to a “lengthy political statement”, but that he wanted it to respond to the imminent “overshoot” of 1.5C, the “catastrophic impacts” of warming and the “tangible progress” being made in the energy transition.
For Turkey, the cover decision became a vehicle to promote what had started out as its voluntary target for electricity to make up 35% of global final energy by 2035. (See: Electrification.)
While early on, Russia publicly challenged the legal basis for a cover decision, given it was not on the official agenda, these procedural objections fell away as the summit continued.
Many other recent COPs have issued cover decisions, setting a firm precedent.
Carbon Brief understands that legal advice from the UNFCCC secretariat confirmed the broad authority of the presidency to initiate a cover decision in Antalya.
Nevertheless, many parties remained unhappy about the existence of the cover decision, the process by which it was put together and the impact it had on time for other negotiations.
“We are also acutely aware that [the cover decision] has taken away our attention from the mandated items of the agenda, which we had to deliver.”
It had quickly become clear that Bowen’s ambitions for a brief cover decision would be in vain, when a lengthy 144-paragraph “reflections” text was released on 16 November.

Simon Evans 13 November 2026, 05:55 GMT NEW: COP31 cover decision ‘reflections’ text Today, Friday 13 November, the COP31 presidency published a “reflections” text on consultations it has been holding with heads of national delegations on a potential “cover decision”. This is not a fully formed draft text, but instead contains an organised…

This document was a compilation of all the issues that parties had put forward for inclusion, ranging from quantified climate-finance goals through to firm timelines for the next assessment report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

Other ideas included that developed countries should reach net-zero emissions by 2030, that certain trade policies should be “phase[d] out” next year and that the largely defunct Kyoto Protocol should be resurrected, with binding carbon targets for developed nations.
The text also included the presidencies’ favoured “35 by 35” electrification target, as well as language on the transition away from fossil fuels. (See: Fossil fuels.)
A second iteration – in reality, the first fully formed draft cover decision – was published on 19 November, consisting of just 80 paragraphs.
This version was immediately criticised for having excised any mention of fossil fuels, as well as deleting the $120bn adaptation-finance target wanted by developing countries. (See: Adaptation.)
It retained the “35 by 35” target, but only as one of a menu of options, listed as areas for “global cooperation” to “keep 1.5C within reach”.

Controversially, this menu of options – indicated by the wording “inter alia”, meaning “among other things” – also included numerical targets for carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), apparently as “quid pro quo” for the quantified electrification target.
The same day, in a highly unusual move, Panama issued an open letter stating that it would “formally object” to any decision not meeting demands including a “cap on oil production”.
A third and supposedly “final” version of the cover decision was published at around 3am local time on Sunday 22 November, already deep into overtime at the summit.

This still did not make any direct reference to fossil fuels or the $120bn adaptation finance target. It also removed language that had called for the next IPCC reports to be published ahead of the second “global stocktake”.
Carbon Brief has seen proposed revisions presented to the presidency by a 126-nation coalition of countries, including the EU, LDCs, AOSIS, AILAC, EIG and Umbrella groups.

They asked for the paragraph above – numbered 36 in the second draft and 40 in the third – to be replaced with a direct link to the first global stocktake, which included the transition away from fossil fuels. (They did not suggest an explicit use of the words “fossil fuels”.)
The group also wanted the sub-paragraph with numerical targets for CCUS to be deleted.

However, a fourth and final version of the “Antalya pact”, published a few hours later, made only minor changes, softening language on CCUS to “increasing” rather than “accelerating”, while also weakening the language around the timeline for the next IPCC reports.
On the last scheduled day of negotiations, Bowen had told journalists: “The world is wondering whether multilateralism can deliver. I think it can.”
But the presidencies’ efforts to secure a cover decision were, ultimately, unsuccessful.

“What is before us is not commensurate with the urgency of overshoot, the scale of the climate crisis or the impacts already being felt…It is the lowest common denominator…[rather than presenting] bold collective ambition on climate action.”

Not all parties were opposed to the Antalya pact. Ghana, for the African group, said it could support the decision, despite the lack of specificity on topics including adaptation finance and trade measures.

Saudi Arabia, for the Arab group, said that they had continued to “engage constructively” on the cover decision, “despite all of the issues that were taken off the table”, including on finance and historical emissions. It also said:
“We cannot reconcile a position that stated so publicly that we need to keep 1.5C within reach and, yet, calling CCUS technologies greenwashing.”

Russia explained its steadfast opposition to “any wording on fossil fuels” – despite the wording agreed by consensus at COP28. It criticised “slogans” around the use of fossil fuels, arguing that even in 1.5C pathways, there was an ongoing role for oil and gas.
While the failure to adopt a cover decision has been widely compared to the collapsed Copenhagen climate talks in 2015, experts told Carbon Brief this comparison was flawed.
Nevertheless, they said it could end the recent trend of COPs attempting to secure a cover decision, as well as sparking renewed reflections on how to reform the process.
Paul Watkinson, the French chief negotiator at Paris COP21, told Carbon Brief:

“This time it is the political bet of the presidency on a cover decision that has not worked…I think this needs a deeper reflection on what we are trying to achieve – there are limits to political signals in a decision – and we ought to think [about] what we can achieve through the COP and how to make it work better.”

The failure of the Antalya pact meant that initiatives on oceans, methane, mountains – and on COP reform itself – were all lost from the formal outcome of the summit. While some may be revisited at future COPs, not all have a clear place on the agenda.
As COP31 ended without agreement on the proposed “Antalya pact”, much of the immediate response focused on perceived shortcomings in the UN climate process.
In his closing remarks, UNFCCC executive secretary Simon Stiell said there were “lessons that must be learned” for the consensus-driven process:
“Clearly, there is also scope to improve, modernise and reform. But not only because of what happened here. But also because we must evolve in this era of implementation.”
In fact, one of the COP31 presidency’s stated priorities had been reforming COPs – or what they described as “strengthen[ing] UNFCCC processes”.
COP reform was discussed during the summit, including at a press conference where Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro told journalists:
“The COP has become an exercise in futility…192 countries will not agree on every single comma and every single period…especially those countries that produce carbon-based fuels.”
In practice, such bombastic statements were far removed from the on-going discussions and country submissions on COP reform, which had already begun in Brazil last year.
These discussions were integrated into the formal negotiations under the heading of “arrangements for intergovernmental meetings” (AIM).
At the Bonn climate talks in June, Australia, along with Turkey, offered to conduct informal consultations on increasing UNFCCC “efficiency” at COP31.

The African group asked for legal clarity and cautioned that “efficiency should not be equated with reducing budgets or removing agenda items” necessary to tackle climate change, according to the Earth Negotiations Bulletin.

Early in the talks, the COP31 presidency published a concept note calling for “forward-looking and exploratory” discussions on what a “strong and effective UNFCCC process” could look like. It also initiated “presidency consultations” on the matter, despite the lack of a clear mandate for doing so.
In the presidency consultations, responses included multi-year planning, retiring old agenda items and “avoiding unnecessary cover decisions”.

Several countries – including Russia, the African group, AILAC and the LMDCs – questioned the need for separate discussions and whether these were solely for the cover decision, given they were already underway in the AIM negotiations.

Russia said it “did not consent to elevating this discussion to high political level” and that it was unclear “why such a significant amount of negotiating time [was] being devoted” to these roundtables without a clear objective.
Drafts of the presidency’s failed cover decision included “high-level consultations” under COP presidencies on “strengthening the UNFCCC process”.

During the final plenary, Peru, for AILAC, called for a “clear rule on votes” and an independent review of the COP process’s efficiency. Peru’s environment director Andrés Martín Garrido Sánchez said:

“To negotiate in good faith is not a courtesy; it’s an obligation. It means not using delays as a strategy. It means negotiating text in the room in the view of everyone, with every party being heard before a decision is gavelled. It means not taking issues hostage…We are not proposing matters against the consensus. This way of negotiating is not leading us to where the world needs us to be.”
With the Antalya pact rejected, these discussions will still continue under AIM in Bonn in 2027.

While efforts to specify that tripling adaptation finance meant $120bn by 2035 failed to make it into any final texts, COP31 did see a breakthrough on channelling carbon-market revenues into the UN adaptation fund.
Disagreements over finance dominated negotiations within the “global goal on adaptation” (GGA).
This followed a “call for efforts” to triple adaptation finance by 2035, which was agreed last year at COP30.
That target was originally proposed by the LDCs as a “tripling of grant-based adaptation finance by 2030 to at least $120bn”.
Last year’s final agreement was considerably weaker and lacked key details – including the baseline for tripling and what kinds of funding would be counted towards it.
Ahead of the start of COP31, the African group requested that the tripling goal be added to the agenda, providing a potential space to discuss these outstanding issues.

This request was rejected. As a result, the question of where the goal should be discussed quickly arose as a fault line. It was debated within the GGA, the climate finance “work programme”, as well as the proposed “cover decision”.
As negotiations got underway, the G77 and China coalition of developing countries argued that adaptation finance should be discussed in the GGA rooms.

The EU, UK, environmental integrity group (EIG), Norway and Canada all wanted adaptation finance discussed under the climate finance work programme. This would place the tripling goal within the broader $300bn target for 2035 – meaning adaptation finance could come from a wide variety of sources, not just developed-country grants.
Over the first week of negotiations, two GGA draft texts were released, both of which included specific references to tripling adaptation finance to $120bn per year by 2035.
This would use a baseline of 2025, when the previous target to double adaptation finance to $40bn per year came to an end.
Over the second week of COP31, parties continued to disagree over the home and baseline for the tripling target.

The first draft text on the cover decision – reflecting ideas put forward by parties – included relatively ambitious language that tripling finance for adaptation “should reach at least $120bn”. However, the “$120bn” was absent from the next draft and an accompanying GGA text.

NGO network Climate Action Network (CAN) reported that France – as co-chair of the ministerial climate-finance negotiations – had proposed a 2019 baseline, which would reduce the tripling target to just $60bn a year by 2035.
For context, the latest UNEP report on adaptation suggests that developing countries will need a total of $305bn every year by 2035 to meet their adaptation needs.
Ultimately, neither the GGA, the climate finance work programme nor the failed cover decision specifically contained a baseline or target figure for tripling adaptation finance.

Bethan Laughlin, senior policy specialist at ZSL (Zoological Society of London), told Carbon Brief that the failure to agree a baseline does a “colossal amount of damage, because it is a continued betrayal of promises for finance of all types”.

Beyond finance, parties worked to establish an expert taskforce that could refine the set of 59 “indicators” for the global goal on adaptation, which had been agreed at COP30, as part of the two-year “Belém-Addis vision”. These are the metrics that countries will use to assess their progress in adapting to climate change.

Speaking to Carbon Brief, Emilie Beauchamp, senior adaptation expert at International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD), highlighted that the indicators had been pushed through in Brazil without full engagement from parties. She added:

“It ties into the bigger picture, which is that [the] Brazilian presidency’s cover decision didn’t leave any space for countries not to adopt these 59 indicators. These are complex and incomplete, which means most countries aren’t happy with them.”

Parties agreed on the need for a “two-tier” approach to resolving this, with a taskforce undertaking technical work on the indicators and then a policy alignment process for testing them. However, the composition of the taskforce quickly became a sticking point, just as it had in Bonn earlier in the year, according to ENB.

The 19 November draft GGA text still contained three options on the taskforce’s composition, including a mix of experts nominated either by regions, the chairs of the UNFCCC subsidiary bodies or by UN organisations and other non-party stakeholders.

Parties also disagreed on references in the GGA text to the Paris Agreement and “common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities” (CBDR-RC), plus on recognition of the importance of the 1.5C goal in limiting the need for adaptation.
While the final decision agreed at COP31 does not mention overshoot or 1.5C, it does provide clarity on the taskforce.
It “agrees” that six experts will be nominated per UN regional group, in addition to three experts nominated by the LDCs and three by small island developing states.
With so much time and focus given to the finance question, smaller technical aspects of the GGA negotiations struggled to find consensus across the two weeks of COP31.

“I think we are seeing these big-number finance issues as absolutely fundamental, but we’re also seeing the technical elements of the process, where the real work of implementation is done, be significantly challenged and, in my view, denigrated into obsolescence.”

Observers told Carbon Brief that there had not been sufficient time given to the GGA, as well as items such as national adaptation plans (NAPs). One said that more than double the negotiating time had been devoted to the cover decision than to mandated items, such as the GGA, MWP and JTWP, over the first week.
Beauchamp told Carbon Brief she hoped that COP32 president Ethiopia would “break this pattern”.
Beyond the GGA, other adaptation items also proved challenging at COP31.

The adaptation fund is the oldest dedicated UN climate fund and was set up as part under the Kyoto Protocol. Now, it is in the process of transitioning to exclusively serve the 2015 Paris Agreement. This will allow it to access 5% of the revenues generated by the agreement’s Article 6.4 carbon market.
This process has previously been delayed by disagreements over the makeup of the fund’s board.

The expectation has been that under the Paris Agreement, the board would have set quotas for “developed” and “developing” nations – the terms used in the treaty – instead of “Annex I” and “non-Annex I” nations, as it has done in the past.

Some parties see this distinction as important, because the UNFCCC annexes clearly separate a small group of predominantly European and industrialised states from other nations, whereas the “developed-developing” division is less clearly defined.
Joe Thwaites, international climate finance director at Natural Resources Defense Council, told Carbon Brief that parties “can’t access” the Article 6.4 “share of proceeds” until this is resolved.
A draft text released on 18 November continued to include references to both “developed countries” and parties “included in Annex I to the convention” within square brackets.

Ultimately, the final decision confirmed that there will be regional quotas instead of “developed” and “developing”, but it also confirmed that developing countries will continue to have a majority of seats on the board.
Thwaites described the resolution of the adaptation fund negotiations as “one bright spot” from the climate summit, noting:

“The decisions at COP31 enable the fund to receive a share of carbon-trading proceeds under the Paris Agreement crediting mechanism, which will not be subject to the politics of national budget processes.”
Negotiations on NAPs, adaptation communications and adaptation committee discussions all ended with procedural conclusions, meaning no substantive agreement was reached.
One adaptation area with more progress was “matters relating to the LDCs”, an agenda item where parties discuss support and adaptation planning for the 44 LDCs.

Despite “difficult negotiations”, on the second Wednesday of COP31, parties agreed to a decision that establishes a “LDCs national adaptation plan implementation platform” under the LDCs expert group.
ENB quoted a delegate saying: “This decision may not make the headlines, but it means a lot for the more than one billion most vulnerable people who benefit from the work under this agenda item.”
As COP31 ended in disputes and finger-pointing, a major complaint by many parties was the failure to agree progress on climate finance.
In their closing speeches, several developing-country figures expressed “profound concern”, accusing developed countries of “refusing to engage” on this “essential” issue.
Finance talks ended with little – beyond decisions to hold more meetings. There was no progress on “tripling adaptation finance”, despite efforts to flesh out this goal. (See: Adaptation.)
Finance negotiations took place amid major aid cuts by developed countries and, as revealed by Carbon Brief, a corresponding 70% drop in the amount of public climate funding being pledged.
COP31 co-president Australia drew heavy criticism from NGOs for failing to commit new funds, along with other major donors, such as Germany, France and Japan.
Meanwhile, pledges to UN climate funds fell to their lowest levels in years, with few new commitments in Antalya.
Two years ago, nations agreed on a “new collective quantified goal” (NCQG), which involves developed countries “taking the lead” in raising $300bn in climate finance a year by 2035.
A variety of sources are expected to feed into this goal, including multilateral development banks, UN climate funds and private finance “mobilised” by public investments.

In recent years, roughly a third of total climate finance has been public finance from developed countries. The provision of funds by these nations now looks less certain, amid economic struggles and pressure to raise military spending.
Developing countries, therefore, came to COP31 looking for assurances.
Finance was discussed across most rooms in Antalya, but negotiations around a climate finance “work programme” – set up at COP30 last year – were the main venue for this push.

Developing countries had wanted to create this space to discuss finance “provision” under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, which says developed countries “shall provide” finance. This is taken to mean public funding – such as aid spending – from developed countries.
(The NCQG, on the other hand, is a “mobilisation” goal, meaning it covers various funding sources, including private finance “mobilised” by public investments.)
This came amid concerns that developed countries were trying to transfer responsibility onto others. Abdulkani Barrow, Somalia’s lead negotiator, told Carbon Brief:

“Africa does not want developed countries’ historical financial responsibilities to become diluted by a general expectation that private investors, developing countries and other financial actors should provide the money.”
However, due to pressure from developed countries, the work programme was set up with a broader remit, including Article 9.1 “in the context of Article 9…as a whole”.
Following initial talks in June, the programme was only added to the COP31 agenda due to a continued push by developing countries. The EU remained “deeply concerned” about its inclusion.
Coming into COP31, developing countries continued to insist that the work programme should focus exclusively on Article 9.1.

Some developing-country groups, notably the Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDCs) and the Arab group, said it should consider ways to secure more from developed countries, including “burden-sharing arrangements”. They also argued for an extensive new set of talks and other activities.
Such ideas were unacceptable for developed countries, who generally wanted a far more limited set of actions that were “non-prescriptive” and “non-punitive”.
They argued that the talks should be based on the existing $300bn mobilisation goal, stressing that they were already contributing tens of billions a year.

Prior to COP31, Wopke Hoekstra, European commissioner for climate, told Bloomberg that “any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water”. (This statement – and choice of words – sparked outrage among civil society and was even quoted by India’s Amandeep Garg in the closing plenary.)
“We made a deal with the whole world community on financing…We don’t think there is any merit in opening it.”
(The work programme was established “without prejudging the process for the implementation of the NCQG”.)
There were a few finance-related issues that the EU and their allies were happy to discuss, including “broadening the contributor base” to include wealthier developing countries.

Developed-country groups also said they wanted the discussions about “tripling adaptation finance” to take place within the work programme, as part of the NCQG. This would mean adaptation finance coming from both their public spending and other sources.
In particular, the EU, the UK and others said they wanted to discuss “access” – helping small islands and other low-capacity nations to better get hold of the finance that already exists.

Ilana Seid, chair of AOSIS, told Carbon Brief that this focus on access presented small-island states with “an interesting dilemma”, because they also needed more finance, noting: “The whole machinery needs to move.”

The developed countries’ stated focus on access amounted to little, with no mention in the final finance decision. The Australian presidency was set to launch an “access declaration” for small islands and LDCs at COP31 – but the event was cancelled, partly due to lack of signatories.

After drafts circulated, the first official work programme text landed at the start of the second week. It contained two lengthy, opposing sets of “options”, which broadly reflected the competing priorities of the developed and developing-country blocs.

There are major divisions between developed and developing countries, including over whether the programme has already started. It follows a proposed text that was being…
The EU, Switzerland and New Zealand reportedly argued that a “no text” option should be on the table. This was reflected in the next iteration, which had a set of brackets around the entire document.
NGOs said the EU was acting as a “villain”. Sehr Raheja, deputy programme manager at the Centre for Science and Environment, told Carbon Brief:
“If they’re derailing the negotiations on this work programme, then that commitment to the NCQG – in my mind – is questionable.”

Co-chairs of the finance negotiations attempted to combine the work-programme discussions with another set of talks on Article 2.1c of the Paris Agreement – which relates to “making finance flows consistent” with climate goals.
Developing countries objected to this effort. They wanted to keep discussions focused on the responsibilities of developed countries, rather than broadening them to all “finance flows”.

As COP31 drew to a close, it became clear that a stripped-back outcome was likely for both the work programme and Article 2.1c negotiations, with nothing substantial on finance provision, tripling adaptation finance or any other stated party priorities.

This was reflected in the final decisions, which contained largely procedural outcomes. Notably, parties did agree to continue discussing finance under the work programme until 2028, rather than ending next year as some developed countries preferred.
Less high-profile finance texts, such as the Standing Committee on Finance, also finished with largely procedural outcomes.
Discussions on how to create a new “just transition mechanism” (JTM) proved one of the most controversial aspects of COP31 and were, ultimately, deferred to COP32.
At COP30 last year, negotiations under the broader “just transition work programme” (JTWP) had agreed to launch the mechanism, a decision seen as a key “legacy” of the summit.
At COP31, parties were expected to agree on the form and function of the mechanism, to allow it to start working.

Following work in Bonn in June and a workshop in Sydney in the autumn, parties began negotiations in Antalya productively, with general consensus emerging on a two-tier structure for the mechanism. This would include a political and governance body, as well as a technical operational arm, according to Earth Negotiation Bulletin (ENB).
Similarly, despite some divergences on the duration and scope of the work programme, there was broad support for the continuation of the JTWP beyond 2026.
This initial work suggested that the JTM – referred to as the Belem-Antalya Mechanism (BAM) by civil society – would have a similar format to that previously suggested by NGOs and academics.
However, a draft text prepared at the end of the first week of negotiations was met with criticism from civil society, due to its lack of substantive detail on the mechanism.

They told Carbon Brief in statements that it was “hollow”, “watered-down” and an “insult to the principles parties agreed in Brazil”, adding that the “exciting potential for COP31 to deliver a real just transition mechanism is hanging by a thread”.
Speaking to Carbon Brief, Dr Leon Sealey-Huggins, a senior campaigner at the charity War on Want, said there had been a “steep decline” in negotiations.

He added that developed parties, such as the EU, Norway and the UK, were pushing for the mechanism to run dialogues, produce reports and connect people. He said that while this was “fine”, it is largely already happening in the JTWP and would have little impact on implementation. Sealey-Huggins continued:

“G77 and China have been really strong on pushing back on that in various different ways. [They are] united in the call for some kind of institutional arrangement that will have longevity, that will have power to implement work and that will do the work of scaling up means of implementation [and] support.”
Over the second week, the key areas of focus became who would set up and run the mechanism, the involvement of non-party stakeholders and how it would be financed.
The G77 and China, African group and LDCs shared proposals on how the mechanism could deliver implementation. The EU and EIG highlighted the role of non-party stakeholders.
Anabella Rosemberg, senior advisor on just transition at NGO umbrella group CAN International, told Carbon Brief that the arrival of ministers in the second week put a “cold wind in our room”.
She said that what should have been a “relatively easy win” for COP31 was disrupted by disagreements in other areas, including finance and mitigation.

Throughout the second week, there was also criticism of the Turkish presidency’s involvement in the JTWP. On 17 November, it was given a “dishonourable mention” in CAN’s “fossil of the day” award. This followed COP31 president Murat Kurum saying during a ministerial roundtable:
“Rather than creating new structures, it would be more favourable to establish a system that better connects existing resources.”
Parties and civil society were quick to criticise the statement, which they viewed as breaching presidential neutrality.

As the summit progressed, negotiations became further mired in disagreement. Rosenberg told Carbon Brief they were hampered by the focus on the cover decision, which “basically captured the oxygen of the negotiations”.

On 19 November, a new JTWP draft text was published. However, the entire body of it was contained within square brackets. Key issues, such as the institutional arrangements for the new mechanism, were still only mentioned as “options”.

A call from the G77 and China for the mechanism to be a “constituted body”, meaning a specialised subsidiary that would house work on the mechanism would be established under the UNFCCC, was not included, observers told Carbon Brief.

Civil society – who originally proposed the mechanism – became increasingly vocal as COP31 moved into its final scheduled day. At a packed press conference attended by Carbon Brief, speakers said it had been “possibly the worst COP in history” and that they “unequivocally reject” the outcomes as they stood.

The final decision, published late on 21 November, sets out a phased approach to setting up the new just-transition mechanism.
It says that in Bonn next year, parties will work out what the mechanism will do and how it will work, with a view to this being formally agreed at COP32 in Ethiopia in November 2027.

In a statement, Gina Cortés Valderrama, political strategist at 350.org said civil society and developing countries “stood firm in the face of a weak” mechanism, which “rich nations were trying to throw over the edge”. She added:

“Damage control is not a victory at this point. This is a failure of ambition and leadership, particularly from the so-called ‘developed countries’, who obstruct the provision of support, and of the COP31 presidency, who sidelined the united calls from 135 countries – almost 80% of the global population.”
Beyond the mechanism, parties discussed a review of the JTWP and the key messages that emerged from the fifth and sixth just-transition “dialogues” held in 2026.

Over the two weeks of negotiations, parties disagreed on language around agriculture and other topics, as well as the inclusion of references to transitioning away from fossil fuels and trade – neither of which made it into the final decision.

At COP30 last year, references to minerals had been included in earlier drafts on the JTWP – the first time they had appeared in a text within the UNFCCC process. However, this did not make it into the final decision in Belém.
At COP31, “critical minerals” were referenced in a COP decision for the first time.

In a statement, Angela Asuncion, Asia-Pacific coordinator and transition-minerals focal point at the Resource Justice Network, welcomed the inclusion as a “notable step”, but added that “the decision by parties to eliminate human rights due diligence across critical mineral supply chains is unacceptable”. She added:

“Stripping away these fundamental safeguards is a profound failure of leadership. By failing to operationalise the BAM and removing human-rights safeguards in critical-mineral operations, governments have once again abandoned frontline communities.”
Negotiations on “loss and damage” resulted in few substantial outcomes at COP31 and only limited recognition of the gap in funding to aid victims of climate disasters.
On top of finance to support emissions cuts and climate adaptation, developed countries are expected to take the lead on this issue.
Loss-and-damage funding has been particularly in the spotlight since the devastating Himalayan floods over the summer.
The Nepali government subsequently requested $20m from the UN fund for loss and damage, which was established with much fanfare at COP27 in 2022.
So far, predominantly developed nations have pledged just $342m to the fund, a fraction of the $2.8bn in funding requests that developing countries have submitted.
The fund’s board does not plan to start distributing finance until December, despite pressure to begin fast-tracking applications in response to urgent needs.
Speaking at a COP31 side event, Nepali environment minister Gita Chaudhary said “disasters do not wait for the paperwork and neither can survivors”. She added:

“The gap between the scale of loss and damage and the resources available in the fund is enormous and growing, so Nepal, therefore, strongly urges developed country parties to honour their commitments.”

Unlike previous years, very little new loss-and-damage funding was announced at COP31 – limited to €15m ($16.5m) from Spain, plus Italy and the EU formalising previous pledges. The fund’s first replenishment process is due to start in 2027.
In negotiations, parties were tasked with discussing a report on the loss and damage fund and deciding what guidance – if any – they wanted to provide for its operation.
Explaining why such guidance might be necessary, Liane Schalatek, an associate director and climate-finance expert at Heinrich Böll Stiftung, told Carbon Brief:

“From developing countries, there have been concerns about things that are happening in the board meetings…There is no sense of urgency from developed countries to figure out how and when we do resource mobilisation.”

An initial text presented two options. The first – favoured by the African group, LDCs and AOSIS – laid out six pages of guidance for the fund, “noting with concern” the gap between funding available and requests made.
The alternative, supported by the EU and Japan, simply stated “no guidance”. They cited concerns about “micromanaging” the fund’s board.

The final text “noted” the loss-and-damage finance shortfall, but contained relatively weak language about the need to scale up funding. One exception was a line “urg[ing] the conversion of pledges as soon as possible”, referring to promised funds that have not yet been paid out.

Meanwhile, there were technical discussions at COP31 involving the joint annual report of the executive committee of the Warsaw International Mechanism (WIM) and the Santiago Network, plus the governance of the WIM.
These two bodies are involved in research and helping developing countries access technical assistance to deal with loss and damage.
One key dispute in these negotiations concerned WIM governance, which has gone unresolved for several years, but has not prevented the body from undertaking its work.
In the end, parties decided to simply defer the issue again, with a footnote in the final decision stating that this does not “prejudge outcomes” on WIM governance.
There was limited progress on negotiations on gender in Antalya, as a small number of parties once again pushed back on language on inclusion.

At COP30 last year, parties agreed on the Belém gender action plan (GAP), which set out specific actions for ensuring gender-responsive climate action and indicators for measuring parties’ progress on gender-related issues.

This year’s summit was expected to be a “simple procedural negotiation”, with parties meant to discuss several reports that were deliverables under the GAP, said Bridget Burns, executive director of the Women’s Environment and Development Organization (WEDO).
“Our experience has shown us that even the most insignificant procedural negotiations can also get quite derailed and that’s somewhat what happened here.”
During the first consultations, on 10 November, the co-facilitators sought parties’ views on three reports prepared by the secretariat, according to Earth Negotiations Bulletin (ENB).
ENB said that several negotiating groups used their time to highlight the need for finance, capacity-building and technology transfer in order to effectively implement the GAP.

The first draft of the text, released late that day, “welcome[d]” the three reports and the work conducted under the GAP during its first year. It also “t[ook] note” of a report on addressing reported cases of harassment at the UNFCCC, but did not significantly mention the need for additional means of implementation.
On the second day of consultations, the G77 and China reportedly asked for stronger language on finance, which was reflected in brackets in the text’s second draft, as shown below.

Later in the first week, several parties objected to the use of inclusive language. They also disagreed over whether they should “welcome” or “take note” of the secretariat’s reports. (The latter is considered to be weaker language.)
As at last year’s summit, Argentina, Paraguay, Russia and the Holy See – the government of the Vatican – raised objections over the use of previously agreed, gender-inclusive language in the draft.
Burns told Carbon Brief that it was “continually jarring” to see the Holy See “huddling with Russia in almost every negotiation stream”. She added:

“The Holy See has been specifically vocal in these negotiations…and, in my opinion, [are] disastrously using the moral capital that they have to drive this process into procedural negotiations that are meaningless to actually changing what has been [previously] adopted in this process.”
The final text, published on 14 November, reflected the lack of consensus, simply saying that the SBI had “considered” the reports and “acknowledged” the work being done to implement the GAP.

Noemi Grütter, head of advocacy and partnerships at the Global Alliance for Green and Gender Action, told Carbon Brief that, despite the lack of progress on the agenda item, important work on implementation is still happening on the ground. She added:
“There is also the reality that we need to build power outside of UNFCCC, because it’s not fast enough. There are countries that are willing [to do that], and I think we need to work with them.”

According to the Guardian, Argentina and Paraguay both intervened over the definition of gender in the plenary during the adoption of the standing finance committee decision in the early hours of Sunday morning.
Negotiations at COP31 on carbon trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement reopened many familiar arguments over how tightly such activities should be regulated.
Beatriz Granziera, senior policy adviser at The Nature Conservancy (TNC), told Carbon Brief:

“Discussions repeatedly came back to familiar trade-offs: practicality versus conservativeness; flexibility versus oversight; and how to scale much-needed participation and investment while maintaining environmental integrity.”
Agreement was, ultimately, reached on both bilateral trading under Article 6.2 and the international carbon market under Article 6.4.
Carbon trading between countries under Article 6.2 is only subject to light-touch rules, such as reporting on the use of the process and a “technical expert review” of national reports.
Across 16 national reports checked so far, these reviews found 543 “inconsistencies”, 115 of which were “significant”. None of the reports were found to be without issue.

An initial draft text at Antalya “note[d these issues] with concern”, adding that “many…are significant” and relate to “environmental integrity” – in other words, whether or not emissions are actually being cut. It asked parties to address issues “at the earliest opportunity”.
However, this entire paragraph disappeared in the final, agreed text. Instead, the decision “takes note” of the information in the technical reports, without asking for any response.
Given its confidentiality provisions, campaign groups have long described Article 6.2 as a “wild west” for carbon trading and the COP31 outcome does nothing to tighten the rules.

Separately, parties were unable to reach agreement at COP31 on how to fund the processes needed to run Article 6.2. Instead, they agreed to continue discussions next year, requesting a technical paper on how “fees or other funding arrangements” would work.
On Article 6.4, negotiations began against a backdrop of calls for a “course correction” on the way the international carbon market is operated.
This came in an open letter from the Project Developer Forum and the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), saying market rules were too “conservative”.
Andrea Bonzanni, senior director at IETA, told Carbon Brief that the “current version of [the market] is failing to attract investment in carbon projects”.
The requests in the open letter appeared in early draft text, after being taken up by the like-minded developing countries and others.
A 14 November draft “request[ed]” the supervisory body to “assess the cumulative impact” that its rules and standards have on the “feasibility” and “cost” of carbon-credit schemes.
It said this was to avoid “excessive compounding of conservative adjustments”, in what amounted to asking that the rules for the Article 6.4 market not be too stringent.
Isa Mulder, at Carbon Market Watch, told Carbon Brief that this looked like market proponents “chipping away at the standards that have been set out”. She added:
“The goal [of Article 6] was to enable higher ambition, not to enable [carbon-trading] activities.”
However, after pushback from the EU and others, the final text adopted at COP31 no longer asks for a formal assessment of the “cumulative impact” of the rules.
Instead, it asks that the supervisory body “take into account” the way different standards “operate together” when making or revising provisions.
Towards the end of the summit, 45 scientists signed an open letter saying that the Article 6 rules “must be consistent with the science”.
With those rules set for a review starting in 2028, Granziera told Carbon Brief:

“Ultimately, the debate [at COP31] reflected different views on what is needed for Article 6 to deliver more effectively as a tool for achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement, which will likely come back to light in 2028.”
For the second year in a row, negotiations on the Sharm el-Sheikh joint work on agriculture (SJWA) collapsed without parties reaching an agreement.
SJWA is where formal negotiations around climate change and agriculture take place under the UNFCCC.
Part of SJWA’s mandate is to synthesise information about work being done in the agricultural space – under both the UNFCCC and other international bodies – in an annual report.

SJWA also held two workshops – one on holistic approaches to agriculture and one on “means of implementation”, usually taken to mean finance – where countries and other partners could share their experiences, as captured in summary reports.

At this COP, parties were meant to discuss the conclusions of these reports and, time permitting, decide on the future of the agricultural workstream under the UNFCCC. (The four-year mandate of SJWA was set to end at COP31.)
Many observers were hopeful of agreeing a text that recognised agroecology as beneficial for humans, climate and biodiversity.

However, in the first negotiating session, on 10 November, the Arab group expressed its view that fertilisers are vital for food security and fertiliser exports are being impacted by the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM). Therefore, it said, the agriculture talks needed to discuss CBAM and other trade measures.
Teresa Anderson, global climate-justice lead at ActionAid, called this a “total curveball” in the negotiations. She told Carbon Brief:

“Everybody’s faces just dropped…Suddenly we knew that the chances of agroecology having a chance had been pretty elegantly spiked by putting in this really complicated political issue into the middle of the agriculture discussions.”
Other observers also expressed frustration to Carbon Brief that the group had brought CBAM into the negotiations, noting that trade measures are being discussed elsewhere in the COP.
At the end of this session, parties were asked to submit their views in writing for consideration, with the LMDCs proposing an extension of SJWA to COP32.

A draft text circulated on the evening of 12 November – after the scheduled start of the negotiations that evening – left many parties unsatisfied, with several stating that elements of the text crossed their “red lines”. The draft presented parties with four options, including “no text”.

Although various parties objected to many parts of the proposed text – including agroecology (opposed by India), CBAM (opposed by the EU) and “food systems” language (opposed by the G77) – the underlying issue was a lack of finance, observers told Carbon Brief.
Marie Cosquer, advocacy analyst at Action Against Hunger, said:

“The main issue is not bad-faith negotiating; it’s the fact that across the UNFCCC, the countries that have a climate debt are not paying it…Unless they move on finance, there is nothing in this negotiation for global south countries.”

With no sight of agreement on the horizon and the scheduled negotiating time drawing to a close, parties suggested that the negotiations end with a procedural text. The co-facilitators put such a text forward on 14 November.

This final text says only that parties “continued consideration” of SJWA and have “requested the subsidiary bodies to continue consideration” of SJWA at the mid-year intersessional meetings in Bonn. The subsidiary bodies are then “requested” to report back at COP32.
The “mitigation work programme” (MWP) stalled repeatedly over the two weeks of COP31, and was ultimately blocked in the closing plenary, with work pushed back to Bonn in 2027.
The MWP – the only formal agenda item at the annual COP that is specifically focused on cutting greenhouse gas emissions – was set to come to an end in 2026.
As such, parties have been wrangling with an existential question over the past year – both regarding the continuation of the programme and what it should work on.

Both in Bonn and at COP31, divisions arose over the challenge of ensuring the MWP is “facilitative and non-prescriptive and…drive[s] greater urgency on mitigation ambition and implementation”, as the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions noted.

At the Bonn intersessional meetings in June, countries were unable to agree on how to balance these two aspects and negotiations were subject to “rule 16”, meaning there was no outcome and discussions were knocked over to the next session.
In the run-up to COP31, submissions from parties made it clear that there was support for the continuation of the programme.

According to Earth Negotiations Bulletin (ENB), as negotiations got underway on 10 November, parties diverged on the duration of the programme – with suggestions including out to 2030 or 2040 – and on a review of the purpose of MWP.
Additionally, Switzerland proposed establishing a permanent mitigation committee that would be similar to standing bodies in other areas of the UNFCCC process. This was opposed by the Arab group.

Speaking to Carbon Brief, Lola Vallejo, diplomacy and partnerships director at the European Climate Foundation (which funds Carbon Brief) and former co-chair of the MWP, said the proposal raised an “interesting question”.
She noted that, alongside the climate finance “work programme”, there is a standing committee focused on finance, but there has not been one proposed for mitigation previously.

Vallejo added that while finance discussions may not be “getting the political traction” many wanted at COP31, “at least there’s no shortage of spaces to discuss”, unlike mitigation, which solely has the work programme.

Observers told Carbon Brief that there was pushback against this proposed mitigation committee, on the basis that there is not a lack of institutions or bodies to tackle the issue, rather, there is a lack of finance and support.

Areas of divergence between parties included connection (or not) to the “global stocktake”, connection to NDCs or other collective goals, mentions of the IPCC and to what extent the “action agenda” can be brought in, according to Vallejo.

Various designs for the continuation of the MWP were proposed in subsequent negotiations, including multi-year work plans and introducing more “focused, solutions-oriented global dialogues” to facilitate implementation.
The extent of the disagreements was evident in a draft text published at the end of the first week of COP31, which contained 177 square brackets and 12 “options”.

In the second week in Antalya, progress continued to stall in the MWP negotiations. A new draft text released on 18 November highlighted that the duration of the programme, links to the global stocktake (GST) and the potential for a committee remained contentious.
While it was cut down from the previous iteration, this was, in part, because contentious issues had been replaced by placeholders without any content, as shown below.

Natalie Jones, senior policy advisor on energy at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, told Carbon Brief that some parties were pushing to weaken language around the MWP’s original mandate to “accelerate action in this critical decade”, as well as language linking the work programme to the GST. She said:

“Some parties want to limit what the GST can say on mitigation. Basically, they want to avoid another sort of transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF) situation at COP33 and avoid any more top-down or sectoral targets or whatever, and they fear that they could come out of the MWP into the stocktake.”

The next day, another draft text was published. This was close to agreement, with just two outstanding options: whether the MWP should take into account any “mitigation-related outcomes” of each stocktake when planning its activities or dialogues, or to have no text on the matter.

The draft text “decides” that one global dialogue will be held every year from 2028 under the MWP, leaving the door open for additional in-person or hybrid dialogues. Furthermore, it decides that the work programme will be extended until the end of 2030 and be renamed the “Sharm el-Sheikh-Antalya mitigation ambition and implementation work programme”.

Speaking to Carbon Brief, Fernanda de Carvalho, head of policy for climate and energy at WWF International, said the continuation of the MWP would be “better than nothing”, but added the process needed to be “significantly strengthened to deliver on its mandate”.
“A few parties keep pretending the link between this process and the GST doesn’t exist; they should just look at the decision that created the MWP.”

Despite a clean text being released on 21 November – with the reference to the Paris Agreement removed from the preamble, but the reference to the GST remaining – parties failed to adopt the MWP in the closing plenary.

Saudi Arabia and Russia both rejected the programme there, with the former stating it was “deeply disappointed by the continued attempts throughout these negotiations to fundamentally alter the facilitative, non-prescriptive and bottom-up nature of the mitigation work programme”.
It said parties had tried to “move it away from its agreed mandate”.
The UK, for the Umbrella group, lamented that the MWP could not be agreed, adding that the “complementarity of the global stocktake has been part of the MWP mandate from the beginning”.
With no agreement in Antalya, work on the MWP will be pushed to Bonn in 2027, with the future of the programme uncertain.
Talks on “response measures” were some of the least contentious at COP31, however, the final plenary still rejected a draft decision on the topic.

At UN climate talks, “response measures” is a forum for discussing the effects of carbon-cutting policies on countries. They are particularly relevant for nations where controls on emissions or deforestation pose a risk to communities and the economy.
In recent years, the forum has been where trade and climate issues have been discussed.

In 2024, COP29 in Baku established a four-year work plan on response measures, including the “cross-border impacts” of climate-change measures. This created a formal space to discuss and assess trade-related climate measures in UN climate talks.

COP30 in Belém established a two-day “global dialogue” on response measures each year from 2026-29. The first was in Bangkok from 21-22 September 2026, focusing on economic diversification and on how to manage impacts on vulnerable populations.

In Antalya, three key disputes emerged. The first was on what activities the forum would undertake in 2027 and, second, how it would consider recommendations from its Katowice Committee (KCI) of experts. The third was on whether – and how – response measures would inform the second “global stocktake”.

At the start of negotiations, countries – including the African group, AOSIS, South Korea and China – called for a wide range of activities next year. One of these included a new “cross-border” impact assessment of response measures.
On 16 November, the EU suggested removing an activity that refers to Article 3.5 of the 1992 UN climate convention, covering trade and an “open international economic system”.

Eventually, countries settled on four different activities. These include a workshop next June for the most affected countries to learn how to report these impacts, plus another workshop at COP32 on “technological solutions” to reduce climate impacts.

As work on the second global stocktake (GST2) gets underway, countries disagreed on how response measures would feed into it. As of 19 November, the same four options remained on the table, including one with “no text”.
One option, supported by G77 and China, “decide[d]” that all of the outputs of the forum – dialogues, workshops, technical reports and case studies – would serve as substantive inputs to GST2.
This option “urged” that the cross-border impact assessment be conducted “before and during” GST2, including metrics such as inflation, trade flows, household income, employment and debt.
Canada and the EU warned that this would change the global stocktake’s “well-established function”, reported Earth Negotiations Bulletin.
However, Switzerland, Norway, EU and the UK supported a compromise option – where countries could submit their views on the “social and economic impacts of response measures” as input to GST2.
Eventually, the option explicitly containing a cross-border impact assessment as an input to GST2 was deleted from the final draft.

Instead, the text “recognises” that inputs to GST2 are “non-exhaustive” and “affirms” that all the forum’s outputs will feed into the stocktake’s technical assessment. This includes work on cross-border impacts – including trade measures – and how to report and analyse them.
At the same time, it “invites” countries to submit their views on the “social and economic consequences” of response measures by 28 February 2027, which would also inform the stocktake.

During the final plenary, the EU told delegates it objected to the adoption of the decision on response measures, on the grounds that it “contains provisions that are highly problematic”, as well as “the lack of recognition of the best available science”.
This was supported by Canada and the UK, with the latter adding:
“We cannot accept any outcome that seeks to undermine and unduly influence the next global stocktake.”

Brazil and Saudi Arabia both expressed their disappointment with the rejection of the text.Brazil said that the draft “excludes the voices of developing countries, the very countries that struggle to address the social and economic impacts of mitigation measures”. It asked for a formal note that the role and mandate of the forum were being “undermined”.
A draft decision on “action for climate empowerment” (ACE) had been set for adoption at COP31, but was unexpectedly torpedoed by Russia in the closing plenary.
This area of the negotiations aims to encourage people to engage in climate action in different ways – through education, training, public awareness and access to information.

COP27 had agreed to a four-year “action plan” on ACE that ends this year. COP31 was due to have agreed a new plan for 2027-2031, with some parties wanting it to address “misinformation and disinformation” related to climate change.

During the Antalya talks, Russia, along with Saudi Arabia and Paraguay, objected to including a reference to countering climate-related “misinformation and disinformation”, reported ENB. It added that Russia described this as amounting to the censorship of other scientific views.
Russia also made repeated efforts to replace previously agreed language on “gender-responsive” action with the phrase “gender-sensitive”.
A draft decision, proposed by the presidency on 21 November, “note[d] the need to enhance efforts to promote and support the integrity of information on climate change”.
The proposal also “recognise[d] the centrality of equity and the best available science for effective climate action and policymaking, as provided by the IPCC”.

It then set out an action plan for continued work from 2027-2031. Notably, while references to “misinformation” had been removed, it still talked of “ensuring that the public has access to reliable, accurate climate information and is equipped with adequate climate literacy skills”.

During the closing plenary, however, Russia said it “reject[ed]” the “censorship of science” and that it “objected” to the draft text on action for climate empowerment. It said discussions had been “held hostage by considerations which are not part of the climate process”.

The EU and the UK for the Umbrella group expressed their “surprise” at Russia’s objection. The UK said this topic was “very important for our group” and that “respect for gender equality and all identities is core to an effective, inclusive and meaningful process”.
The COP president told the plenary that, “in light of the objection from the Russian Federation”, the issue of action for climate for empowerment would be deferred until the Bonn talks in June 2027.
In a statement, campaign group Climate Action Against Disinformation said:

“The ACE action plan should have been a milestone for truth at COP31. Instead, the Russian federation – the epicentre of climate disinformation – blocked its adoption, standing alone against 193 other[s].”

After the creation of three annual “dialogues” on trade within the COP30 Belém “global mutirão” decision, the topic was not expected to feature on the official agenda, even if it was likely to come up in other negotiating tracks.

But, in the end, the rejection of not only the cover decision, but also agreements on “response measures” and agriculture, meant that trade was entirely missing from the COP31 outcome. (See: Response measures and Agriculture.)
(A request from the African group to add trade to the COP31 agenda was also rejected.)

Trade and climate featured strongly in the first “reflections” text on a cover decision, which was a compilation of suggestions from parties.Paragraph 119 of the first draft “call[ed] on” developed countries to “phase out unilateral…trade-restrictive measures” by the end of 2027. Commonly cited examples of what this might refer to include the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism and deforestation law. (See: Agriculture and food security.)
The phase-out call was, expectedly, cut from the second iteration of the cover text.
Speaking to Carbon Brief, global policy advisor at Greenpeace East Asia Yao Zhe said:
“No one thought it would survive, probably even the ones [who] proposed it. But I see it as an indication that [countries] are persistent in pushing the trade angle.”
