This could include ensuring consistent, smooth and appropriately tailored interaction from debt referral/signposting to resolution, including clear and reliable communication channels and collaborative working with third-party advisors to have as positive a customer experience as possible and support sustainable outcomes for customers.

The first theme that the panel examined was how suppliers engage with customers who are receiving support from third-party debt advice organisations. These customers are already experiencing financial difficulty and taking the initial step to ask for help can be a difficult decision. Effective collaboration between suppliers and the debt advice sector can reduce the burden on customers who are going through financial difficulties. In contrast, poor coordination between suppliers and advisors can lead to additional barriers to getting the support needed. Feedback from stakeholders, particularly local debt advisors and charities, identified this as an area needing attention

All suppliers spoke about working with FCA-authorised debt advice organisations to help customers access advice and support, with StepChange, Citizens Advice and IncomeMax all commonly referenced as partners. They pointed out that customers’ financial difficulties often extend further than energy bills and that independent debt advice plays an important role in providing holistic support.

All confirmed their policy to accept the MaPS Standard Financial Statement (or Scottish equivalent), which summarises a person’s financial situation and helps debt advice providers to support those struggling with their bills. Suppliers described a range of approaches to working with these organisations, from signposting customers to available support through to more established referral pathways and formal partnerships. Some suppliers spoke about working on new initiatives such as the Citizens Advice Consumer Energy Debt Advice (CEDA) service with Money Advice Trust and StepChange.

All suppliers emphasised the importance of engaging with customers in debt as early as possible, working towards proactive identification before financial difficulties escalate. 100Green told the panel that it prioritises early conversations with customers and individualised, human-centred support, using direct phone call conversations to identify potential difficulties and signpost customers to relevant support organisations.

Fuse Energy, a digital-first supplier, contacts customers as soon as a payment fails, using app notifications to let these customers know when a further payment attempt will be made. In recognition that customer disengagement is a significant hurdle in managing debt, the supplier offers tailored repayment plan options, including self-service payment plans and access to advisors where customers need additional support.

ScottishPower identifies early signs of financial difficulty through payment behaviours, account information, and PSR indicators, using each customer interaction to build a fuller understanding of their circumstance and proactively direct customers towards specialist support.

A common practice suppliers spoke about for this theme was adapting their debt processes to support individual circumstances. OVO spoke about its strategy of segmenting customers to provide a more bespoke debt journey, using insights into customer behaviour and payment patterns to better understand their needs. It uses around 30 customer segments to inform the tone and timing of communications, and how customers are directed to specialist collections or vulnerability teams.

The supplierrecognised that the range of available support can sometimes feel overwhelming for some customers and highlighted the importance of its relationship with external debt advice organisations. Its approach focuses on connecting customers with appropriate support when they need it, to prevent additional barriers to engagement.

Its Extra Support package provides a centralised hub aimed at customers already in or at risk of fuel poverty that connects customers with the right support at the right time. In addition, it also uses the Lightning Reach referral portal to consolidate multi-agency support and make it easier for vulnerable households to access and apply for support.

In the last year, OVO has streamlined access to financial support through Lightning Reach, so customers not eligible for its Extra Support package are automatically matched with other available support through a single application process. This development resulted in positive customer feedback.

Good Energy told the Expert Panel it has increased its investment in customer vulnerability roles and has upskilled more debt specialists to work closely with the vulnerability team. It has also refined its debt pathways to provide more tailored support, with customers directed towards different routes based on their identified circumstances and needs. This includes allowing longer intervals between stages of the debt journey where appropriate, giving customers more time to engage and access support.

Several suppliers spoke about the importance of having dedicated teams in place to support customers with more complex needs, recognising that some circumstances require additional expertise and a more tailored approach than frontline advisors may be able to provide. So Energy is an example of this. Last year, it commissioned an independent review of its vulnerability support led by Helen Pettifer and drawing on feedback from customers, frontline staff, and senior leadership. The findings informed the development of a dedicated specialist vulnerability team of experienced advisors, who were given the flexibility to spend as much time as needed with customers to handle more complex cases.

Good Energy has also introduced processes to engage with external debt advice organisations where no formal partnership exists. This included proactively contacting customers following communications from an advisor with the offer to pause the debt journey while repayment options are explored.

Working collaboratively with external debt advisors was also emphasised by Ecotricity, which focuses on working with customers and their advisors to find affordable and sustainable solutions tailored to individual circumstances. This includes offering a Customer Support Fund, a scheme encouraging customers to make regular payments towards their debt by offering 50% write-off.

Likewise, several suppliers spoke about similar approaches to incentivising debt repayment through matched payment schemes. ScottishPower’s Hardship Fund helps eligible customers reduce arrears by crediting their energy account. In 2025, 10,800 customers were supported via this fund, with an average value of the debt written off standing at £1,139. To effectively identify the right customers for this fund, the supplier uses credit reference agency data to identify potential financial vulnerability before using Open Banking, with customer consent, to assess income and expenditure.

Octopus Energy referenced the success of its You Pay, We Pay scheme, which is part of a £60 million tailored support package that offers matched payments when customers pay towards their debt. The supplier reporteda marked positive impact on customer behaviours and helping people get out of debt, with more than 1,000 customers having cleared their outstanding balance via this scheme by August 2026.

British Gas also highlighted its work with the British Gas Energy Trust to provide financial assistance to customers experiencing difficulties. This includes grants of up to £1,700, financial assistance payments, and providing customers with essential white goods and vouchers. The Trust also funds around 40 local and specialist organisations to deliver advice and support to help reach customers in their communities.

The Expert Panel wanted to hear about suppliers’ existing partnerships with the debt advice sector, as well as their processes for dealing with an organisation with whom they do not already have a relationship. Strong partnerships with debt organisations can help facilitate a smooth communication loop and a deeper understanding of a customer’s circumstances. However, as customers may choose the support of a wide range of debt advice organisations for multiple reasons, it is important that suppliers can guarantee the same quality of service regardless of which organisation is chosen.

Multiple suppliers, including E.ON Next, British Gas and OVO spoke about expanding their dedicated direct charity support line. This provides the organisations involved with a direct line to contact the supplier on a customer’s behalf, allowing them to bypass the queue and receive immediate support when dealing with highly vulnerable customers.

ScottishPower highlighted its dedicated Third-Party Team and network of 21 partner organisations, providing intermediaries with direct access to specialist support for complex debt, billing, PAYG, and metering queries. The supplier is also one of three participating in the CEDA pilot, which provides direct referral pathways into independent debt advice. Across participating suppliers, the pilot has supported around 9,000 customers and delivered over £2.93 million in personal financial uplift.

A direct referral route into a dedicated team forms part of British Gas’s strengthened partnership with StepChange. The company has also welcomed a secondee from the charity to support and train its advisors. After a customer is spotted struggling with debt or in a vulnerable situation, a ‘warm’ referral is made to the ring-fenced StepChange team, which assesses the customer’s financial circumstances, identifies any opportunities to maximise their income and access any additional benefits or support that they may be entitled to. Through this partnership, 97% of customers on repayment plans are maintaining regular payments. The supplier has also seen an 84% increase in payments and around 24% of customers having reduced their debt balance by an average of £1,166 after going through the process.

E.ON Next has focused on improving the route for external debt advisors to access support on behalf of customers, including through a dedicated advisor line available to at least 600 charities. It works closely with debt advice organisations including National Debtline, StepChange and Citizens Advice, offering secure transfers and 14-day account holds after referrals, to give customers time to engage with specialist advice. The supplier is also trialling new approaches with Citizens Advice through its CEDA trial, using real-time access to budgeting information for customers to help achieve sustainable repayment arrangements more quickly.

The supplier has also expanded its work with organisations supporting customers with wider needs. This includes new partnerships with Surviving Economic Abuse to support customers in abusive or coercive situations, and with Warm Welcome Spaces to reach customers who are accessing community support for essentials such as warmth and food. Italso highlighted its partnership with Lightning Reach, which helps customers to access financial support through its Energy Fund and wider support available through the platform. This forms part of its broader approach to income maximisation and signposting customers to additional financial support.

The Expert Panel heard that there is an emphasis on partnership working at EDF, which works with a range of organisations including IncomeMax, Citizens Advice Plymouth and Charis Grants to support customers experiencing financial difficulties. Customers can be referred to these organisations at any stage in their debt journey, with the supplier pausing debt collection activity while they engage with external support to help reduce stress. The company encourages its partners to make onward referrals where appropriate so that customers can continue accessing support to address their wider financial circumstances.

Utility Warehouse told the panel that it has multiple long-standing signposting arrangements with organisations including StepChange, Citizens Advice, National Debtline, PayPlan and MoneyHelper. It particularly highlighted its ongoing partnership with Citizens Advice Plymouth, which involves advisors providing specialist support to struggling households, including debt advice and write offs, income maximisation reviews and practical advice on energy efficiency improvements. Through this partnership, the supplier has supported thousands of customers with debt advice and case management, securing hundreds of thousands of pounds in debt write-offs and financial assistance.

It has also taken a more proactive approach over the past year to explore and develop partnerships with external organisations, resulting in a commercial partnership with Post Office Plus’s two concept stores (in Barnsley and Derby).

Utilita emphasised that effective signposting begins with listening to customers and understanding their individual circumstances. Conversations can reveal wider pressures on household finances. The supplier works with organisations including Christians Against Poverty, StepChange and GamCare, helping advisors to direct customers towards support appropriate to their circumstances.

Octopus Energy also highlighted the importance of connecting customers with specialist external support, particularly where their needs extend beyond what an energy supplier can provide. It has a direct referral route to PayPlan for independent debt advice, alongside a partnership with InBest to help customers identify additional benefits entitlements. It was also the first supplier to participate in the Economic Evidence Abuse Forum pilot, which aims to support customers experiencing economic abuse by providing opportunities for debt write-off and access to additional financial support.

Alongside these partnerships, the company has a team of qualified social workers that provides additional support to customers with complex needs, including assistance with benefits application and income maximisation.

Outfox Energy spoke about identifying customers who may need additional assistance to manage their accounts. Through a partnership with Haste, it identifies customers who have the means to pay their bills but struggle to understand their balances or arrange repayment plans. In some cases, this has led to social services involvement to help customers manage their accounts.

E highlighted its longstanding partnership with Fuel Bank Foundation, which has led to development of a collaborative referral process to connect customers with support beyond what the supplier can provide directly. As customers are often in crisis when they first seek assistance, the partnership explores following up with them after their immediate needs have been addressed. The company believes this will behelpful for creating an opportunity to discuss wider financial difficulties and access to debt advice.

This could include providing communications that reflect a wide range of needs, including mental health considerations and accessibility requirements, such as Braille or support for customers with cognitive impairments, ensuring the information is clear, accessible, and appropriate to individual circumstances.

This year, the panel wanted to hear about how suppliers are ensuring their communication methods are suitable for a wide range of customer needs. This involves making information available in different formats, understanding how customers prefer to communicate, reducing barriers to engagement, and adapting services to individual needs where possible.

All suppliers spoke about the need for tailored communications that cater for the broad range of needs and preferences across their customers to avoid barriers in engagement. As some communication needs can be complex and require specialist knowledge beyond supplier expertise, many highlighted the value of working with external organisations to better understand those needs and make their communications more accessible. For example, So Energy spoke about working with Mencap in the design of its easy-read guides for bills and smart meters.

Similarly, ScottishPower has partnered with Plain Numbers to improve the clarity and accessibility of customer communications. This was initially rolled out with a focus on price cap communications, but the company has since applied its learnings to billing, achieving a Plain Numbers accreditation for its approaches. The redesigned bill presents key information first, with other details broken down into clear, easy-to-read sections to help customers better understand their energy costs.

Many suppliers told the Expert Panel how they are prioritising input from organisations with lived experience knowledge of particular vulnerabilities. EDF worked with the Alzheimer’s Society following feedback from customers with lived experience that revealed some struggled to remember what the PSR is for. To address this, the supplier developed a letter explaining the PSR and its benefits, which was then reviewed by the Alzheimer’s Society to ensure it was clear and accessible.

Translation services across multiple languages, alongside large print, audio, Braille and transcription, form part of Outfox Energy’s approach to meeting different communication needs. The supplier reported growing use of its alternative format services.

E.ON Next reported on its work with the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute to redesign its debt communications for customers with mental health conditions. Drawing on feedback from people with lived experience, it introduced new debt templates with clearer layouts, simplified information, with a more empathetic tone to reduce potential stress and encourage engagement. Since introducing these redesigned communications at the start of 2026, the supplier reported a 3% increase in customer contact via phone, with half then resolving their issues during the conversation.

A common challenge identified by suppliers around this theme was customers having to repeatedly explain their circumstances to different teams or organisations. This can be particularly difficult for customers with complex needs; suppliers highlighted the importance of continuity and tailored support.

For example, Utility Warehouse has established a specialist non-arrears vulnerability team for customers with complex needs who require frequent contact, reducing the need for the repeated disclosure of circumstances. The supplier has also improved its vulnerability recording systems, moving away from more lengthy assessments towards natural conversations that focus on understanding individual needs and providing tailored support.

E.ON Next highlighted its ongoing development of its NextCare tool. This enables staff to record more detailed information about customers’ vulnerabilities and better understand their individual circumstances. This supports a “tell-us-once” approach that reduces the need for customers to repeatedly disclose information when accessing support.

British Gas shared how it embeds inclusive communications into its wider customer service processes. When customers disclose vulnerability or accessibility needs, these are recorded on systems and automatically trigger relevant support in future interactions.

Ecotricity highlighted its approach to providing consistent and personalised support, including case-managing customers with specific communication needs so they can always speak to the same person and avoid repeating explanations. The supplier also emphasised the need for clear, jargon-free language and giving customers greater flexibility over how and when they contact the supplier.

Octopus Energy also spoke about the importance of reducing customers having to repeatedly explain circumstances. It launched a charity referral trial with Together for Short Lives, enabling customers who have already disclosed their situations to the charity to receive tailored support from the supplier’s specialist team without any repetition. It is looking to expand this approach to other charities and has invested in specialist vulnerability training across its teams to help colleagues respond to a wide range of customer needs.

The company also pointed to the scale of its communications to customers and illustrated the careful measurement of impact and effectiveness in the choice of tone and channel. For example, it has achieved expert accreditation from AbilityNet.

Many suppliers spoke about equipping their frontline staff with the training and specialist knowledge needed to recognise different customer needs and tailor their interactions. For example, OVO has focused on making it easier for frontline staff to access the information and guidance they need to support customers through its tools such as Advisor Assist and Vulnerability Toolkit. It has also invested in additional specialist training, including suicide awareness training, to help staff to respond appropriately when customers disclose potentially distressing circumstances.

Vulnerability training is mandatory for British Gas’s 5,000 frontline colleagues, including annual refreshers aligned to policy and process changes. The supplier told the panel that this forms part of embedding inclusive communications throughout the organisation.

The growing role of AI and other digital technologies in customer support was a notable theme across this year’s panel hearings. The Expert Panel heard how suppliers are proactively utilising these technologies to their full extent – while recognising the importance of retaining alternative communication channels for customers who cannot or prefer not to digitally engage.

Fuse Energy spoke about its Plugs AI assistant, embedded throughout its customer service operations to ensure inclusive communication. Able to respond to both simple and complex questions, Plugs AI understands the context of the question and the information it holds internally. Queries made to Plugs AI are responded to within seconds but if it cannot handle a query or if a customer would prefer to speak to a human, a specialist agent is available to pick up the same conversation. This chat is routed to a specialist team such as billing and payments, switching and tariffs, or general support. The supplier believes this approach to customer service helps deliver its strong complaints performance and reports Plugs AI has averaged a customer satisfaction score of 98% each week so far in Q4 2026.

EDF presented on its AI-powered Bill Explainer, which aims to present billing in a clearer and more customer friendly way. After successfully completing the pilot scheme, the supplier launched the Explainer at full scale, with around 70,000 customers having used it at the time of reporting. Outfox Energy has also utilised AI assistance throughout its telephone and digital platforms. This includes real-time, AI-powered insights, agent scripting and summary of conversations with proposed next steps.

British Gas highlighted how it has developed its use of technology for customer service, including real-time alerts, large-language models (LLMs), and speech analytics to better identify customer needs and monitor customer outcomes. It explained that this approach provides more consistent assurance over customer outcomes and enables customer needs to be identified in a scalable and repeatable way.

Alongside new technologies, many suppliers also highlighted improvements made to existing services and equipment to make them more accessible. E, for example, told the panel about its regular website accessibility reviews, which have led to the introduction of features that allow customers to tailor browsing to their needs. These include adjustments to colours and content, reading guides, and accessibility settings designed for customers with low vision, ADHD, and older users. Good Energy, meanwhile, trained its AI tools to reduce jargon and produce friendlier, more accessible responses, and provide automated and alternative debt communications for PSR customers.

Several suppliers demonstrated to the Expert Panel how their communication channels extend into community engagement. These suppliers highlighted the value of maintaining this direct contact, particularly for customers who may face barriers seeking support through the standard channels.

Utilita gave the example of its high street hubs, which are located across the UK and available for anyone to drop into, with no requirement to be a Utilita customer. This recognises the importance of free community spaces in reducing social isolation and providing opportunities for people to engage who may not otherwise do so.

Similarly, OVO outlined its refreshed approach to its OVO in the Community events, first launched in 2024 with the purpose of building trust through local influence, physical presence and practical support. The update aimed to better reach customers who may benefit from additional support, focusing on 14 locations with high deprivation and collaborating with the Warm Spaces network to engage a broader range of energy customers. Finally, 100Green highlighted its community energy schemes, which enable residents living near renewable generation – including areas experiencing high levels of fuel poverty – to benefit from lower-cost electricity. To communicate these schemes effectively to the local communities, the supplier has worked with external organisations to develop clear, accessible communications that help customers understand the scheme and encourage participation.

This could include communicating the benefits of PAYG meters clearly and appropriately, supporting customers to use them as a budgeting tool where suitable, while ensuring the messaging and service reflect both the advantages and the safeguards in place for customers in vulnerable circumstances.

This year, the Expert Panel wanted to know how suppliers are recognising and championing PAYG as a potentially useful budgeting tool for customers while ensuring it remains suitable for their individual circumstances.

Many suppliers emphasised the importance of recognising customer choice. As a PAYG-specialist supplier, Utilita reported that many customers value the control it gives them over their budgets and the reassurance of avoiding unexpected bills. It highlighted the lack of a standing charge in its tariffs and stressed the importance of respecting customers’ preferred top-up methods – recognising that some customers value visiting a shop in person rather than using an app or online service.

E,another PAYG meter specialist, highlighted that customers come to the supplier with the expectation of being able to pay for their energy this way. The supplier has spent significant time ensuring it provides the tools customers need to manage their usage and spending effectively. Customers can control when they receive credit or low-budget alerts via the MySmartE app, and E is trialling automatic top-ups when customers receive low credit alerts. Customers can also view their energy usage in half-hourly intervals, compare this with previous periods, set their own budgets, and receive immediate confirmation of payments. Additionally, it undertakes account reviews, including safeguarding conversations with customers for whom PAYG may not be suitable.

Other suppliers echoed customer preference on PAYG account management, with 100Green, ScottishPower and EDF reporting that even some customers who have transitioned from legacy meters to smart PAYG will prefer to top up their accounts physically. Some suppliers, including Octopus Energy and EDF,told the panel that top-ups are available at all three major outlets (PayPoint, Payzone, and the Post Office) to allow customers to continue to use their preferred method. EDF has also mapped customers against their nearest outlet to check coverage.

While recognising the benefits of PAYG and respecting customer choice was a key element of many suppliers’ hearings, equal importance was placed on ensuring that PAYG remains safe and suitable for individual circumstances, with appropriate safeguards in place. All suppliers stressed the additional checks they have put in place following Ofgem’s intervention in 2024.

100Green said that when a customer requests a PAYG meter, it explores their reasons to make sure it is the right option for them. Similarly, Utility Warehouse told the panel its approach is meter-type agnostic, focusing on customer suitability and choice rather than actively promoting PAYG. Its reviews of customers at risk of self-disconnection reinforced the importance of allowing for customer choice, with more than half of the customers reviewed choosing to remain on PAYG.

British Gas described the significant work it has put into suitability checks around PAYG, resulting in a multi-layered safeguarding ladder. This starts with an affordability assessment and the consideration of alternative payment options before exploring any household vulnerabilities that could make PAYG unsuitable. This also ensures customers can make an informed choice, with any refusal recorded and assessed. When PAYG is agreed, the customer receives information on available safeguards, including emergency credit, alongside ongoing monitoring for self-disconnection.

As part of the PAYG aftercare processes, the supplier monitors customers’ use of emergency credit and reliance on Additional Support Credit, proactively contacting them to check PAYG remains suitable for their circumstances. Customers also have access to a dedicated 24-hour PAYG helpline to help them stay on supply. It also spoke about its commitment to provide non-repayable Additional Support Credit to eligible customers who cannot afford to repay, reporting at the panel hearing that it has provided £1.7 million in non-repayable support.

E.ON Next also highlighted its approach to ensuring PAYG remains safe and suitable for customers, including a dedicated mini business team. It monitors smart PAYG meters for potential self-disconnection, using low-balance alerts and consumption data to identify customers who may be struggling to stay on supply. The supplier also outlined its Safe and Reasonably Practicable assessment process, which accounts for factors such as health conditions, accessibility needs and repeated self-disconnection. Where PAYG is no longer considered suitable, customers can be moved to credit payment without a credit check, then supported to stay on supply during the transition. The supplier’saftercare process for PAYG customers includes follow-up contact to review customers’ circumstances and ongoing support needs.

The Expert Panel heard from multiple suppliers about how they are using smart PAYG technology to give customers greater visibility and control over their energy usage and spending. Features such as remote top-ups, real-time usage monitoring and budgeting alerts can help customers to manage their accounts more easily, with several suppliers demonstrating how they have improved to these digital tools in the last year.

OVO and So Energy highlighted their investment in digital tools for PAYG customers to manage their accounts. Now OVO has moved PAYG services into its app, customers can top up, view their top-up history, and access key energy usage information in one place. It continues to develop the app to offer more tailored support, with plans including greater visibility of debt balances and access to additional support credit. Likewise, So Energy customers can track their energy usage in real time through its app or website.

Through ScottishPower’s app, PAYG customers can quickly and simply top up and monitor their balance and energy usage, giving them greater control over their spending. The supplier emphasised how this visibility helps customers budget through smaller, regular payments and avoid unexpected bills. It has also made proactive interventions to support customers in the PAYG process, including its targeted Friday SMS campaign, which reaches around 3,000 customers each week with reminders to check and top up balances ahead of weekends to help reduce the risk of self-disconnection.

Many suppliers spoke about how they use data on energy usage and spending habits from customers to identify when a customer may be struggling to stay on supply. For example, Ecotricity outlined its process for monitoring self-disconnection. This is more straightforward for smart meter customers as the supplier will receive an alert when a customer disconnects themselves. For traditional meters, it calculates a customer’s usage and works out how that reflects against their top-up patterns. If a risk is identified, a reminder is sent to the customer to top up.

Staff training around PAYG was a recurring theme, with suppliers highlighting the importance of equipping teams with the knowledge and skills to support PAYG customers effectively. Despite having a small PAYG customer base, Fuse Energy outlined its approach to training staff and its PlugAI tool on the relevant information to support these customers and potential switchers. Outfox Energy has developed a dedicated PAYG help page that covers the advantages and disadvantages of PAYG, the additional support available to customers in vulnerable circumstances, and where customers can seek help if they are struggling to top up.

For some suppliers, this PAYG training is reflected in how the teams are structured, with the establishment of dedicated specialist teams. Good Energy spoke about its specialist PAYG support team, which ensures accounts are healthy and regularly checks for new vulnerabilities, while British Gas has a dedicated team for managing PAYG meter mode changes, which handles suitability conversations and explains self-disconnection monitoring.

Earlier this year Octopus Energy established a dedicated sensitive PAYG care team, focused on proactively engaging with at-risk customers, such as those who are frequently self-disconnecting or reliant on Additional Support Credit. This includes a matched top-up scheme, similar to the supplier’s You Pay, We Pay initiative, which aims to encourage more sustainable top-up habits and reduce debt on customers’ meters.

EDF also demonstrated an extensive PAYG training package that fully equips its teams to promote and support customers who have or may have a PAYGmeter. Examples of required training include PAYG basics, its benefits and how to top up. Additionally, training on Additional Support Credit is being rolled out to equip EDF Energy Specialists to have the right conversations when customers require credit. This ensures customers are not being placed at risk of increased debt or being left in a vulnerable position.

The supplier alsotold the panel about its PAYG communications campaigns. Its Autumn campaign aims to support customers over the summer period by reminding them to keep their meters topped up to help prevent debt from building up ahead of the winter, when usage typically increases. Another example is its No/Low Key Charge campaign, part of EDF’s ongoing safeguarding approach for this cohort of customers. It contacts those who have topped up less than £5 in 35 days to offer support and encouragement to top up.

This guide closes the monitoring phase of the sixth year of the Vulnerability Commitment, which found all participating suppliers to be compliant with its requirements. Throughout 2026, Energy UK has continued working with Paul Spence, the Advisory Board, and its signatories to strengthen the Vulnerability Commitment. This has been done through an expanded focus on debt and affordability, greater engagement with the debt advice sector and increased opportunities for shared learnings. This work has taken place against a backdrop of continued affordability pressures and rising levels of customer debt.

Looking ahead to 2027, Energy UK will build upon this year’s supplier shared learning sessions and the involvement of the MaPS and wider debt advice sector. Further opportunities for collaboration and knowledge sharing will be developed, bringing together signatories and external stakeholders to strengthen supplier approaches to customers experiencing financial difficulties.

The 2026 Vulnerability Commitment hearings provided a valuable opportunity to examine how suppliers are adapting their approaches to affordability, vulnerability and consumer support during a period of continuing financial pressure on households. As in previous years, suppliers demonstrated a clear commitment to improving support for consumers in vulnerable circumstances. The strongest examples showed a shift away from viewing debt primarily as a collections issue and towards a broader focus on affordability, prevention and sustainable consumer outcomes.

This is particularly important this year as we anticipate energy prices increasing significantly this winter. With debt and arrears also still at record levels, it has never been more important for the Vulnerability Commitment to deliver for consumers facing these increasing pressures – with a particular onus on suppliers to deliver the positive outcomes they are keen to promote in relation to smart PAYG, and use tools they’ve developed to support people falling into debt.

The themes emerging from the 2026 hearings build upon issues identified in the 2025 Good Practice Guide. Rising energy debt, increasing PSR membership and difficulties engaging consumers before they reach crisis point remain prominent challenges. However, the evidence presented this year suggests suppliers are developing a more sophisticated understanding of vulnerability and affordability.

A consistent message across hearings was that energy debt rarely exists in isolation. Consumers presenting with energy arrears are often experiencing wider financial hardship linked to changes in circumstance such as bereavement, illness, unemployment or relationship breakdown.

These circumstances are frequently dynamic and situational rather than easily captured through traditional vulnerability indicators. This reinforces the importance of suppliers considering vulnerability beyond PSR membership alone. While the PSR remains a valuable mechanism for identifying and supporting many consumers, support systems that rely primarily on PSR data risk overlooking financially vulnerable households whose circumstances have not yet been formally identified.

One of the most encouraging developments observed during the hearings was a greater focus on earlier intervention. Several suppliers are attempting to engage consumers shortly after bills become overdue, rather than waiting until debt becomes deeply entrenched.

The strongest approaches employed supportive rather than punitive communication. Rather than focusing solely on payment collection, suppliers demonstrated an increased willingness to understand the barriers preventing payment and to explore solutions tailored to individual circumstances.

Particularly noteworthy were examples of data-led segmentation to tailor customer communications. These suppliers demonstrated how they adapt communication methods, contact timing and support offers according to customer characteristics and engagement history even when they have large portfolios. However, segmentation must remain subject to ongoing review to ensure consumers are not directed into inappropriate pathways or excluded from support opportunities.

The broader challenge remains one of trust and engagement. Suppliers continue to report difficulties reaching consumers before circumstances deteriorate. While communication strategies have become more sophisticated, many approaches still rely heavily on consumers disclosing information voluntarily. The next stage of development may require more proactive identification of emerging financial vulnerability while maintaining consumer trust and appropriate safeguards.
A second area of progress was supplier engagement with debt advice organisations and independent advisers.
The most effective models recognised that sustainable solutions often require a whole-household perspective rather than a narrow focus on energy debt alone.
These approaches reflect a growing recognition that independent advisers can often understand and address the root causes of financial difficulty more effectively than suppliers acting alone.

However, it was not always clear how suppliers would engage with advisers who were not formal referral partners. Consumers should not experience different outcomes because of which regulated advice organisation they choose to work with or be forced to switch advisers – where they may need to re-start the difficult process of disclosure and engagement from the beginning.

The hearings also highlighted limitations in how success is measured. Referral volumes alone do not demonstrate positive consumer outcomes. A referral may not result in adviser contact, a completed assessment or an affordable arrangement. As suppliers develop partnerships, suppliers should explore ways to understand consumer outcomes after referral.
A particularly welcome development this year was examples where suppliers had a stronger emphasis on sustainability of outcomes rather than initial interventions.

Several suppliers demonstrated efforts to measure whether support remained effective over time. Examples included monitoring whether repayment plans remained affordable, tracking ongoing engagement and assessing whether consumers re-entered debt after receiving support, including debt matching or write-offs.

This consumer-outcomes focus represents an important evolution of good practice. The key question is not whether support was offered, but whether the consumer’s situation improved and remained stable afterwards. Progress in this area will need to continue to align with Ofgem’s shift to more outcomes-focused regulation.
The hearings also revisited the role of PAYG, particularly smart PAYG, in supporting consumers experiencing affordability challenges.

Suppliers presented smart PAYG as a tool that can help many customers budget effectively while enabling earlier identification of potential issues through data and alerts. Technological innovations have created opportunities for faster interventions than are possible with traditional PAYG systems.
However, PAYG offerings must be accompanied by robust safeguards. This winter it will be vital for suppliers to demonstrate that PAYG can deliver good consumer outcomes, even in challenging times.

Repeated use of Additional Support Credit, long periods without top-ups or unusually low consumption should trigger welfare-focused reviews rather than purely account-management responses. Such reviews should examine affordability, benefit entitlement, debt deductions, as well as offerings and information on more sustainable options like energy efficiency opportunities and whether another payment method may be more appropriate.

There also remains a risk that smart PAYG discussions focus predominantly on technological capability without sufficiently demonstrating customer benefit. Suppliers should continue to evidence how innovation improves outcomes rather than assuming technology itself represents good practice. For example, it is important for suppliers to demonstrate whether smart PAYG alerts and predictive analytics allows them to analyse vulnerability earlier, or improve consumer engagement. This is particularly relevant in Scotland, where lower historic smart meter penetration means some consumers remain harder to reach and may require enhanced engagement.

The 2026 hearings demonstrate good progress in several areas. Suppliers increasingly recognise that vulnerability is complex, that affordability challenges often extend beyond energy debt and that long-term outcomes matter more than short-term interventions.

The strongest examples combined early engagement, tailored communication, collaboration with independent advisers, flexible repayment approaches and a focus on sustainable solutions. These approaches move beyond debt management towards helping consumers maintain financial stability.

However, important challenges remain. Consumer engagement continues to be difficult, outcomes evidence remains inconsistent across suppliers and support models that depend heavily on PSR membership risk missing financially vulnerable households whose circumstances have not yet been identified.

Looking ahead, the most important test for the Vulnerability Commitment is not how many initiatives suppliers can demonstrate, but whether those initiatives measurably improve consumer outcomes. A focus on consumer outcomes should also enable support to be adaptable as businesses grow and develop. Some suppliers have demonstrated how their approach to vulnerability has adapted as their business model has changed, and this approach may be useful for fast growing relatively new entrants or firms that merge.

Future development should continue to focus on what happens after support is offered: whether consumers can access it easily, whether it is appropriate to their circumstances and whether it delivers lasting improvements to affordability, resilience and wellbeing.

articles.title: ‘Implementation COP’ ends without overall consensus as real economy action races ahead
articles.standfirst:
Overview Hard-fought negotiations in Antalya ended without reaching consensus on an overarching outcome and only procedural progress on some negotiation items. Against a backdrop of worsening climate impacts, geopolitical instability and a second fossil fuel-driven energy crisis in four years, COP31 failed to secure the necessary political and diplomatic leadership in the negotiations to accelerate […]
The post ‘Implementation COP’ ends without overall consensus as real economy action races ahead  appeared first on E3G.
paragraphs: Hard-fought negotiations in Antalya ended without reaching consensus on an overarching outcome and only procedural progress on some negotiation items. Against a backdrop of worsening climate impacts, geopolitical instability and a second fossil fuel-driven energy crisis in four years, COP31 failed to secure the necessary political and diplomatic leadership in the negotiations to accelerate implementation of the Paris Agreement and demonstrate the collective response needed in this era of overshoot.

Progress on climate action and the energy transition, although under attack by fossil fuel interests in negotiation rooms, is unstoppable in the real economy as volatility and energy insecurity drive countries and sectors to seek to realise the economic benefits of clean, renewable energy and the national security implications of freeing themselves from fossil fuels. In Antalya, that momentum was clear, led by over 70 countries backing the electrification pledge, over 20 countries announcing fossil fuel transition roadmaps, and partnerships driving green industrialisation, adaptation and oceans initiatives.

Despite the lack of overall consensus today, some progress was made, and multilateralism remains alive and essential. The UN process is the only forum where every country has a voice and is crucial for setting global goals and bringing governments and all actors together around real-world delivery as well as formal negotiations. Countries rejecting this weak deal did so as they saw this was the only way to protect the integrity of the UNFCCC, Paris Agreement and the IPCC science going forward.

There can be no doubt this outcome shows the geopolitical strains before us – and makes the road to Addis Ababa harder – but there is also momentum happening, and a collective call to not simply agree to lowest common denominator but rather to continue to maximize the economic opportunities and necessities before us.
Kaysie Brown, Associate Director, Climate Diplomacy & Geopolitics, E3G, said

“Antalya faced two simple tests. Could it rally the world to answer 1.5C overshoot with support of the science and faster action on emissions, adaptation and the finance to pay for both? And could it live up to its own billing as the “COP of delivery”? Underneath both was a bigger question: can climate cooperation still hold in a fractured world?

Antalya struggled to deliver on the first test and passed the second outside the negotiating rooms. Governments rejected a cover text that did not send the signals needed to show seriousness in responding to overshoot and the centrality of science. They should never have been forced into that choice.

But some agreement was reached across negotiation rooms, and delivery, meanwhile, is real: this COP proved that the Action Agenda that has become the engine of implementation. Neither that progress nor the necessity of multilateralism disappears after Antalya. The UN process is still the only place where every country has a voice and laggards can be held to account. It is only as strong as the political commitment governments bring to it, and the road to Addis Ababa and in real world partnerships and investments is now where that commitment must be advanced.

We leave Antalya unclear about what happens on critical issues such as the Antalya to Addis Ababa roadmap on adaptation finance and work on oceans, mountains, forests and beyond as well as with the upcoming IPCC resumed session and the implications for the next global stocktake.”
Cosima Cassel, Programme Lead, Climate Diplomacy & Geopolitics, E3G, said:

“This COP was the first in the era of overshoot. Warming above the 1.5C limit is now unavoidable. The science is clear – every fraction of a degree matters to avoid the most devastating impacts of climate change. COP31 needed an urgent response which matched the scale of that challenge. In the face of significant geopolitical headwinds, stubborn blockers, a challenging Presidency setup, and attempts to undermine the science itself, we leave Antalya without a substantive negotiated outcome.

The months ahead are decisive, starting with the IPCC’s December decisions on budget and timelines that will shape the evidence base for the second Global Stocktake. And at this crucial moment on the road to the next Global Stocktake, much now lands on Ethiopia’s desk. Ethiopia must engage early and work with the UK’s G20 presidency, through China’s BRICS presidency and with others to unblock and bridge divides. Progressive countries must engage, align and actively support that effort throughout the year if COP32 is to deliver meaningful progress on mitigation, adaptation finance and a just transition.”
Alden Meyer, Senior Associate, Climate Diplomacy & Geopolitics, E3G, said:

“As escalating climate impacts devastate communities and ecosystems across the world, COP31 needed to show countries coming together to confront the climate emergency. Instead, reluctance from developed countries to step up on climate finance, combined with opposition from Saudi Arabia and other petrostates to implementing the COP28 agreement on transitioning away from fossil fuels, led to a disappointing outcome.

Yet beyond the negotiating rooms, momentum continues to grow. Governments, cities, businesses and investors are advancing clean energy, methane action, green industrialisation, adaptation, health, oceans and forest protection through the Action Agenda. That spirit of collaboration stands in stark contrast to the adversarial dynamics that too often dominate the formal negotiations. Unlike negotiated text, these real-world initiatives cannot be vetoed by opponents of climate action.”
Heather McKay, Programme Lead, Finance and Resilience, E3G, said:

“While presidencies and parties are stalling, the outside world is moving at pace. This risks signalling that COP finance conversations are out of step with the real world. However, the failure to find consensus at COP31 is ultimately a call for greater ambition. The case for action is clear. Countries, development banks and the private sector are already moving ahead with efforts to finance resilience. Now we need to scale up finance and ensure that countries and communities most exposed to climate impacts can access it on affordable terms. COP31 missed the chance to set out how to scale up adaptation finance equitably, and to connect that investment with an ambitious just transition away from fossil fuels.”
Matt Webb, Associate Director, Global Clean Power Diplomacy, E3G, said:

“This outcome is disappointing but if we step back from the negotiating rooms and look at the real world, the shift to clean energy is irreversible—and it is gaining pace. Clean energy investment is now double that of fossil fuels, and renewables have drawn level with coal in terms of global electricity generation.

We saw that momentum reflected in the wider Action Agenda in Antalya rather than the negotiations. Over 20 countries came forward with fossil fuel transition roadmaps, and we’ve seen major new backing for the global electrification pledge which will help drive fossil fuels from transport, cars and industry. Getting strong fossil fuel language into a consensus text is tough – but the direction of travel is unmistakable.”

articles.title: Energy UK welcomes ambitious UK-EU agreement on energy and climate cooperation
articles.standfirst:
Energy UK has welcomed the conclusion of negotiations to link the UK and EU Emissions Trading Systems (ETS), announced at today’s UK–EU Summit. The agreement is a major step toward deepening energy cooperation, lowering costs for consumers, bolstering confidence for investors and strengthening energy security on both sides of the Channel.  The industry body said…  Read more 
The post Energy UK welcomes ambitious UK-EU agreement on energy and climate cooperation   appeared first on Energy UK.
paragraphs: Energy UK has welcomed the conclusion of negotiations to link the UK and EU Emissions Trading Systems (ETS), announced at today’s UK–EU Summit. The agreement is a major step toward deepening energy cooperation, lowering costs for consumers, bolstering confidence for investors and strengthening energy security on both sides of the Channel.

The industry body said it was pleased that the UK and EU had recognised the mutual benefits of linking emissions trading systems, which will enable both sides to decarbonise faster and at lower cost, and exempt British companies from facing a new tax on exports to their largest market.

Energy UK notes that the UK will benefit from an exemption to the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) costs from 2028. The faster that implementation of the linkage agreement can take place, the faster that both UK and EU customers can benefit from lower costs. For example, Energy UK’s Securing Tomorrow report found that the removal of the CBAM on electricity could reduce energy costs.

The energy sector also strongly supports the ambition to conclude negotiations next year on the UK’s participation in the EU’s Internal Electricity Market. Closer integration of UK and EU electricity markets would deliver significant benefits for consumers and the wider energy system; including reducing the costs of inefficient cross-border trading, strengthening the investment case for hybrid interconnectors, and creating opportunities for GB participation in European balancing platforms, capacity mechanisms and cross-border power purchase agreements.

“Today’s agreement is a real milestone. Linking our carbon markets is good for consumers, good for investment, and good for the climate. Negotiators on both sides deserve credit for getting it over the line.

“Linking our respective carbon pricing regimes will strengthen industrial competitiveness and enable faster and more cost-effective decarbonisation. We urge both sides to implement this linkage at pace, to ensure the benefits of today’s deal are felt as quickly as possible.

“We also welcome the ambition to conclude negotiations next year on the UK’s participation in the EU Internal Electricity Market, which could play an important role in driving down electricity costs for British households and businesses.

“Putting the acrimonious debates of previous years behind us, this summit outcome shows that working together on issues like emissions and electricity trading is a win-win, enabling both the UK and EU to strengthen our economic and energy security.”

articles.title: Bus delays, benefit review relays and BOMAD for cowboys
articles.standfirst:
Afternoon all, Alan, Stephen and John walk into a bar, and the barman says, “What’ll it be Andy?” Alan says cut benefits. Do not be confused here (Andy) – the removal of entitlement to health and disability benefits from under 25s is expected to save half of that bill in 2036 through some individuals receiving … Continued
The post Bus delays, benefit review relays and BOMAD for cowboys appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: Alan, Stephen and John walk into a bar, and the barman says, “What’ll it be Andy?”

Alan says cut benefits. Do not be confused here (Andy) – the removal of entitlement to health and disability benefits from under 25s is expected to save half of that bill in 2036 through some individuals receiving less. Stephen’s order is imminent, but he’s been told it can’t be pricier than his last one so his options are limited. But if John was hoping for a cheap round, Alan has spent 280 pages laying bare an unsurprising reality: solving deep and long-standing challenges in society tends not to be free.

If you’ve been hiding under a rock this week it’s possible you didn’t notice Alan Milburn’s review and you might have no idea what I’m on about. He has done an incredible job at making an issue that has often languished at the bottom of the priority list a grade-A political hot topic. We are already seeing the benefits of that, from the government’s extension of the job guarantee scheme to a funded college place for every 16–18 year old who wants one. But boy does the government have some stuff to sort out this winter on its plans for benefits…(Timms review cheat sheet below)
Ofgem’s new energy price cap comes next week and our resulting Chart of The Week ain’t pretty.

Late again? Using bus location data, the excellent Tom Forth has built a tracker for how long bus journeys in England and Wales actually take (not Scotland, upsetting one RF colleague who tells me that Lothian Buses won Bus Operator of the Year). You can pick any two stops, and it gives you the published and average journey times against the time actually needed if you want to be on time nine journeys in ten. Self-centredly considering Westminster serving buses, the 148 from Camberwell Green needs a buffer of over 20 minutes compared to the published journey time. For commuters fed up of overly optimistic Google Maps, this is the website for you…

Trial and error. Most AI productivity studies ask how well people work with the machine, but a new NBER paper asks the more awkward question of what they can do once it’s gone. In a three-month trial 133 patent lawyers at eleven US firms were randomly given (or denied) a custom drafting assistant, with blinded expert attorneys marking all their work. AI lifted drafting quality by 0.38 standard deviations at ninety days, and narrowed the gap between juniors and seniors. But when AI was withdrawn from everyone, the lasting benefit showed up only among senior lawyers, while junior lawyers showed no average gain. Firms tempted to swap trainee hours for chatbots may find they’ve saved on juniors today and run short of seniors tomorrow.

How low can you go? Ask why the UK isn’t building enough homes and eventually an economist will point at land prices. This interesting blog offers a corrective to anyone who thinks the slump would end if only land prices would fall. Land should be valued at whatever is left once build costs and developer profit are accounted for, but with construction inflation outpacing new home values for the last few years, the residual is getting squeezed. Slower, pricier planning applications (decisions now take more than three times as long as 15 years ago) increase risk for landowners, and outside options like data centres, supermarkets and storage units make for wallet-padding alternatives. Good luck getting to those 1.5 million homes built any time soon.

Keeping it in the family. The issue of the Bank of Mum and Dad is not a new one, shows this blog. The author built a database of 20,000+ upper-class people and their familial ties in Dallas, Texas over its first 122 years until 1963. They found that nearly four-fifths were closely related in a ‘hairball’. And being in this ball paid off: where wealth, status and power were knotted together through family, more than four in five had upper-class descendants in Dallas after 1940, twice the rate for the upper class as a whole. If you’re interested in how status and connections matter as much as money, come to our event in just over a week’s time examining the earnings and mobility gaps of graduates from different socio-economic backgrounds

This week was all about Milburn; but soon it will be Timms’ turn, with the Review of Personal Independence Payment (PIP) due before the end of the month. It aims to make sure PIP is “fair and fit for the future” but spending more money is off the table, with the Review pledging to stay within the OBR’s spending forecasts.

Expect plenty of recommendations on making the current PIP system more humane. Rightly so: there’s lots of evidence the system is traumatising, with claimants describing being treated with suspicion and disdain. For more on PIP’s pitfalls – and possible alternatives – check out our recent High Resolution episode.

Scotland shows a better approach is possible without explosive cost. Its Adult Disability Payment (ADP) replaced PIP four years ago, with the same eligibility rules and payment rates but a kinder delivery. Crucially, this has not permanently increased award rates or sizes. ADP’s award rate for new applicants was 32 per cent in the first half of 2026, lower than PIP’s 36 per cent.

The harder task comes when the Government must produce a welfare White Paper that reconciles Timms with Milburn. Yet our survey of 2,500 PIP recipients found young claimants’ conditions differ less from older claimants’ than is often assumed – 16-24-year-olds are less likely to report depression than 25-54-year-olds for example. The important thing is having the best system (our suggestions here) for all ages, rather than different conclusions driven by two very different independent processes.

Next week Ofgem will announce January’s Energy Price Cap and it is set to soar by £443 to £2,166 in January (according to Cornwall Insight). This week’s chart looks at monthly dual fuel bills for typical households since 2019. The bars show bills before any government support; the diamonds show the winter of 2022-23 after the £400 discount. Once you account for the £400 Energy Bills Support Scheme discount households received in 2022-23, bills will be around £50 higher in real terms this January than they were in January 2023, at the height of the previous energy price crisis. The chart doesn’t include the £100 Household Energy Payment scheme this January or the £150 Council Tax rebate from 2022, but including them wouldn’t change the picture. We know that energy price shocks hit poorer households hardest, which is why the Government’s decision to spread limited support thinly across four-in-five households is the wrong approach. It’s those with typical or higher energy use and low incomes that will find this hardest to bear. Doubling support to half the number of households, with support based on energy use and income, would do a far better job of protecting vulnerable households this winter.

articles.title: Andy Burnham’s EU ‘reset’ deal highlights the problems of incrementalism
articles.standfirst:
Andy Burnham’s EU ‘reset’ deal highlights the problems of incrementalism sam.macrory Fri, 20/11/2026 - 16:07 This prime minister has largely completed Keir Starmer’s EU legacy. 5 Comment Jill Rutter Institute for Government Yes Prime Minister Andy Burnham addresses a media conference during the EU-UK Summit at the European Council building in Brussels. International relations Brexit Trade Immigration Foreign affairs Labour Burnham government
No

It may have been Andy Burnham’s cabinet lining up in Brussels today to shake hands with EU leaders, but this PM’s team have picked up the baton from Keir Starmer and his lead negotiator Nick Thomas-Symonds. Today’s “deals” mostly reflect the files opened at the UK-EU summit in May last year. The one which closed summarily at that summit, when the UK decided the price was too high to join the EU’s Security Action for Europe programme, has remain closed, but the UK announced last December that it would reassociate for one year with the EU’s Erasmus+ programme. 

Since then, negotiations have focussed on easing life for most agri-food exporters, through an agreement to “dynamically align” UK sanitary and phytosanitary laws with the EU, removing the need for checks at the EU border which have seen UK exports decline very substantially since Brexit. The UK will also link its emissions trading scheme (ETS) with the EU’s, allowing UK exporters to avoid the bureaucracy and costs of the EU’s Carbon Border. And there will be a new Youth Experience Scheme (YES) which will allow up to 100,000 young EU citizens (aged 18-31) to work or study in the UK every year for a maximum of three years – with the same number of young Brits able to move to individual EU countries. The prime minister explicitly lauded this scheme as bringing hope to a generation that policy-makers had neglected (and who, by implication, were victims of a Brexit vote they could not participate in). 

None of these “deals” come into force yet. The language on both agreements is that “negotiations have been concluded”, and that the agreements aim to be applied in 2028. The precise language speaks of “looking forward to the conclusion of these agreements (SPS and ETS) along with the Youth Experience Scheme”.  

Opponents are arguing that these breach the UK’s red lines by effectively moving us inside the single market for agricultural goods, that the UK has become a rule taker by accepting the EU design of emissions trading, and that the YES is tantamount to freedom of movement through the backdoor. However, the UK parliament could still decide not to accept new EU rules (though at the price that access newly gained would be lost) and the YES is a souped up version of working holiday schemes that the UK already has with nations like Australia, Canada and South Korea. Indeed, the EU could say that 100,000 is proportionally very low compared to Australia’s 45,000 annual quota. The big concession will come when/if the UK discounts tuition fees for EU students at UK universities – something not conceded to any of these other countries. That remains to be negotiated within the next six months. The language in the joint statement avoids pegging agreement to charging domestic fees and it remains to be seen whether the EU will settle for less.

Related content

Burnham’s Brexit Mission: From Brussels with Love?

Burnham’s Brexit Mission: From Brussels with Love?

The FT’s Stephen Bush joins the podcast team to discuss a big week on the international stage for the prime minister.

Listen to the podcast

Attention is now shifting to Made in Europe

But one of the major focus points in the negotiations was not on the table last year. Since Keir Starmer launched his reset, the EU’s “Made in Europe” agenda – designed to protect the EU’s industrial base from Chinese incursions – risked leaving the UK outside the EU’s procurement and subsidy wall and excluded from critical supply chains. The EU itself has been divided on whether Europe for these purposes includes the UK (and other friendly countries such as Canada, Japan and South Korea) or whether Europe should be interpreted more narrowly to comprise only single market members. 

The final joint statement contains a lot of commitments to work together in “a partnership for economic resilience” with a “Dialogue on Economic Security” (their caps) and to cooperate in managing critical supply chains. There is no explicit reference to the UK coordinating external tariffs – but quite a lot of implication that the UK needs to avoid becoming a backdoor to allow other countries to avoid EU controls.

We don’t know how Andy Burnham will manage the future EU options debate 

The UK government is going to move swiftly into action on getting the necessary legislation to allow the SPS and ETS deals to be implemented onto the statute book, with Burnham suggesting that job will be done this parliament when the agreements are completed. He then proposed “brainstorming” future options with the EU before the next summit, around this time next year – though quite how much time or inclination the EU has for that in the aftermath of a series of difficult election results in Spain, France and Poland remains to be seen.  

The 10 year plan, due this side of Christmas, may reveal more about what Burnham wants to say to the British public about his thinking on future options. The risk for the prime minister is the vacuum he has created is being filled by his critics who are already weaponising elements of these deals to argue that “control” is being handed back to Brussels. But it may make him think that if these limited moves trigger such a reaction, he might as well try to move further, faster after an election.

The UK and the European Union: What is the current relationship?

The UK and the European Union: What is the current relationship?

The UK-EU summit on 20 November 2026 concluded some new agreements between the UK and EU.

Read our explainer
Today’s summit on Brussels followed an agenda set by Keir Starmer, and one constrained by Labour red lines. But even these limited changes have reignited the Brexit debate, notes Jill Rutter, an outcome which may persuade the prime minister to be much less cautious than his predecessor The UK and the European Union: What is the current relationship? Opponents are arguing that these breach the UK’s red lines by effectively moving us inside the single market for agricultural goods, that the UK has become a rule taker by accepting the EU design of emissions trading, and that the YES is tantamount to freedom of movement through the backdoor. However, the UK parliament could still decide not to accept new EU rules (though at the price that access newly gained would be lost) and the YES is a souped up version of working holiday schemes that the UK already has with nations like Australia, Canada and South Korea. Indeed, the EU could say that 100,000 is proportionally very low compared to Australia’s 45,000 annual quota. The big concession will come when/if the UK discounts tuition fees for EU students at UK universities – something not conceded to any of these other countries. That remains to be negotiated within the next six months. The language in the joint statement avoids pegging agreement to charging domestic fees and it remains to be seen whether the EU will settle for less.
The FT’s Stephen Bush joins the podcast team to discuss a big week on the international stage for the prime minister.

But one of the major focus points in the negotiations was not on the table last year. Since Keir Starmer launched his reset, the EU’s “Made in Europe” agenda – designed to protect the EU’s industrial base from Chinese incursions – risked leaving the UK outside the EU’s procurement and subsidy wall and excluded from critical supply chains. The EU itself has been divided on whether Europe for these purposes includes the UK (and other friendly countries such as Canada, Japan and South Korea) or whether Europe should be interpreted more narrowly to comprise only single market members.

The final joint statement contains a lot of commitments to work together in “a partnership for economic resilience” with a “Dialogue on Economic Security” (their caps) and to cooperate in managing critical supply chains. There is no explicit reference to the UK coordinating external tariffs – but quite a lot of implication that the UK needs to avoid becoming a backdoor to allow other countries to avoid EU controls.

The UK government is going to move swiftly into action on getting the necessary legislation to allow the SPS and ETS deals to be implemented onto the statute book, with Burnham suggesting that job will be done this parliament when the agreements are completed. He then proposed “brainstorming” future options with the EU before the next summit, around this time next year – though quite how much time or inclination the EU has for that in the aftermath of a series of difficult election results in Spain, France and Poland remains to be seen.

The 10 year plan, due this side of Christmas, may reveal more about what Burnham wants to say to the British public about his thinking on future options. The risk for the prime minister is the vacuum he has created is being filled by his critics who are already weaponising elements of these deals to argue that “control” is being handed back to Brussels. But it may make him think that if these limited moves trigger such a reaction, he might as well try to move further, faster after an election.

articles.title: Auto and machinery among the hardest hit in AI downside scenario
articles.standfirst: Electronics faces the greatest exposure to shifts in AI data centre investment, while a slowdown would have wider repercussions across global industries.
paragraphs: Electronics faces the greatest exposure to shifts in AI data centre investment, while a slowdown would have wider repercussions across global industries.
The AI data centre boom has been an important pillar of global economic growth over the past few years, but uncertainty around the outlook has been rising on both sides.

AI investment has consistently exceeded our expectations this year, with further upside possible as AI adoption accelerates and demand for computing power continues to grow. At the same time, rising financing stress, bloated stock valuation, grid bottlenecks, and social backlash against data centre construction could slow or derail the AI buildout.

In both scenarios, the electronics sector is the most affected because it supplies vital IT equipment for AI data centres. Electronic components and boards are hit particularly hard because much of the value added occurs in the subsector, with the impact concentrated in the US and Asia.

In the downside scenario, the impacts go beyond AI-related segments as the wider economy is affected. Motor vehicle production falls sharply as a material negative wealth effect weighs on consumer spending and households refrain from big-ticket purchases.

The combination of weaker consumer spending, lower investment activity, and softer industrial demand drags on a wide spectrum of industries. Weaker investment constrains capital-reliant machinery sectors, while softness in end markets affect upstream sectors such as steel and chemicals.

The post Energy UK responds to the Government’s announcement on the budget for AR8 appeared first on Energy UK.
paragraphs: Responding to the Government’s announcement on the budget for the Contracts for Difference (CfD) Allocation Round 8, Energy UK’s chief executive, Dhara Vyas said:

“UK customers are likely to face bill increases of over £400 in the New Year, as conflict abroad causes prices to spike for the second time in five years. In an increasingly uncertain world, energy security is national security. Ensuring that the UK can continue to attract investment to expand our own sources of domestic, clean power is crucial. Alongside electrification, the clean power transition is the best route to ensure that we can secure the jobs, growth and lower-cost energy system of the future.

“The CfD auctions have long proven to be a successful way of securing domestic clean power, giving developers the confidence to make crucial, long-term investment decisions, delivering value for money and protecting consumers from price volatility.

“The Government has been clear that it’s focused on securing cheaper energy supplied by clean power. Today’s announcement of a £1 notional budget for the auction is designed to drive a competitive price, so that the next auction round delivers renewable projects at a cost that is fair for consumers – and the energy industry shares this ambition. It will therefore be crucial that developers have clarity and confidence in how budgets will be subsequently revised. AR8 is a significant opportunity to strengthen our energy security and boost economic growth, confirming that Great Britain continues to be an attractive place to invest.”

“The oil industry is not disappearing. But the assumption that demand will grow with every new car, every journey and every expanding economy is beginning to fail. Investors need to stop treating yesterday’s growth story as tomorrow’s investment case.” Mark Campanale, Founder and CEO, Carbon Tracker

The International Energy Agency’s World Energy Outlook 2026 arrives amid an energy crisis that has renewed calls for investment in fossil fuel production. Yet behind the immediate disruption, the report reveals a more fundamental change in the global energy system.

For decades, economic growth and rising mobility have driven increasing oil consumption. It was an extraordinarily successful growth model, supporting investment across a vast global industry. That relationship is now weakening.

The IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario sees oil demand levelling off around 103 million barrels per day by 2030, before gradually declining. Its Current Policies Scenario shows continued growth, while an additional response to the energy crisis could accelerate the shift away from imported fuels.
These are different possible futures, not predictions. But the underlying structural change is increasingly visible across both.
Electrification allows economies to expand mobility and other energy services without equivalent increases in fossil-fuel consumption.
As a prime example the IEA estimates that electric vehicles are already displacing around 2.3 million barrels of oil per day globally in 2026, despite slower growth in some major vehicle markets.
Crucially, the IEA also finds that much more substitution is already economically competitive using today’s technologies.
That has important consequences for investment: the WEO finds that a difference of just 4% in oil demand between two of its scenarios in 2035 translates into a 13% difference in oil prices.
Such sensitivity raises fundamental questions about the economics of new oil production, particularly higher-cost projects that depend on sustained demand and strong prices over decades.

The Middle East crisis has demonstrated the continuing importance of oil, but also the increasing exposure of economies dependent on internationally traded fuels. Electrification and renewable energy offer not simply alternative energy supplies, but a way to reduce that exposure.
The world will continue to consume substantial quantities of oil for many years. But growing demand for energy services no longer guarantees growing demand for oil.
The old energy system does not have to disappear for the new one to take the lead.
For investors, the issue is not that oil demand disappears, but that the demand growth needed to justify new investment fails to materialise.
