articles.title: Europe must maintain momentum on energy and climate cooperation at the EU-UK Summit
articles.standfirst:
Story The 2026 EU–UK Summit will take place on 20 November in Brussels, hosted by European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham attending.   Recent statements by both leaders at COP31 have given renewed political impetus to closer cooperation. UK Prime Minister Andy […]
The post Europe must maintain momentum on energy and climate cooperation at the EU-UK Summit   appeared first on E3G.
paragraphs: The 2026 EU–UK Summit will take place on 20 November in Brussels, hosted by European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham attending.

Recent statements by both leaders at COP31 have given renewed political impetus to closer cooperation. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for a new era of British climate leadership as the UK published its clean electrification roadmap, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen set out the EU’s ambition to accelerate electrification. Both leaders backed the COP31 35-by-35 goal. The EU’s Electrification Action Plan aims to double electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 46% by 2040. These signals create an opportunity to turn shared ambition into closer practical cooperation.

As the Iran war is driving up prices of oil and gas again, both the EU and UK have a strategic interest in accelerating deployment of clean energy to reduce dependence on fossil fuels and strengthen energy security. Neither the EU nor the UK can fully realise the benefits of electrification in isolation.

Closer cooperation can help unlock the potential of North Sea offshore wind, improve electricity market integration and support more competitive, resilient industrial supply chains. Progress in these areas would bring benefits to both sides, from more affordable and secure energy to stronger industrial competitiveness and a more coherent approach to global climate diplomacy.

The political conditions for closer EU–UK cooperation are increasingly favourable. The previous summit in May 2025 demonstrated the appetite for collaboration on climate and energy, recognising the mutual benefits of accelerating clean energy deployment, driving economic growth, strengthening security and improving affordability. The November summit offers an opportunity to build on that foundation, moving from broad political commitments towards concrete milestones and a roadmap for cooperation in 2027.

“With the worst drought on record this past summer driving up food bills and energy bills going through the roof this winter, the danger of fossil fuel dependence is becoming impossible to ignore. This summit is a major opportunity for the UK to work with the EU to build a far more secure, inter-connected and electrified energy system that can drive down energy bills and bolster energy security. This is the only solution that can end the power of dictators and autocrats to hold our economies to ransom by weaponizing fossil fuel supplies.”

“It has been a while since the UK-EU relationship has felt so full of possibility. It gives the summit new relevance as the moment to lay the foundations a stronger Europe needs for security, international relevance and affordability at home, via commitments and clear milestones. The UK and EU would both materially benefit from more efficient energy system ties; joint, ambitious projects for a competitive and clean industrial transition; and a shared plan to build climate security through decarbonisation, resilience and diplomacy.”

“The EU and UK have a shared strategic goal to reduce dependence on fossil gas and electrify their economies. This will require huge amounts of clean electricity. It is difficult to see how this can be delivered without fully exploiting the offshore wind potential in the North Seas. Neither UK nor EU can do this alone – they need to work together. Making the UK a full member of the North Seas Energy Cooperation would be an important step.”

“This Summit is an opportunity to advance talks on the UK’s reintegration into the EU electricity market. At a time of shared energy security and affordability challenges, deeper electricity market integration can help lower energy bills, strengthen energy system resilience and unlock the potential of North Seas wind to deliver greater energy independence.”
Ellie Belton, Programme Lead for Clean Econonmy at E3G, said:

“Building a shared UK-EU agenda for cooperation on trade and industrial policy will strengthen Europe’s economic security in a more volatile world. Extending ‘Made in Europe’ provisions to UK businesses and co-developing solutions to mitigate CBAM tensions with global partners will reduce strategic dependencies and build a more resilient clean economy. This is the best pathway to accelerating industrial decarbonisation in a new era of geoeconomic competition.”
Katharina Osthoff, EU Foreign Policy Specialist and Lead, said:

“The EU and UK face many of the same climate and China-related risks, but still too often assess them separately. They need to think of security more broadly, as the next crisis in Europe could start with a shock to food markets or disruption to a critical supply chain. Both should use this summit to coordinate more closely on the climate security agenda and establish early consultations on trade defence and investment screening. Otherwise, a decision taken on one side of the Channel may create a new vulnerability on the other.”
Manon Dufour, Executive Director, E3G Brussels (EN, FR) – EU politics | manon.dufour@e3g.org
Luke O’Callaghan-White, Programme Lead for EU energy transition luke.ocallaghanwhite@e3g.org
Simon Skillings, Senior Specialist at E3G London | simon.skillings@e3g.org
Artur Patuleia, Senior Policy Advisor | artur.patuleia@e3g.org
Ellie Belton, Programme Lead for Clean Economy at E3G | ellie.belton@e3g.org

E3G’s briefing, Closing the North Seas delivery gap: Political leadership to deliver affordability and security from offshore wind, sets out the key actions needed from European leaders to successfully deploy the 300GW of offshore wind ambition. Offshore wind in the North Seas is a strategic opportunity to secure clean homegrown electricity, promote integration of the European market, and transform the region into a clean industrial powerhouse. articles.title: Modernising post-government employment rules is long overdue
articles.standfirst:
Modernising post-government employment rules is long overdue ellie.slee.lamb Wed, 18/11/2026 - 10:20 Reform of the business appointment rules is an important part of the bigger picture on opening up the civil service 5 Comment Hannah Keenan Institute for Government Yes Civil service Civil servants Civil service reform Burnham government
No

Restrictions on the type of work an official can do after leaving the civil service are governed by BARs – the business appointment rules. Once administered by the advisory committee on business appointments (ACOBA), the BARs for senior (directors general and permanent secretaries) civil servants and special advisers is, as of 2025, overseen by the civil service commission, the arms-length body that regulates recruitment into the civil service.  

It is a system which, the institute has long argued, is in need of overhauling – and so a new report by the civil service commission is welcome. It sets out recommendations which will, if accepted, contribute to a more porous and expert civil service, and government should reform the BARs in line with the review recommendations. It will then need to go much further to open up the civil service. 

Business appointment rules have been harming the civil service 

While developing people and skills is crucial, part of creating an effective workforce will always mean being able to access experience and expertise from outside when it is required. Something with which the civil service has long struggled.  

There are a whole host of reasons, cultural and structural, behind that. But BARs are one part of the picture. As the Institute’s research from 2022 set out, the BARs have been acting as a disincentive for external applicants, in particular senior ones to technical roles. The rules could, in theory, restrict you from taking up work in your field of expertise for up to two years after leaving the civil service. And in process terms, even if there are ultimately no restrictions on your future employment, it might take you months to get clearance to take up that role – by which time the window may well have closed. That is very real uncertainty, and a very real disincentive for outsiders to take up a role in the civil service. It is not the only reason external experts don’t come in, but it is a factor. 

Government should act on the commission's review 

That the civil service commission, which already regulates entry, is leading this work on exits for senior officials is a good start; career shapes are shifting and the service should be encouraging – with appropriate ethical safeguards – careers that move in and out of government. The rules have not been meaningfully updated since the 1970s, and no longer reflect the reality of modern work or the skills the service needs. This review should result in a much-needed update.  

Two things are particularly welcome. First, a recognition that the current rules conflate sector expertise with improper advantage, and that this must change. The civil service needs experts, and there should be a sizeable chunk of them who are able to come into government and return to their field of expertise without being unduly punished for doing so. Second, the recognition that much of this is about culture and process efficiency, rather than only about the rules themselves. There is no point updating the rules if the myths around them still hold, or if it will still take months for officials to receive the all-clear on low-risk roles.

The government should act on the commission’s review, reforming the system so that it provides greater clarity for officials, and more proportionality. The review recommends, for example, that for fixed-term appointments of a year or less, conditions should be agreed upon before employment is taken up. As the Institute has previously argued, it should be possible, before joining a role, to see very clearly what restrictions on your activity will look like after you leave. 

Opening up the civil service will need far more than BARs reform 

These recommendations are still only one small piece of the civil service’s ongoing struggle with porosity. As the cabinet secretary said in her recent lecture, “we disincentivise our brightest talent from stepping outside the Civil Service to gain vital experience, and bringing that critical knowledge back”.  

Unblocking this problem requires a series of inter-linked initiatives. More recruitment, especially in central government departments, needs to be done externally. New talent can’t find its way in if many job adverts are still only visible to civil servants. That in turn means addressing the underlying reasons, or perceptions, that drive recruitment from the existing pool of civil servants: security vetting takes too long; onboarding is patchy; there’s no consistent training offer so new team members need to already ‘get’ government; the recruitment process favours internal candidates anyway.

The government is making good steps on some of this, including the new national school of government and public service, and the decision to scrap the ‘success profiles’ currently used to recruit. There are pockets of excellence that show it can be done differently without the system falling over, such as the recruitment exemptions in place for the AI Security Institute.  

Being able to bring in more external people while controlling the size of the civil service also requires better tools to increase the number of leavers from the civil service. A sharper practice and culture around poor performance management, and tighter workforce planning are all part of the same picture.

BARs reform is a helpful piece of the puzzle of breaking open the civil service. But it is only one part of a much bigger ambition on porosity and reform.

paragraphs: The government should adopt recommendations set out in the civil service commission’s review into the rules, and the practices, regulating post-government jobs – but this is one part of the puzzle of breaking open the service, writes Hannah Keenan

Restrictions on the type of work an official can do after leaving the civil service are governed by BARs – the business appointment rules. Once administered by the advisory committee on business appointments (ACOBA), the BARs for senior (directors general and permanent secretaries) civil servants and special advisers is, as of 2025, overseen by the civil service commission, the arms-length body that regulates recruitment into the civil service.

It is a system which, the institute has long argued, is in need of overhauling – and so a new report by the civil service commission is welcome. It sets out recommendations which will, if accepted, contribute to a more porous and expert civil service, and government should reform the BARs in line with the review recommendations. It will then need to go much further to open up the civil service.

While developing people and skills is crucial, part of creating an effective workforce will always mean being able to access experience and expertise from outside when it is required. Something with which the civil service has long struggled.

There are a whole host of reasons, cultural and structural, behind that. But BARs are one part of the picture. As the Institute’s research from 2022 set out, the BARs have been acting as a disincentive for external applicants, in particular senior ones to technical roles. The rules could, in theory, restrict you from taking up work in your field of expertise for up to two years after leaving the civil service. And in process terms, even if there are ultimately no restrictions on your future employment, it might take you months to get clearance to take up that role – by which time the window may well have closed. That is very real uncertainty, and a very real disincentive for outsiders to take up a role in the civil service. It is not the only reason external experts don’t come in, but it is a factor.

That the civil service commission, which already regulates entry, is leading this work on exits for senior officials is a good start; career shapes are shifting and the service should be encouraging – with appropriate ethical safeguards – careers that move in and out of government. Two things are particularly welcome. First, a recognition that the current rules conflate sector expertise with improper advantage, and that this must change. The civil service needs experts, and there should be a sizeable chunk of them who are able to come into government and return to their field of expertise without being unduly punished for doing so. Second, the recognition that much of this is about culture and process efficiency, rather than only about the rules themselves. There is no point updating the rules if the myths around them still hold, or if it will still take months for officials to receive the all-clear on low-risk roles.

The government should act on the commission’s review, reforming the system so that it provides greater clarity for officials, and more proportionality. The review recommends, for example, that for fixed-term appointments of a year or less, conditions should be agreed upon before employment is taken up. articles.title: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time
articles.standfirst:
Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon…
The post Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time appeared first on Carbon Brief.
paragraphs: Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.
Since 1850, the three nations – and other major fossil-fuel exporters – have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 in the form of gas, oil and coal that has been burned in other countries.
Carbon Brief’s analysis of extraction-based CO2 emissions is based on figures compiled by Robbie Andrew, a senior researcher at Norwegian climate institute CICERO.
It shows that Australia is responsible for more than twice as much global warming when including emissions from its fossil-fuel exports, while Saudi Arabia has caused more than four times as much.
Australia has been under pressure for continuing to expand its fossil-fuel production ahead of the UN climate summit in Antalya, where it is co-president with host nation Turkey.

In contrast, nations that are heavily reliant on energy imports – such as Japan or Germany – are responsible for far lower shares of planet-warming emissions, if responsibility passes to fossil-fuel producers.
There are many different ways to assign historical responsibility for current global warming.
Carbon Brief has previously published analysis based on territorial emissions, the consumption of imported goods, according to colonial rule or based on historical emissions per capita.
This year is expected to be around 1.5C hotter than pre-industrial temperatures. Next year is forecast to be the hottest on record, at around 1.7C of warming.
This year-to-year variation is due to natural variability, such as El Niño. However, approximately 100% of global warming to date is the result of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.
The burning of fossil fuels since the industrial revolution is the largest contributor to this.
Since there is a direct link between each tonne of CO2 and each fraction of a degree of warming, historical fossil-fuel emissions can be tied to responsibility for current climate change.

This is typically calculated on the basis of historical territorial CO2 emissions, according to where in the world the fossil fuels are burned. It is also possible to assign historical responsibility on a “consumption” basis, according to where goods are used.
Historical emissions are often counted by country, but this puts the focus on populous nations. Alternatively, responsibility can be assigned per capita, based on today’s populations.
A less-familiar way to look at the question of historical responsibility is to consider where fossil fuels are extracted. This puts the spotlight on major fossil-fuel exporters.
The figure below shows that Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the largest CO2 exporters of all time, based on emissions from exported fossil fuels since 1850.

(The allocation is based on extraction taking place within current national borders. Emissions under the former USSR, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia are allocated among constituent countries, based on their share of emissions at the time of separation.)
Other major CO2 exporters, based on their overseas sales of fossil fuels since 1850, include Venezuela, Iran, Norway, the United Arab Emirates and Canada.
Between them, these major coal, oil and gas producers have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 over the past 175 years, according to Carbon Brief’s analysis.
The analysis shows that overall, the US and China retain the largest responsibility for historical warming under extraction-based accounting, despite having been net CO2 importers since 1850.
The US has large resources of coal, oil and gas, but was nevertheless a major oil importer until after the shale revolution in the early 2000s.
China remains a major oil and gas importer, describing itself as “rich in coal, lacking oil and gas”.
Russia remains in third place, as shown in the figure below, despite gaining responsibility for an extra 69bn tonnes of CO2 from exported fossil fuels.
The UK becomes the fourth-largest historical emitter, climbing above Germany due to the latter’s reliance on fossil-fuel imports.
Saudi Arabia becomes responsible for the world’s fifth-largest share of historical warming when including its fossil-fuel exports, which increase its cumulative emissions more than fourfold.
Australia also climbs up the rankings, becoming one of the top-ten largest emitters when including its fossil-fuel exports. This more than doubles its share of historical emissions.
Nations that drop down the rankings under extraction-based accounting, due to their reliance on fossil-fuel imports, include Germany, India, France and COP31 host Turkey.

Japan is a particularly notable example, as it is almost completely reliant on fossil-fuel imports. The nation is the sixth-largest emitter on a territorial basis and the 34th-largest on an extraction basis.
When considering population sizes, major fossil-fuel exporters have the highest extraction-based CO2 emissions since 1850, as shown in the figure below.
Small nations that export large amounts of oil and gas are particularly prominent on this list, including Brunei, Kuwait, Qatar, Norway and Trinidad and Tobago.
Andrew tells Carbon Brief that while the extraction-based accounting offers an alternative perspective on historical responsibility for warming, it also raises complex questions. He explains:
“At the end of the day, it’s not solely the responsibility of extracting countries that fuels are combusted; it’s joint responsibility between extractors, producers and consumers.”
He adds that responsibility for past decisions is shared by many actors. For example, he notes that oil production in the Middle East was historically “developed by and for western powers”.
National emissions under extraction-based accounting come from a dataset developed by Robbie Andrew and covering the period from 1850-2025.
Emissions are allocated to the country that extracted the relevant fossil fuels, regardless of where the coal, oil or gas was burned.

The allocation is based on current national borders. Emissions that took place within the former USSR, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia are allocated among their present-day constituent countries, based on the relative shares of emissions at the time of separation.
Andrew notes that the dataset is a draft release, based on available data.
Population data for 2025 is taken from the UN Population Fund.

The post Save the date: What industry actually thinks about the future of the EU ETS appeared first on E3G.
paragraphs: As negotiations on the future of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) enter a crucial phase, strong and often competing claims are being made about what the system and different design choices mean for European industry. But how do the companies and investors affected by the ETS actually think? What are their preferred design choices for the future of the system?

The event will present the results of a business poll by Norstat, commissioned by E3G in collaboration with CISL-Corporate Leaders Group Europe, Jacques Delors Institute, EPICO and Bellona. It covers the views of over 1,000 representatives from companies and investors affected by the EU ETS across nine EU Member States: Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, Czechia, Romania, Greece and Lithuania.
Taking place just days ahead of the 11 December Environment Council, the event will provide a comprehensive picture of business attitudes and preferences on the future of the EU ETS, including:
The findings will also allow comparisons across the nine countries surveyed and between company profiles, such as between those that receive free allocations and those that do not.

Following the presentation of the polling results, a panel discussion with business representatives, policymakers and think tanks (final speakers to be confirmed) will reflect on what the findings mean for the future of the EU ETS and the ongoing negotiations – followed by a Q&A session.

articles.standfirst:
Responding to the publication of Alan Milburn’s review From a Welfare State to a Working State: A new settlement for the next generation commissioned by the Department of Work and Pensions, Rachel Cary, Head of Industrial Strategy at Energy UK, said: “Young energy professionals are at the heart of the energy industry workforce, so it…  Read more 
The post Energy UK responds to the Milburn Review on youth unemployment appeared first on Energy UK.
paragraphs: Responding to the publication of Alan Milburn’s review From a Welfare State to a Working State: A new settlement for the next generation commissioned by the Department of Work and Pensions, Rachel Cary, Head of Industrial Strategy at Energy UK, said:
“Young energy professionals are at the heart of the energy industry workforce, so it is positive to see the challenge of youth unemployment taken seriously in this review.

“Alan Milburn is right to say that apprenticeships are the best opportunity to get young people into skilled employment, so it is positive to see proposals to ringfence apprenticeship funding to increase investment in skills.

“Our members already offer a wide range of rewarding, entry-level opportunities, including apprenticeships, that serve as a launchpad for an exciting and rewarding career in a rapidly evolving industry.

“As the energy industry continues to grow, we will need people from every background and skill level. Making entry easier will be key to delivering the future energy system, but it is also important that viable pathways for retraining and upskilling of the existing workforce remain open.

“Wider reforms are still needed to the apprenticeship system and cutting funding for apprentices over the age of 25 could have a negative impact on developing these skills at a time when our industry needs a skilled workforce at all levels.

articles.title: Northern Ireland’s “government in name only” is failing to deliver
articles.standfirst:
Northern Ireland’s “government in name only” is failing to deliver sam.macrory Tue, 17/11/2026 - 20:11 Dominant parties in Northern Ireland don't seem to pay a price for their inability to deliver better outcomes. 4 Comment Jill Rutter Institute for Government Yes Stormont is the home of the Northern Ireland Assembly and Executive, but both government and parliament need to work better in Northern Ireland. Devolution Northern Ireland protocol Sinn Féin Democratic Unionist Party Social Democratic and Labour Party Deputy first minister of Northern Ireland First minister of Northern Ireland Northern Ireland executive
No

The last Conservative government finally persuaded the DUP to re-establish the Executive in February 2024 – two years after it collapsed when the DUP withdrew over the implementation of the then Northern Ireland Protocol. Rishi Sunak had failed to persuade the DUP that the Windsor Framework was sufficient reason to return, and it took almost another year for the DUP to extract enough concessions to agree to go back in. 

Initially it looked as though relations between Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O’Neill and deputy First Minster Emma Little-Pengelly were going well, as the new team launched with a spirit of optimism, common purpose and a willingness to get to grips with deep-seated policy problems. But initial progress has since stalled and relations have deteriorated to such an extent that the DUP are now refusing to join joint activities with the First Minister. This left Northern Ireland with no political representation at the prime minister’s recent National Economic Council with the leaders of the devolved governments. 

But a bigger problem is what Sam McBride of the Belfast Telegraph termed “government in name only” at our webinar on Northern Ireland. Decisions are not being made. The much poorer performance of the health service in Northern Ireland than in the other parts of the UK is still not being addressed, despite years of reports detailing how it needs to be rationalised. The NI Executive is rejecting the latest bail out offer from Westminster – and refuses to contemplate extra local revenue raising, preferring instead to look to UK taxpayers to underwrite them. They know the UK government usually blinks first and the moral hazard merry-go-round of failing to take tough decisions continues. 

There is a lack of accountability when voting is little affected by delivery 

In theory, Northern Ireland should have politicians capable of facing up to long-term decisions because power sharing means they face minimal electoral jeopardy. Indeed, identity voting reduces the electoral penalty for poor performance. But so far there is no evidence that the dominant parties pay a price for their inability to deliver better outcomes in Northern Ireland. 

Sinn Féin have benefited from Michelle O’Neill’s decision to stand with the citizens of the Garvaghy Road in opposition to the controversial Drumcree march, even if the DUP’s response has hamstrung the Executive. A recent LucidTalk poll put the party at an impressive 28 per cent, despite the other main nationalist party, the SDLP, being seen to have been making a good fist of Opposition. The incentives to play to the base will only increase as the next elections approach.

On the other hand, accountability may finally be catching up with the DUP, who are shedding votes to a reenergised UUP (who they displaced in the mid-2000s as the principal unionist party) on one side and to the even harder line TUV (Traditional Unionist Voice) on the other. That same poll showed the three unionist parties all in the lowish teens, with the UUP just edging ahead. Advocacy of Brexit, failure to deliver in government and the move from insurgent to party of government all seem to be catching up, and the battle over Assembly seats is hotting up for next May.

Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset should reduce the tension over the Windsor Framework

Any search for stability is also dependent on decisions in Westminster over relations wit the EU. The move for GB to dynamically align with EU sanitary and phytosanitary rules, expected to be signed off, should reduce the divergence between NI – still following most single market rules –and the rest of the UK. If Andy Burnham aims to go further when he sets out his options, the differences would diminish – though so too would any “best of both worlds” advantage. But if the Conservatives or Reform UK looked like approaching government, Northern Ireland would be forced yet again to address the consequences of a breakdown in UK-EU relations over their desire to leave the ECHR. It is far from clear any Executive could cope with those pressures. 

Northern Ireland needs its institutions to work better

The Good Friday Agreement set up institutions (with slight modifications since) designed for power-sharing arrangements, but both government and parliament need to work better in Northern Ireland. In our webinar, David Sterling, the former head of the Northern Ireland Civil Service, pointed to the possibility of the three smaller parties going into opposition when the next Executive is formed. Ann Watt explained what Pivotal, Northern Ireland’s independent policy think tank, would be looking at in their new project on possible reforms to make Stormont more effective. Andy Burnham has hinted the government is looking at that too. And Ulster University’s Deirdre Heenan asked (somewhat plaintively) what level of divergence in public service standards between different parts of the UK a responsible government in Westminster could really tolerate – a great issue to throw back at a prime minister whose big idea is devolution. 

Whatever his answer, Andy Burnham will, at least, face scrutiny for his decisions. For now, Northern Ireland’s politicians seem to keep getting away without making any.

articles.title: The Economic Importance of Motorcycles to Europe
articles.standfirst: In 2024, motorcycle-related activity supported €35.1 billion in GDP, 481,600 jobs and €20.6 billion in tax revenues across the EU and the UK. This study shows how manufacturing, sales, repairs and events ripple through supply chains, and how trade barriers and competition shape Europe’s global position. It also models how more motorcycle commuting could cut travel time, costs and CO₂ emissions.
paragraphs: A Report for the European Association of Motorcycle Manufacturers (ACEM)

In 2024, motorcycle-related activity supported an estimated €35.1 billion in GDP, 481,600 jobs and €20.6 billion in tax revenues across the EU and the UK. These figures capture the sector’s own operations, its supply chains and the wider spending it supports, including spending by employees and visitors attending motorcycle events.

The analysis covers motorcycle manufacturing, sales and repairs, as well as accessories, sports and promotional events. Drawing on official statistics, industry data and economic modelling, it traces how these activities support businesses across the economy. For every €1 of GDP generated directly by the sector, a further €2.30 was supported elsewhere.

International trade is another important part of the picture. Around half of EU motorcycle and parts production was exported in 2024. The report examines Europe’s position in global markets and how trade barriers, growing competition and regulatory complexity affect the industry’s opportunities to invest and expand.

The study also explores how motorcycle use can reduce commuting times, operating costs, emissions and demand for urban space. Around 6.4 million people across the EU and the UK already commute by motorcycle. Under a modelled scenario in which 5% of car commuters switched to motorcycles, the report estimates potential annual savings of 28 million days of commuting time and 2.6 million tonnes of CO₂. It also considers how motorcycles can complement public transport and other modes within urban mobility plans.
Associate Director of Economic Consulting, Continental Europe

Stefan Gorgels is Associate Director for economic consulting services in Continental Europe, focusing on economic impact analysis and econometric analysis. He has a strong academic background in economics and extensive experience in managing consulting and research projects for national and international clients.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Stefan was a manager at DIW Econ - the consulting arm of the German Institute for Economic Research - where he managed economic consulting and research projects for a wide range of clients, including companies, industry associations, German government ministries and the European Commission.
Stefan Gorgels holds a B.Sc. in Economics from Maastricht University, an M.Sc. in Economics from the Barcelona Graduate School of Economics and a Ph.D. in Economics from New York University.

Before joining Oxford Economics in 2025, Johanna worked at DIW Econ, the consultancy firm of the German Institute for Economic Research. During her time there, Johanna led several high-profile projects assessing the economic impact of different industries and institutions, as well as projects addressing socioeconomic and environmental issues. Johanna holds an M.Sc. in Economics and Management from Leibniz University Hannover.

articles.title: COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions
articles.standfirst:
UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to…
The post COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions appeared first on Carbon Brief.
paragraphs: UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to answer readers’ questions.
Carbon Brief readers submitted questions via CB Connect on topics including the UK’s “climate leadership”, the COP31 electrification target, as well as the roadmaps on deforestation and fossil fuels.
Despite recent criticism over the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, Miliband argued that the UK is still seen as a climate leader, due to its “ambitious targets on net-zero”.
Pushing back on a question about COP reform, Miliband explained how he is “quite pro the institution of the COP”, given its role in bringing countries together for climate action.
He emphasised the importance of action on methane and the UK’s “support” for the “35×35” electrification pledge.
Carbon Brief: Well, thanks very much for joining us. I know you’re very busy and we’ve got some reader questions. It’s great that you’ve got time to answer some.
CB: How, in your experience at COP31 so far, has the UK’s decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field and the rumoured rollback of its EV targets affected the UK’s standing as a climate leader?

EM: People see us as showing leadership. People don’t see us as rolling back, and I think what people see is a government that is driving the agenda on electrification and clean power. Because after all, we have a clean power 2030 target, which is world-leading.
[We] have the most ambitious targets on net-zero, the [nationally determined contributions] NDCs, of frankly, any country in the world. [We] are legislating for no new oil and gas licences.

And what I’m trying to do here is also bring a new dimension to this, which is the whole national security dimension. Because I think, if you’re serious about national security, you need to be serious about climate. And those parties – and those people – who aren’t serious about climate, I don’t think they’re serious about national security. Because this is a national security issue for, I think – frankly – every government across the world.

So I think, look, people see British leadership. People are looking forward to our [presidency of the] G20 [in 2027], where climate resilience [and] debt development will be central to the agenda as well.
CB: Are you confident that the UK can still meet its 2030 NDC target [to cut emissions 68% below 1990 levels]?

EM: Absolutely, we’re going to go all out to meet it. I think that’s so important, and that is the whole principle of the NDCs, is [that] you drive towards seeking to meet them. Obviously, it’s stretching. We inherited, from 2024, a difficult situation from the previous government, but we’re going to go all out to do what we can.
CB: Great. With the UK and other developed countries facing increasing fiscal pressures, how can you go about ensuring developing countries receive the financial and technical support that they need?

EM: Look, I think the biggest thing we need to do, cognisant of those fiscal pressures and the situation facing developing countries, is multilateral development bank (MDB) reform. So making sure that the MDBs work to the maximum for developing countries.

There’s lots of evidence out there and I was speaking about this at the World Bank annual meetings about the fact that the MDBs could do more to leverage their balance sheets. You know, potentially hundreds of billions of pounds – dollars – more that could be helping developing countries. Helping developing countries with climate resilience, helping them with relieving the debt burden in terms of the financing of the debt.

And, you know, one of the things that we’re going to be doing as part of our G20 is convening those MDBs to, in a friendly way, you know, point to the best practice of some of them, push the others to do more. I feel from our discussions that this is absolutely possible – for us to do more.

So yes, there are more fiscal constraints in developed countries, including in Britain, but it doesn’t mean we can’t make a difference. And I think it’s really, really important to say to your viewers: we are serious about, not just our national leadership on climate, but our international leadership as well, and we believe we can make a difference.

CB: It’s become part of the narrative that the COP process has run its course, and that people should focus more on mini-coalitions, groups of middle powers. What would you say to that, and how would you like to see the COP process reformed?
EM: I mean, I’m quite pro the COP process – not the process, but I’m quite pro the institution of the COP – and I’d say that in two respects.

One, if you look at the sweep of history, I was at the Copenhagen COP of 2009, [which] ended in acrimony. We were heading for a 4C world back then. Now, we’re heading for a 2.5C, 2.6C world, according to the latest UNEP emissions gap report – one of my favourite publications.

And look, 2.6C is bad, right? And we’ve got to do a lot more as a world, but we have made progress. And why? Because of multilateralism, because of the institution, being part of the COP, driving people forward.

That’s one part of it. The second part of it is [that the COP is] a place where these “coalitions of the willing” are formed. If I think about what I’ve done while I’ve been here [in Antalya] – I was at an event on forests, coalitions of the willing acting on the forest leaders’ partnership, acting to protect the forest. An event on electrification, a big focus of the Turkish presidency. An event on industrial policy, green industrial policy. Countries working together. An event this morning on methane, really crucial. We’re trying to, with a coalition of the willing, get it onto the COP agenda. And then, an event on climate security.
So that gives people, your viewers, a sense of why I think this [COP process] matters. You know, it’s not simply a talking shop. I think it is also a place where action happens.
CB: You mentioned the electrification pledge put forward by the Turkish presidency. Is the UK a signatory to that yet?

EM: We support the electrification pledge, absolutely, and you know we want to drive forward. It’s stretching for the UK, but we think it’s the right thing to do. And why? Because – it’s really important to say this – because electrification is a way of getting off the fossil-fuel rollercoaster. Clean-energy electrification is the way I think about it.
[Three hours after Carbon Brief’s interview with Ed Miliband, the UK government confirmed its endorsement of the 35×35 electrification pledge.]

And if there’s one lesson we’ve got to learn from these two wars that we’ve seen – Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran war – it’s [that] you can’t have security on the basis of fossil fuels. It’s not even – even [for a] country like America, a massive fossil-fuel producer is affected by higher prices. But for fossil-fuel importers, covering 75% of the world’s population [including the UK], we are price takers. And you know the fossil-fuel rollercoaster is terrible for the cost of living. That’s why clean energy, clean electrification, is the answer. Electrify now!

CB: The UN climate convention and the Paris Agreement both commit countries, including the UK, to implement “climate-change education, training, public awareness and participation”. Why doesn’t the UK have a national programme on this, particularly given the flood of misinformation in this area?
EM: We need to do more. You’re completely right. Look, I am always ambitious to do more, and more climate education – well, more public information – is important.

I did the first annual climate and nature statement in 2025. It was repeated in 2026 by [environment secretary] Mary Creagh. I was in the House of Commons for that, and that whole institution was part of me believing, as energy secretary, that it was important to find ways to inform the public.

And I fully acknowledge we need to do more. We need to do more. But we need to do more to both tell people about what is happening, in terms of climate and nature, but also say there are answers, because it can’t just be a council of despair. It’s also got to be a council of hope – not false hope – but a council of honesty, but also hope.
CB: Great. How would you like to see the Brazilian roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation taken forward? Are you keen to see those as part of the formal negotiated outcome [at COP31]?

EM: I think what’s interesting about this goes back to your question about the coalition of the willing. Look, there’s obviously no secret that there are countries that are obstacles to the fossil-fuel roadmap being part of – central – to the COP decision. And we took a decision last year that there was a big enough coalition of the willing – I think there are 80 countries or more – to drive this forward.

I think the Brazilians are to be incredibly commended for having produced this fossil-fuel roadmap. I think we should now be thinking, as individual countries, how can we build on that work ourselves? Because it’s doing exactly what I hoped it would do, which is to grapple with the important issues that we face.

I think we have to accept there are some countries – in a world where you have to operate by consensus – where not every decision is going to get into the COP decision. But it doesn’t mean we can’t make progress on it, and I think that’s really true in this case.
CB: Great. One final question from my end, if I may. What’s an outcome that you’re going to be looking for at the end of this COP, that you’re going to be happy to take home to the UK?

EM: I think the most important thing is action to drive forward the climate agenda, and that’s what I want to see. You know, it goes back to the point about the cost. Some of it is about the formal decision-making, but a lot of it is about the real, tangible outcomes that have happened over a couple of weeks.

And if I think about what I’ve done here, you know, if we can get methane and the importance of methane – which, as you know, and as your viewers will know – is such an important short-term difference we can make in terms of preventing the rise in temperatures, and we can get that onto the agenda of the COP. If we can show progress on other aspects of the real economy – what’s happening in the real economy – all of those things are going to be important.

I think there’s something else, though, which is, these events of countries coming together. They contradict those people who say, you know, people are giving up on climate. Because you’ve got more than 190 countries that are coming together [at the COP], reaffirming their belief in the Paris Agreement, reaffirming their belief that they need to make efforts, as part of the Paris Agreement, to meet the climate goals – and working together on these issues.
It doesn’t mean they aren’t hard, but it does show that there is really important global commitment, which I’ve been hearing, to this agenda.
This interview was conducted by Dr Simon Evans at the COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, on 12 November 2026. Filming by Josh Gabbatiss and Daisy Dunne, with editing by Joe Goodman.

articles.title: Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31
articles.standfirst:
The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in…
The post Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31  appeared first on Carbon Brief.
paragraphs: The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in 2026, according to Carbon Brief analysis.
Developed countries are required under UN climate treaties to provide “climate finance” and have traditionally announced multi-year pledges to feed into their global commitments.
Most of these pledges expired in 2025 and, since then, the US has withdrawn from international climate efforts and many European aid budgets have been cut.
A civil-society tracker shows that only six nations have announced new multi-year pledges, including just one major donor – the UK.
Germany, France and Japan are among the key contributors that have so far failed to set out plans for new climate finance, while none is expected from the US.
As a result, the total amount of public climate finance pledged over the next few years amounts to just $11.7bn a year in spending, down from recent levels of around $40bn.
Experts tell Carbon Brief that global conflict, fiscal constraints and the rise of the far right are all making it harder for developed-country governments to pledge new funds.
As the COP31 summit in Turkey gets underway, developing countries are stressing their urgent need for new finance, after nations agreed to a new global target just two years ago.
Under the Paris Agreement, developed countries are obliged to provide climate finance to help developing countries cut their emissions and prepare for climate disasters.
This financial assistance can be channelled through multilateral development banks, UN climate funds and investments “mobilised” from the private sector.

But a large chunk is also expected to come directly from the public coffers of developed countries – primarily their foreign-aid budgets. This public spending has made up roughly a third of climate finance flowing to developing countries in recent years.
The EU, the US and others agreed just two years ago that they would “take the lead” on scaling up annual climate finance from $100bn in the early 2020s to $300bn by 2035.
Donor countries have traditionally supported such goals by announcing multi-year targets that indicate how much they plan to spend on climate finance.
Nearly all of these pledges expired in 2025 – and hardly any major donors have announced new ones to replace them, covering the period out to 2030.
This lack of new commitments is captured in a tracker of old and new financial commitments by climate NGOs NRDC and E3G.
Carbon Brief analysis of this data, based on an annualised breakdown of targets, shows that developed countries had previously pledged around £42bn a year in public finance.
As the chart below shows, based on current pledges, this has fallen by around 71% to £11.8bn, on average, over the remainder of the 2020s.
Not all contributors announced public climate-finance pledges in advance for the pre-2026 period. Some did not hit their stated targets, while others exceeded them.
While official data for 2025 is not yet available, bilateral public finance reached £43.9bn in 2024, broadly in line with the amount pledged by developed countries.
International climate finance has been consistently dominated by five nations – Japan, Germany, France, the US and the UK.
These countries – together with the EU – have provided around 90% of all the bilateral, public climate finance going to developing countries in recent years.
Of these key players, only the UK has announced a new pledge, committing £6bn ($8bn) of aid between 2026-27 and 2028-29, plus £6.7bn ($8.9bn) from outside its aid budget.
This accounts for half of all the annual funds pledged from 2026 onwards – averaging $5.7bn a year.
The European Commission makes up most of the remainder, with an average annual contribution of $4.5bn promised out to 2027.

Rather than a new pledge, this is due to the commission promising to spend €28bn ($31.8bn) over its 2021-2027 budget period. Its post-2027 contribution is currently being discussed as part of wider EU budget negotiations.
Canada has promised to spend CA$5.3bn ($4.1bn) by 2030, averaging $860m a year. The Netherlands, Switzerland, Belgium and Luxembourg have also pledged relatively small sums.

Overall, despite developed countries committing to scale up climate finance, these new pledges are either less ambitious – or only slightly more ambitious – than previous ones. This can be seen in the chart below.

The UK’s pledge appears more ambitious, but this is because the government has changed how it counts climate finance to include $8.9bn in “additional” public finance. When only the like-for-like aid components are compared, the new pledge amounts to a drop in ambition. (For more details, see the methodology.)
The most significant absence is the US, which committed to reaching $11.4bn in annual support by 2024 under the Biden administration.

Since president Donald Trump took power, the US has – for the second time – withdrawn from the Paris Agreement and shrunk its aid budget. It will not provide any official climate finance in the coming years.
Another notable absence is Australia, which is jointly hosting the upcoming COP31 summit, alongside Turkey. Josie Lee, policy and advocacy lead at Oxfam Australia, tells Carbon Brief:

“If Australia fails to announce a climate-finance pledge as president of negotiations, it would send a problematic message to those resisting action on climate change that might serve to embolden their agenda.”

Japan is the largest overall contributor of public climate finance, but it has not traditionally announced targets for this type of spending. Instead, the government set out overall goals that also bundle in finance “mobilised” from the private sector.
As a result, its public-finance ambitions have not been included in this analysis.
So far, the Japanese government has not announced any new multi-year climate-finance pledges, from either the public or the private sector.
Europe provides the majority of international climate finance, but European governments have massively cut their aid spending in recent years, citing economic strain and defence spending needs.
Germany and France, the two largest European climate-finance contributors, both pledged to reach €6bn ($6.8bn) per year by 2025. Neither has committed to anything beyond that.
Both nations have slashed their aid budgets in recent years, including funding for climate programmes. Germany missed its 2025 climate-finance goal due to these cuts.

Dr Anja Carolin Gebel, a senior policy advisor at Germanwatch, tells Carbon Brief that this issue has become more politically fraught since the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) won the 2025 election and began leading a coalition government:
“The issue of climate change – and, subsequently, climate finance – has taken a back seat in the current government coalition.”
There has also been a political shift in France, Gaïa Febvre, international policy coordinator at Réseau Action Climat, tells Carbon Brief. She adds:
“The upcoming presidential election and the growing influence of the far right are likely to make new international financial commitments politically more difficult.”
Other significant European donors are also undergoing political turmoil.
Spain’s centre-left government has triggered a snap election for the end of November, making a new climate-finance pledge during COP31 less likely.
Following a narrow election win, a centre-left bloc in Sweden is still in the process of trying to form a new coalition government.
Some nations have signalled that their climate finance will continue flowing, even though they have not officially set out specific new pledges.

The Dutch government, for example, has said it will provide “at least” €300m ($334m) of specific climate funding annually out to 2031. However, it has also indicated that its total public climate finance is likely to be considerably higher in both 2026 and 2027.

To highlight the lack of new pledges, developing countries are championing a “climate-finance work programme” at COP31, which could provide a space to discuss scaling up public climate finance from developed countries.

In response, the EU has stressed that its member states are the “largest providers” of public climate finance and called on developing countries to submit overdue plans for cutting emissions. The EU and its member states provided a record €32.3bn ($40bn) in 2025.
Against this backdrop, EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra recently told Bloomberg that “any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water”.

Joe Thwaites, international climate finance director at NRDC, who runs the commitment tracker, tells Carbon Brief that “developed countries would be wise to show how they are continuing to lead on climate finance”. He says:

“The lack of new announcements is making the finance negotiations tougher than they need to be. The debate around the climate-finance work programme is arising because developing countries have little clarity about how much public climate finance there will be in coming years.”
Update: This piece has been updated to include a pledge for the 2026-2030 period from Luxembourg.
This analysis is based on the climate-finance commitments tracker, run by the NGOs NRDC and E3G, supplemented with additional research.

Only the 23 “developed” countries that are obliged to provide climate finance are considered in this analysis, plus the EU. This includes western Europe, the US, Australia, Canada and New Zealand. Japan and Norway both provide substantial sums of climate finance, but have not announced specific public-finance pledges and therefore are not included.

Carbon Brief converted multi-year pledges into single years, with 2025 used as the baseline “pre-2026” year. Some countries committed to reaching a certain amount “by 2025”, in which case that value is used. Others said they would provide a total amount over several years, in which case the average value per year is used. Belgium, Switzerland and the US only set initial targets as far as 2024, so their 2024 values were used instead of 2025.

These values were compared with the average annual contribution for the remainder of the 2020s, based on the new pledges from the UK, Canada, Belgium, Switzerland and the Netherlands. Some climate finance has been committed by the Netherlands, but this is not expected to be its total contribution. The EU, Portugal and Greece have earlier pledges that extend into the latter half of the 2020s, although the latter two make very small contributions.

NRDC and E3G include all the UK’s newly pledged public finance in their tracker, including $8.9bn in “additional” public finance, which covers “equity, debt, guarantees, insurance and export credit” to mobilise private finance.

In previous Carbon Brief analysis comparing the UK’s new climate-finance target to its old one, this funding was not included. This is because the government did not previously count these funds towards its climate-finance goals, instead focusing exclusively on aid spending.

This analysis does not include pledges that some countries, including Germany and France, have made to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF). However, these pledges would not substantially change the main finding, shifting the overall reduction from 71% to 70%.

articles.title: Clean and secure: India–EU–UK cooperation is key to building diversified cleantech supply chains
articles.standfirst:
The week before COP31, the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit (BRES) in Delhi demonstrated India’s ambition and action on clean energy, and the opportunities for partners such as the EU and UK. The message is clear: India, the EU and UK are well positioned for deeper cleantech cooperation. Brand new trade agreements offer a foundation for […]
The post Clean and secure: India–EU–UK cooperation is key to building diversified cleantech supply chains appeared first on E3G.
paragraphs: The week before COP31, the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit (BRES) in Delhi demonstrated India’s ambition and action on clean energy, and the opportunities for partners such as the EU and UK. The message is clear: India, the EU and UK are well positioned for deeper cleantech cooperation. Brand new trade agreements offer a foundation for discussions about how market access can be turned into investible projects. The partners have complementary strengths across five key cleantech value chains, where collaboration can build domestic manufacturing capacity in India and diversify sourcing and markets for the EU and UK. Deeper India–EU–UK clean energy dependencies would therefore mean benefits for both industrial competitiveness and energy security for all partners.

With disruptions in West Asia again exposing the cost of relying on concentrated and vulnerable fossil fuel supplies, securing reliable, affordable renewable energy is increasingly inseparable from economic resilience and industrial competitiveness for India, the EU and the UK alike. Recent comments from Indian Prime Minister Modi reflected this shift, when he stated that: “Energy security is directly linked to economic security. And we all know that the future of energy security lies in clean energy. If we continue to remain excessively dependent on fossil fuels, the global economy will continue to face repeated disruptions.”

This is not just rhetoric. The IEA estimates that renewables avoided more than $100 billion in coal and gas import costs for India between 2011 and 2025, with cumulative savings projected to more than double by 2030. India has now surpassed 300 gigawatts (GW) of renewable capacity, reached over 50% non-fossil installed capacity five years ahead of the target in its 2030 climate action plan (NDC), and become the world’s second-largest solar module manufacturer. The direction of travel is even more ambitious, with a vision of achieving around 2000 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2047.

India can build on its trade agreement discussions with the EU and UK to cooperate on developing cleantech value chains, with benefits for all partners. There is considerable untapped potential; in 2024, bilateral trade between India and the EU accounted for just 1% of their respective imports of solar PV modules, wind generators and lithium-ion batteries.

This cooperation should focus on specific value chains where combining the partners’ respective capabilities can improve competitiveness and supply chain resilience. Discussion at a recent roundtable convened by the International Solar Alliance (ISA), Dalberg and E3G identified opportunities across five cleantech value chains that are particularly critical to delivering a clean, resilient power system (see table below).

India’s expanding manufacturing base, engineering capabilities, competitive costs and a large growing domestic market complement EU and UK strengths in research, innovation, industrial expertise and investment. For India, these partnerships can strengthen domestic manufacturing and improve access to advanced technology. For the EU and UK, deeper partnerships with India offer opportunities to diversify sourcing and expand markets for technology, equipment and investment.

The timing is right, with new trade agreements to build on. The India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) has been in force since July 2026; the India–EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) is expected to be signed in December 2026 and enter into force in early 2027.
Turning market access into investible projects however requires immediate practical action. The discussion at our roundtable identified key priorities for how to advance delivery:
India–EU–UK cooperation can build competitive clean tech industries, diversify supply chains and widen access to affordable clean technologies across the Global South.

Clean electrification offers a shared agenda connecting energy security, industrial competitiveness, and emissions reduction. Existing partnerships, including through the International Solar Alliance (ISA), provide routes for delivery while engagements with diplomatic initiatives such as the Global Energy Transition Forum, and the Global Clean Power Alliance could open further opportunities. The challenge now is to turn shared interests and trade frameworks into commercially viable partnerships at pace and scale delivering investment, competitive manufacturing, skilled jobs and reliable clean energy across all three economies and beyond.

The post Biggest YEP Awards ever showcase energy’s top talent appeared first on Energy UK.
paragraphs: The brightest up-and-coming talent of the energy industry has been celebrated once again at the Energy UK Young Energy Professionals (YEP) Forum’s annual awards ceremony.

The YEP Awards spotlight excellence among UK energy professionals with up to ten years of experience in the industry. The 2026 event, hosted by award-winning magician Pete Heat, attracted the most nominations in the ceremony’s twelve-year history.
The evening brought together industry leaders and political figures to celebrate the YEPs, including Minister for Energy Michael Shanks MP who delivered a keynote speech to almost 300 attendees.
Julian Leslie FREng FIET, Director of Strategic Energy Planning and Chief Engineer at National Energy System Operator (NESO), also took to the stage before getting the awards underway.
Rising Star, judged by Titi Oliyide CEng MIET, Senior Consultant, Energy Advisory and Projects, Lloyd’s Register and in partnership with Engage Consulting:
Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Focus, judged by Rob Salter-Church, Director of Regulation, National Grid Electricity Transmission (NGET) and in partnership with SGN:
Customer Champion, judged by Paul Spence, Independent Chair, Vulnerability Commitment and in partnership with Centrica:
Communications and Engagement, judged by Bob Roberts, Director of Communications, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero:
STEM Trailblazer, judged by Aadil Qureshi, Co-Founder and CEO, Heat Geek and in partnership with SSE:
Team of the Year, judged by Ben Parsons, Partner, Oaklin and in partnership with NESO:
Supply Chain Innovator, judged by Marisa Steyn, Partner, Gardiner & Theobald and in partnership with Waterstons:
Audrey Gallacher Award for Excellence, judged by Laura Sandys CBE, Chair, Green Alliance and Energy Digitalisation Taskforce:
YEP of the Year, judged by Dhara Vyas, Chief Executive Officer, Energy UK and in partnership with RWE:

“2026 marks our biggest YEP Awards ever. The calibre and volume of nominations this year highlights some of the exceptional people making an impact that drives the energy industry forward at every level.
“The event is always an inspiring moment to celebrate the incredible talent, ideas and dedication of the people who will continue to shape and lead our industry for years to come.

“The energy industry is creating jobs, driving investment and powering economic growth across the country, and the YEP Forum plays a great role in helping early career colleagues to connect, develop and flourish.”
Energy UK would also like to extend a big thank you to NESO for continuing to sponsor the YEP Forum for a third year into 2027, as well as all other sponsors of the YEP awards.
Kayte O’Neill, Chief Operating Officer at NESO and NESO YEP Forum Executive Sponsor, said:
