The post Securing Tomorrow: Growth, resilience and UK-EU cooperation appeared first on Energy UK.
paragraphs: The UK and EU share a common energy challenge: delivering secure, affordable and clean energy in an increasingly uncertain world.
This report sets out how closer cooperation on electricity markets, carbon pricing and North Sea development can strengthen energy security, cut costs and support economic growth.
To request this report in an alternative format, email [email protected].

Separating the UK and EU electricity markets has cost consumers over €500m, and explicit trading is inefficient up to 25% of the time. Recoupling markets would cut those costs and make hybrid interconnectors like Nautilus and LionLink viable.
Without a CBAM exemption pathway for GB electricity, EU imports from GB could fall by over 50%. That would add up to €4.6bn a year to EU consumer costs and up to 2.4MtCO₂ in annual emissions.

Nine NSEC countries have committed to 120GW of offshore wind by 2030 and 300GW by 2050. The UK could provide over 40% of 2030 capacity, but current projections fall short of the targets without closer coordination.

In recent years, continental prices in Belgium, Denmark, France or the Netherlands topped €200/MWh, GB prices stayed below that 74% of the time. On tight winter days, more imports displaced expensive gas and eased price spikes. Europe still needs 318GW of cross-border capacity by 2040, almost double the 167GW projected for 2030, and the current pipeline falls short.

The UK needs full NSEC membership and recognition in the Industrial Accelerator Act’s Union origin framework from day one. Its Strategic Spatial Energy Plan should also be aligned with regional planning from the outset.

The UK and EU face a shared energy security challenge: how to build a clean, affordable, and resilient energy system in a world of growing geopolitical uncertainty, supply chain vulnerabilities and climate-related risks. Meeting this challenge will depend increasingly on cooperation, interconnected infrastructure and access to diverse sources of energy.

Current arrangements for trading electricity between Great Britain (GB) and continental Europe are inefficient and increasingly costly. The separation of UK and EU electricity markets following Brexit has cost British and European consumers over €500m.[1] As renewable generation and the North Sea take on a more strategic role in Europe’s electricity system these costs are likely to grow. Without closer cooperation, barriers to cross-border trading and developing shared infrastructure will constrain the efficient use of Europe’s energy resources.

This is particularly important in the North Sea, where the nine countries involved in the North Sea Energy Cooperation (NSEC), including the UK, have committed to 120GW of offshore wind by 2030 and 300GW by 2050. GB alone could account for more than 40% of North Sea offshore wind capacity by 2030. Realising this potential will require countries to plan and deliver infrastructure together, supported by electricity markets that enable power to flow efficiently across borders.

This paper identifies three priorities that should form part of a single strategic agenda: aligning carbon pricing arrangements, reintegrating UK and EU electricity markets, and coordinating the development of the North Sea. Together, these measures would strengthen energy security, unlock investment and help deliver a more affordable and resilient European energy system.

First, carbon pricing arrangements must support continued trade in low-carbon electricity between the UK and the EU. As discussions on linking emissions trading systems progress, it will be important to agree how GB electricity should be treated under the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), including a pathway towards exemption. Without this, analysis suggests that imports of clean GB electricity could fall by more than 50%, EU consumer costs could increase by up to €4.6 billion annually and carbon emissions could rise by up to 2.4MtCO₂ per year.[2]

Second, closer integration of UK and EU electricity markets would deliver significant benefits for consumers and the wider energy system. Recoupling markets reduces the costs of inefficient cross-border trading, strengthens the investment case for hybrid interconnectors such as Nautilus and LionLink, and creates opportunities for GB participation in European balancing platforms, capacity mechanisms and cross-border power purchase agreements.

Third, closer coordination on the North Sea on infrastructure, spatial planning and supply chains will be essential to realising the region’s full potential. This means ensuring that national plans are developed in a coordinated way, maximising opportunities for shared infrastructure and hybrid projects, and securing full UK membership in the NSEC and in the Industrial Accelerator Act’s Union origin framework from the outset.

The decisions taken today will shape Europe’s energy system for decades. Closer cooperation offers both the UK and EU an opportunity to strengthen energy security, unlock investment and reduce costs. The prize of integration is significant, and the cost of fragmentation is one neither side can afford.

A decade on from the UK’s referendum on EU membership, political arrangements have changed, but geography, physics and economics remain the same. The UK and EU remain linked by electricity interconnectors, shared offshore energy resources, critical supply chains, and similar climate ambitions. In an era defined by geopolitical uncertainty and growing energy security concerns, effective cooperation is more important than ever.

Recent shocks have reinforced this reality. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exposed Europe’s vulnerability to international fossil fuel markets, while recent conflict in the Middle East has highlighted the continued risk associated with dependence on internationally traded fuels. As a result, both the UK and the EU are increasingly pursuing electrification and low-carbon energy not only as a route to decarbonisation but also as a means of strengthening economic and energy security.

This is reshaping the nature of energy security. Historically, security centred on ensuring access to the fuels needed to generate electricity and meet demand. As the UK and Europe transition towards increasingly electrified, low-carbon energy systems, resilience will depend not only on reliable generation, but also on access to diverse energy sources, flexible resources and interconnected infrastructure. This allows countries to draw on one another’s resources when domestic supply is constrained, making the wider system more resilient to disruption. In this context, trusted international partnerships and closer UK-EU energy cooperation are becoming strategically essential.

Interconnection between European markets, particularly across the North Sea nations, is increasingly important to managing the variability of renewable generation and strengthening system resilience. Interconnectors act as ‘shock absorbers’, allowing electricity to flow from areas of surplus to areas of scarcity and giving countries access to a wider pool of generation. For example, combining wind generation in GB with nuclear generation in France can smooth fluctuations in output and reduce short-term variability in generation by up to 30%.[3]

The value of interconnection was also illustrated by the April 2025 Iberian blackout, where links with France and Morocco were critical to supporting the restoration of the electricity system. Cross-border flows provided access to essential system support, including black start capability, voltage, frequency and inertia control. As European electricity systems become more variable and decentralised, and risks to critical energy infrastructure grow, this contribution to system stability and security of supply will be paramount.

The economic case for greater interconnection is equally compelling. Cross-border electricity trades in the day-ahead market already account for 39.5% of EU and Norwegian electricity demand.[4] Analysis of the EU’s Ten-Year Network Development Plan (TYNDP 2024) estimates that by 2040, every €1 invested in expanding cross-border transmission capacity will reduce needed generation costs by more than €2 through access to increased flexibility.[5]

Delivering a resilient and integrated European power system by 2040 will require 318GW of cross-border capacity, almost double the 167GW projected by 2030. This means a further 151GW must be delivered during the 2030s at an estimated cost of at least €150 billion.[6] However, the current project pipeline falls significantly short of this ambition. Given the long lead times associated with planning, consenting and constructing major infrastructure, the window for making the investment decisions needed by 2035-40 is already closing.

The shortfall is also unevenly distributed, with eleven countries collectively representing almost 80% of EU electricity generation, projected to miss the EU’s 2030 interconnection target.[7] Crucially, some of the largest gaps are concentrated in key European electricity markets, including Germany, the Netherlands, France and the Republic of Ireland, which together represent almost 50% of EU GDP. [8] This risks leaving some of Europe’s most economically significant markets without the cross-border capacity needed to realise the full benefits of an integrated electricity system.

The challenge also includes the underutilisation of existing capacity. The Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators’ (ACER) 2025 Monitoring Report found that EU TSOs spent €4.3 billion managing 60TWh of grid congestion in 2024, equivalent to Austria’s entire annual electricity consumption.[9] Much of this congestion reflects insufficient cross-border and zonal electricity capacity. Despite the EU’s Clean Energy Package requirement for TSOs to make at least 70% of physical transmission capacity available for cross-zonal trade, core region TSOs made just 54% of physical transmission capacity available on the most congested lines in 2024, meaning Europe captured only 40% of the €580 million in potential welfare gains.

The UK has a critical role to play in addressing Europe’s growing interconnection gap and strengthening the resilience of its energy system. As a major player in offshore wind development, with significant potential to support the deployment of hybrid assets and integrated offshore infrastructure in the North Sea, the UK is central to realising the benefits of greater regional cooperation. The following sections examine the choices on carbon pricing, electricity market arrangements, infrastructure and supply chains that will determine whether the UK and EU can turn this shared opportunity into reality.

The North Sea is becoming the strategic centre of Europe’s future energy security, providing the clean power and cross-border flexibility that electrified economies will depend on. The nine NSEC countries, including the UK, have committed to reaching 120GW of offshore wind capacity by 2030 and at least 300GW by 2050, 100GW of which will be made up of joint projects like offshore hybrid assets.[10] These targets represent the backbone of Western Europe’s future decarbonised electricity system, underpinning the energy needs of more than 260 million people and industries that account for roughly 60% of Europe’s GDP.[11]

As part of the Hamburg Declaration, TSOs have committed to identifying 20GW of economically viable cross-border projects, including hybrid interconnectors by 2027. This represents almost one-sixth of the additional interconnection capacity needed to deliver an optimised European electricity system during the 2030s.[12]

The UK is already a leading player in the expansion of the North Sea energy system. Five new interconnector projects have been approved, including GB’s first two hybrid projects, Nautilus (1.4GW to Belgium) and LionLink (1.8GW to the Netherlands). Together, these will increase GB’s interconnector capacity with continental Europe by more than 6GW.

Despite rising costs, supply chain constraints and wider market pressures slowing offshore wind deployment in the EU, the UK remains Europe’s leading offshore wind market. Following the successful CfD Allocation Round 7 (AR7) in 2026, a record 8.4GW of capacity was secured, strengthening an already substantial project pipeline. The UK could therefore account for more than 40% of North Sea offshore wind capacity by 2030, supported by its national target of 43-50GW, the largest national target in the region.[13] Yet greater cooperation to unlock investment is essential: current projections suggest the North Sea will reach only 87GW by 2030 and 257GW by 2050, falling short of the NSEC targets.[14]

GB is currently a net importer of electricity from the EU. In the year to September 2025, interconnectors enabled imports of around 43TWh, equivalent to 13% of total supply, while 12TWh was exported.[15] However, this relationship is set to change, with GB set to become a net exporter by 2030, supplying European markets with low-cost, low-carbon electricity.[16] This gives the UK an increasingly important role in Europe’s efforts to secure affordable clean energy, strengthen energy security and support reindustrialisation.

The opportunity is significant for both sides. For GB, interconnection will allow surplus North Sea wind to reach European consumers, generating export revenues rather than being curtailed. Hybrid interconnectors offer potential to link multiple markets through an integrated North Sea network, improving resilience, flexibility and access to affordable energy. For the EU, GB’s growing renewable surplus can provide a source of clean power, displacing more expensive gas generation when continental supply is constrained. The North Sea is more than a location for offshore wind development: it is the infrastructure through which a more secure, affordable and interconnected European energy system can be built.

Realising the North Sea’s potential will require countries to plan infrastructure together rather than develop national strategies in isolation. The Hamburg Declaration recognises this, with a commitment to coordinate planning and permitting, strengthen supply chains and develop the workforce needed to deliver the region’s offshore ambitions.

The UK’s Strategic Spatial Energy Plan (SSEP) will therefore need to be developed in active dialogue with the national network plans of other North Sea countries and NSEC’s work on a coordinated offshore energy infrastructure plan. It is not yet clear how effectively these processes will align. The UK should ensure that its SSEP interfaces with the emerging regional planning framework from the outset, rather than seeking to reconcile national and regional plans at a later stage.

The benefits of interconnection are well established, but current trading arrangements between GB and continental Europe do not make the most efficient use of available capacity. Under explicit trading, electricity and interconnector capacity are bought and sold separately, based on forecasts of market prices. This means electricity does not always flow in the direction that market prices would indicate. Implicit trading, by contrast, allocates electricity and interconnector capacity together, allowing power to flow automatically towards markets where it is most valuable. This was the arrangement in GB before 2021 and remains standard across much of Europe. Energy UK analysis suggests that explicit trading creates inefficiencies up to 25% of the time.[17]

Scenario A: Consider a winter day when wind generation in GB is exceptionally weak and electricity demand is high. Gas generation must increase to meet demand, with the final units of generation often disproportionately increasing wholesale prices which regularly exceed £100/MWh. Efficient interconnection can help reduce these costs by allowing GB to access cheaper electricity from neighbouring markets, displacing the most expensive gas generation. As Figure 1 illustrates, during periods of high gas generation in recent years, increased imports have coincided with lower wholesale prices. More efficient trading could therefore help to narrow the £100/MWh gap between spot prices of £200/MWh and £300/MWh during these kinds of events, reducing volatility.
Figure 1: Gas and import proportions and spot price at maximum periods of gas generation on tight winter days[18]

Figure 2 shows a day of extremely low wind. Gas generation was high throughout, but the relationship between import levels and the wholesale price is evident. Increased imports displace the most expensive gas generation, reducing price pressures. On 20th January 2025, the evening spike in demand alongside reduced imports caused a huge spike in spot prices, where implicit trading may well have dampened the price spikes.

Scenario B: Consider the summer of 2022, when the French nuclear fleet was blighted by extended maintenance shutdowns,[20] and Norwegian hydro generation fell to the lowest level in a decade. This contributed to increased scarcity across continental markets connected to GB. As shown below, in Figure 3, Britain was able to increase its power generation and export much more, switching from a net importer to a net exporter of power for eight consecutive months.
Figure 3: Monthly data for Norwegian hydropower generation, French nuclear generation, and GB net imports[21]

In general, the correlation of stress events between GB and the interconnected continent is low. Looking at periods where prices in Belgium, Denmark, France, or the Netherlands exceeded €200/MWh since 2024, the price in GB was below €200/MWh 74% of the time.[22] With this in mind, efficient interconnection serves both sides. GB’s power system diverges enough from its interconnected neighbours to make it a real asset to be coupled with, acting as a buffer to high prices.

Furthermore, GB has different weather patterns and a different profile of electricity generation to interconnected nations on the continent. This diversity is a strength to all those who can tap into it. Figure 4 demonstrates how GB’s power system would contribute to this diversity. For example, GB greatly bolsters dispatchable capacity, increasing gas by 84% and biomass and waste by 118%. As Britain accelerates towards its Clean Power 2030 goal, the benefits to both sides only get stronger.
Figure 4: Capacity of power generation technologies in Belgium, Denmark, France, the Netherlands (Connected EU), with GB added[23]

The costs of fragmented trading are not limited to periods of system stress. Analysis has shown that consumers in GB and the EU lost an estimated €500m in the first three years following decoupling.[24] Interconnector operators also stand to lose more than €1bn in congestion income, weakening the commercial case for future investment.

Offshore Hybrid Assets (also known as multipurpose interconnectors) are interconnectors that connect offshore wind farms to multiple countries. Through combining generation and transmission assets, these projects are cheaper than conventionally building them separately. However, developers have stated that without market coupling they cannot be operated effectively.[25] Future projects will likely be delayed, not connect to GB, or not go ahead at all as a result, increasing the cost of meeting the Ostend Declaration target of 300GW of offshore wind by 2050 by £13bn.[26]

The scenarios above illustrate the cost of fragmentation during periods of system stress. However, the cost is not confined to periods of crises, and market fragmentation is imposing a daily economic penalty and weakening the investment case for the cross-border infrastructure Europe needs to secure its energy future.

Beyond more efficient cross-border trading, closer market integration could enable greater coordination of balancing services, allowing GB and EU operators to share flexibility and access a wider pool of reserves. It would also provide a stronger basis for coordinating cross-border capacity and adequacy. As electricity systems become more interconnected and the challenge of managing volatility grows. these arrangements are increasingly important. Yet GB’s exclusion from the IEM makes coordination more complex. GB assets could make a greater contribution to European adequacy and system management, but this requires closer alignment of market arrangements and operational frameworks. In particular, regulators on both sides currently lack a common framework for coordinating restrictions on cross-border flow during periods of system stress.

Closer market integration could also create new commercial opportunities including cross-border power purchase agreements (PPAs) between GB generators and EU industrial consumers seeking long-term access to clean electricity and greater price certainty, which remain limited between GB and EU markets. Without market coupling, day-ahead prices are determined through separate auctions, while cross-border capacity is not allocated through a single, integrated process. This creates additional uncertainty for generators and buyers seeking to manage price and delivery risks, constraining the development of cross-border contracts at scale. Market coupling could help to address these barriers alongside greater regulatory alignment on Guarantees of Origin (GOOs), Renewable Energy Guarantees of Origin (REGOs), balancing arrangements and relevant contractual arrangements.

The cost of market fragmentation extends beyond electricity trading. Differences in carbon pricing arrangements, and how these are recognised at the border, risk creating a further barrier to cross-border trade just as the UK and EU seek to deepen their energy relationship. The evidence points to a clear risk that CBAM could make cross-border electricity trade more expensive, reduce flows of clean electricity from GB and weaken the investment case for future interconnection. The consequences would extend beyond the immediate cost to consumers, undermining the wider benefits of an integrated North Sea energy system.

Afry’s 2024 impact study highlights the scale of the potential costs.[27] Its modelling projects that EU electricity imports from GB could fall by more than 50% once CBAM costs take effect in 2027, rising to over 85% by 2040. This would represent a loss of 53TWh of clean electricity annually, equivalent to Denmark’s entire electricity demand. EU consumers could also face annual wholesale electricity cost increases of €2.3 to €4.6 billion, including €740 million in Germany, €524 million in France and €344 million in the Netherlands. The impact on future investment could be equally significant. Annual congestion rents, an important source of revenue underpinning the business case for interconnectors and hybrid assets, could fall by 50% to 90% across all GB-connected borders. Afry estimates this could undermine the business case for future interconnector projects by €75 million and €170 million per GW in a single year.

The consequences would extend beyond electricity costs and investment. A study by the London School of Economics suggests that applying CBAM to electricity imports from GB risks reducing UK renewable electricity exports to the EU by up to 164 GWh in a single year.[28] Conversely, avoiding CBAM charges on electricity from GB could prevent the EU from needing to import an additional €2bn in gas imports annually, as increased fossil fuel generation would otherwise compensate for reduced renewable imports from the UK.[29]

The climate consequences are equally counterproductive. The studies project that total carbon emissions across the EU and GB increase by 1.5 to 2.4 MtCO₂ annually in the initial years following CBAM implementation, equivalent to the annual emissions of up to 8.3 million cars. This reflects increased curtailment of GB renewable generation, alongside greater gas and coal generation in the EU to compensate for reduced imports.

There is an opportunity for the UK and EU to address this as part of an agreement on ETS linkage. Recognising the equivalent carbon costs already faced by GB electricity generators would help avoid additional charges on electricity traded across the Channel, protecting consumers and industry on both sides. The two parties should ensure that the benefits of ETS linkage are reflected in the treatment of electricity under CBAM from the outset, rather than leaving cross-border trade exposed to unnecessary costs during implementation. This would be a practical near-term win for both sides, supporting clean electricity flows, reducing costs and preserving the investment case for the interconnectors and offshore infrastructure needed to strengthen Europe’s energy security.

A competitive European energy system will also depend on the strength of the industrial capabilities and supply chains that underpin it. Offshore wind already supports tens of thousands of jobs, with the Hamburg Declaration providing a platform for further growth across manufacturing, ports, engineering and specialist supply chains. The UK’s Clean Energy Industries Sector Plan, the subsequent Electricity Network Sector Growth Plan and Great British Energy’s £300 million Supply Chain Fund collectively demonstrate a growing commitment to strengthening domestic supply chains, coordinating infrastructure investment and addressing critical manufacturing bottlenecks. Importantly, the Sector Plan also recognises the value of alignment with EU processes. [30]

But these supply chains are European and the same manufacturers, installation vessels and specialist engineering firms serve projects across the North Sea. National procurement frameworks, such as Ofgem’s Advanced Procurement Mechanism and emerging EU initiatives should therefore be designed to support coordination and interoperability across borders.[31] Exploring joint procurement of critical, supply-constrained components through the North Sea Energy Cooperation (NSEC) should be a practical near-term priority. Better coordination of demand would help secure manufacturing capacity, achieve economies of scale and reduce the risk of countries competing against one another for limited supplies, driving up costs and delaying delivery.

A more immediate risk to this integrated supply chain comes from the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), currently progressing through the EU legislative process. Its Union origin framework, which determines which manufactured components qualify for EU support schemes and public procurement, has become increasingly restrictive through successive drafts. The European Parliament’s draft report proposes that Union origin requirements for low-carbon technology support schemes should apply by default only to EU27 manufacturers, with the inclusion of third countries subject to a delegated act and seven conditionality criteria.

The UK’s status under the IAA has been left to be resolved during the remaining legislative negotiations. For the UK’s offshore wind sector, which is an important part of the wider North Sea supply chain, this creates material uncertainty. Under the proposals as currently drafted, UK-manufactured components could be excluded from EU support schemes, including Contracts for Difference (CfDs), unless the UK secures qualifying third-country status. This risks the creation of barriers within supply chains that are already deeply integrated across the region.

The Commission would have powers under the current proposal to extend the list of eligible countries, and the UK is understood to be well placed to secure inclusion. However, providing clarity from the outset would offer greater certainty for manufacturers and investors on both sides of the Channel. The UK and EU should therefore work towards an agreed arrangement that recognises UK-manufactured components in the Union origin from the Act’s entry into force. This would reflect the deeply integrated nature of their clean energy supply chains, support investment in manufacturing capacity across the region and give practical effect to their shared commitments under the Hamburg Declaration.

The UK and EU have a shared interest in building a more integrated, resilient and secure energy system. But realising this opportunity requires progress on several interconnected fronts: closer participation in the Internal Electricity Market, linkage of the Emissions Trading Systems, and an agreement on mutual recognition and CBAM treatment. These are not separate policy issues, but essential components of a wider strategic partnership.

The consequences of delay are increasingly tangible. Uncertainty over market arrangements and Offshore Bidding Zones continues to complicate the investment case for major projects in the North Sea, while creating risks for the integration of GB into planned European energy islands. Meanwhile, investment decisions that will shape the North Sea energy system of the 2030s and 2040s are being made now.

The window to act is short, and the frameworks being designed today will either enable closer UK-EU integration or make it structurally harder to achieve. The choice is between a coordinated North Sea energy system that delivers greater resilience, security and shared prosperity, and continued fragmentation that leaves both sides more exposed to future shocks. The question is no longer whether cooperation makes sense, but whether the political will exists to deliver it before the opportunity passes.

articles.title: Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31?
articles.standfirst:
More than 92,000 people have registered to attend the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, potentially making it the largest…
The post Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31? appeared first on Carbon Brief.
paragraphs: More than 92,000 people have registered to attend the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, potentially making it the largest COP in history.

Carbon Brief analysis of the provisional lists of delegates, published by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), reveals that more than 14,000 delegates have been registered as “host country guests”.
For comparison, the final list for COP30 in Belém, Brazil, last year included only around 1,300 delegates in this category.
As with COP30, Donald Trump’s US government has not sent a delegation. Other no-shows include Israel and Myanmar.

It was reported ahead of the summit that Taliban officials from Afghanistan had been registered for the event as observers; however, there are no delegates from observer states in the provisional lists.
With more than 3,000 “virtual” delegates signed up to attend the summit online, the total number of people registered for the event surpasses 95,000.
With 92,934 participants registered, COP31 is provisionally the largest COP in history – topping COP28 in Dubai, which was attended by more than 80,000 people.

This total is based on the delegates that have registered to be at the summit in person. The UNFCCC releases the final figures – based on participants collecting a physical badge at the venue – after the summit has ended.
The chart below shows how the provisional figures for COP31 compare to the final totals in previous COPs – going back to COP1 in Berlin in 1995.

The participant lists provided by the UNFCCC are divided between the different types of groups and organisations attending the summit. The largest group at COP31 is for delegates representing parties. These are nation-states, plus the European Union, that have ratified the convention and play a full part in negotiations.
This group adds up to 18,812 delegates – the second largest after COP28.

(In keeping with recent COPs, the UNFCCC has published spreadsheets that name every single person that has registered for the summit – excluding support staff. Previously, COPs have typically included thousands of “overflow” participants in which countries and UN agencies could nominate delegates without their names appearing on their official lists.)

For consistency with Carbon Brief’s analysis of previous COPs, the above chart includes overflow delegates as a single group. However, the participant lists do divide the overflow delegates between parties and observer groups. Including the overflow numbers takes the total for party representatives to more than 34,000.

Unusually, COP31 has a very large number of “host country guests”. This is a category that has only been included in the COP participant lists over the last few years. The provisional number for COP31 – 14,285 – far exceeds the final number of host guests at COP30 (1,324), COP29 (1,651) and COP28 (4,202).

The map and table below present the delegation size – split between party and overflow badges – for all the countries registered for COP31. The darker the shading, the more delegates that country has signed up.
Unsurprisingly, host nation Turkey has registered the largest delegation for COP31 – with 2,950 people.
Following behind are Brazil (1,994 people), Nigeria (1,506), China (1,021) and Indonesia (978).
The rest of the top 10 is made up of Australia (835), Uganda (627), Italy (607), Japan (588) and Kazakhstan (557).
The UK comes someway down the list with a delegation of 255.
The smallest delegation comes from North Korea (two), followed by Eritrea and Nicaragua (three) and San Marino and Trinidad and Tobago (four).
(It is worth noting that some countries – such as Brazil – allocate some of their party badges to NGOs, which can artificially inflate the size of their official delegation.)

The UNFCCC’s participant lists typically provide a title – such as Mr, Ms, Sr or Sra – for each registered delegate. In the past, this has allowed Carbon Brief to work out the balance of men to women in the delegations that each country has sent to a COP.

(This analysis always carries the caveat that the titles are designated by UNFCCC and not by Carbon Brief. In addition, Carbon Brief recognises that gender is not best categorised using a binary “man” or “woman” label and appreciates that the UNFCCC’s lists may not be wholly accurate.)
Overall, the COP31 provisional list suggests an average gender balance of party delegations of 59% men to 41% women.
As the chart below shows, COP31 is slightly less balanced than the last two COPs, but broadly continues a trend that has seen COP delegations become a more even split between men and women.

(Note: Since COP28, the UNFCCC has also used titles that do not indicate gender – such as Dr, Prof, Ambassador and Honourable. Therefore, for this analysis, these non-gendered titles – which make up 1.3% of party delegates at COP31, for example – have not been included.)
Including overflows, there are two delegations of only men at COP31 – Eritrea (three people) and North Korea (two). There are no delegations that are only women.
The full list of COP31 party delegation sizes can be found here.
(For previous COPs, see Carbon Brief’s delegate analysis for COP21, COP23, COP24, COP25, COP26, COP27, COP28, COP29 and COP30.)
After party delegates, observers of the negotiations are typically the next biggest group at COP summits.

These delegates receive their observer status through their not-for-profit organisation. This can be a UN body, a “specialised agency” – such as the World Bank or International Atomic Energy Agency, an intergovernmental organisation – such as OPEC or the Inter-American Development Bank – or an NGO.

The vast majority of observers at COP31 – more than 12,000 – are representing NGOs. These can include charities, such as WWF, 350.org and Amnesty International, as well as philanthropic organisations, such as the Rockefeller Foundation and the IKEA Foundation, and lobby groups, such as the International Gas Union and the UK’s National Farmers Union.
At COP30 last year, the UNFCCC registration process introduced the option for observers to disclose the “immediate source(s) of funding” for their participation.

Of the 12,413 NGO observers registered for COP31, 14% chose not to disclose funding. The most common funders were NGOs (56%) and academic or research institutions (12%). Around 8% declared funding from “private sector or business”.
In addition, observers were “invited to declare their participation's alignment with the objective of the convention and the goals and principles of the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement”.
Overall, 13,108 delegates selected “yes” for this section, with the remaining 2,247 delegates leaving the answer blank.

Finally, there are 3,645 media representatives registered to attend COP31 in person, which is provisionally the second-largest media group in COP history – behind COP3 in Kyoto, Japan, in 1997 (3,712).

The way that media organisations are described in the list is very inconsistent, which makes overall totals difficult to tally. Nonetheless, the Turkish Radio and Television Corporation (TRT) is comfortably the most-represented media group at COP31 with more than 200 delegates.
Other media outlets with at least a dozen participants include CNN, the Associated Press, Financial Times, Bloomberg, Agence France-Presse, Reuters and Sky News.
Update: This article was updated on 11/11/2026 to add further analysis on gender balance, observers and media at COP31.

articles.title: Analysis: Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use
articles.standfirst:
Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn…
The post Analysis: Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use appeared first on Carbon Brief.
paragraphs: Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 (GtCO2), according to new figures from the Global Carbon Project.

The 21st edition of the annual “global carbon budget” report, published today, says that this small decline is largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
The Global Carbon Project’s projections for fossil fuel and cement CO2 emissions in 2026 are preliminary, with a range that spans a fall of -1.5% to a rise of +0.6%.
This means a small increase in emissions can not be ruled out.
Emissions from land-use change, such as deforestation, are projected to rise in 2026.
This is primarily driven by peat fires and forest degradation in south-east Asia and is linked to the development of a strong El Niño event this year.
As a result, total CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and land use are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026 – marginally above 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.

Research published alongside the report by the same team in Nature Climate Change finds that the growth in solar, wind and electric vehicles (EVs) now offsets around two-thirds of the emissions that would otherwise come from rising energy demand.
However, the deployment of these technologies is not yet enough to push global emissions into a sustained decline, according to the study.
(For more on previous editions of the Global Carbon Project’s annual report, see Carbon Brief’s coverage in 2025, 2024, 2023 and 2022.)
Total global CO2 emissions, which combines fossil fuels and land-use change, are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026, up from 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.
The increase in 2026 comes entirely from a projected rise in land-use emissions, which are more challenging to estimate than fossil emissions.
(The global carbon budget groups emissions from fossil fuels and cement production as “fossil emissions”. Carbon Brief follows this convention throughout this piece.)
If land-use emissions had stayed at 2025 levels, total emissions would have fallen slightly in 2026 to around 42.6GtCO2.

Each edition of the global carbon budget updates the historical record as new data and methods become available. The chart below shows total emissions in this year’s budget compared with the five previous editions.
This year’s estimates of historical fossil emissions are around 0.3GtCO2 per year higher than in last year’s budget.

This is largely because the report now estimates a smaller “cement carbonation” sink in the wake of research published this year in Communications Sustainability. In other words, it estimates that cement is able to slowly reabsorb less CO2 over its lifetime than previously thought.
Estimates of land-use emissions have also been revised, including a spike in 2018 – visible in the chart above – linked to updated cropland data for Colombia.
The updated numbers show that total emissions have grown by 0.3% per year over the past decade (2016-25), compared with 1.7% per year over 2006-15.
Fossil emissions grew about 0.9% per year in the past decade, compared with 1.9% the decade before. Over the same period, land-use emissions have declined.
While the slowdown reflects real progress, a plateau in emissions is still a long way from the rapid declines needed to reach net-zero emissions and stabilise global temperatures.

With human-caused warming reaching 1.37C above pre-industrial levels (1850-1900) in 2025, the report estimates that the remaining carbon budget to limit warming to 1.5C, with a 50% chance, is 150GtCO2 from the start of 2027. That is less than four years of 2026 emissions.
Meanwhile, the budgets for 1.7C and 2C are 510GtCO2 and 1,035GtCO2, respectively – or around 12 and 24 years of current emissions.
Fossil emissions made up around 88% of total CO2 emissions over the past decade, with land-use change making up the remaining 12%.
This is a marked change from the first half of the 20th century, when land-use emissions were larger than those from fossil fuels.
The figure below shows global emissions, split into fossil and land-use components.
Global per-capita fossil emissions peaked in the early 2010s and have since slightly declined. At around 4.6 tonnes per person in 2026, they are about 4% below that peak.
It is worth noting that this global average hides very large differences between countries. For example, 2025 per-capita emissions in India are only 2.2 tonnes, compared with 14.5 tonnes in the US.
Land-use emissions come from deforestation, forest degradation, wood harvest, peatland drainage and fires. They are partly offset by forest regrowth and new forests.

Net land-use emissions averaged 4.9GtCO2 per year over 2016-25, down from 6.2GtCO2 per year over 2006-15, marking a decline of around 21%. This decline holds across all three of the “bookkeeping” models used by the Global Carbon Project to track land-use emissions.
(For more on trends in global land-use emissions and how they are calculated, see Carbon Brief’s explainer.)
Land-use emissions are projected to rise to 5.1GtCO2 in 2026, up from 4.4GtCO2 in 2025.
The report attributes the increase to peat fires, almost all ignited by people, and forest degradation in south-east Asia due to drier conditions associated with El Niño.
Uncertainties in land-use emissions are much higher than for fossil emissions given the challenges in tracking them.
While 2026 shows a nominal increase, it is only slightly above the average over the past decade.
Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Indonesia together accounted for 2.6GtCO2 of land-use emissions per year over 2015-25, or around 54% of the global total.
The figure below shows how land-use emissions for these three countries and the rest of the world have changed since 1960.

Global fossil CO2 emissions are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026. However, challenges associated with precisely measuring and projecting 2026 means this could end up anywhere between a 1.5% decline and a 0.6% increase.
The figure below provides a breakdown of fossil emissions over time by major country and region, including China, the US, the EU, India and the rest of the world.
The global carbon budget report sets out the following projections for 2026 in major economies:
The figure below shows how each country or region contributed to changes in global fossil emissions in each year between 2023 and 2026.
A growing number of countries are cutting emissions while growing their economies.

The report finds that 40 countries, together accounting for 26% of global fossil emissions, significantly reduced their emissions while their economies grew over 2016-25. This compares with 22 countries in the previous decade.
Coal accounts for around 41% of global fossil CO2 emissions in 2026, oil 33% and gas 21%. Cement accounts for around 2%, after the carbonation sink is subtracted.
Oil is the main driver of the decline in global fossil emissions in 2026. Oil emissions are projected to fall by 1.9% (with a range of -2.6% to -1.2%), or 243m tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2).

The left panel of the figure below shows that this is one of the largest annual falls in the record, with the exception of 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic. Other large declines occurred during the global financial crisis in 2009 and in the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1992.
The chart on the right shows how oil emissions are projected to fall in every major region in 2026.
The global carbon budget links most of the oil decline to higher prices and reductions in output after the Iran conflict resulted in the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
Petrol and diesel prices in the US, China and EU were 10-50% higher than in 2025, depending on the fuel and the period.
A study published in parallel by the team behind the global carbon budget reveals that growth in EVs accounted for around a fifth of the overall drop in oil emissions in 2026.
This is consistent with Carbon Brief analysis published in September that estimated that global fossil-fuel emissions were set to fall in 2026 amid the Hormuz crisis.
By contrast, coal emissions are projected to rise by 0.6% (-0.6% to +1.7%), with a strong increase in emissions in India partly offset by sharp falls in the EU and US.
Gas emissions, meanwhile, are projected to fall by 0.3% (-1.6% to +0.9%) – making them effectively flat.
Coal emissions grew rapidly in the 2000s, at around 4% per year, but have risen only slightly since 2013. Even with continued growth, 2026 coal emissions are only around 6% above their 2013 level.
Oil emissions remain about 1% above their pre-pandemic level in 2019.
The figure below shows the contribution of each fuel to the change in global emissions between 2023 and 2026.
The annual global carbon budget report tracks both the sources of CO2, from fossil fuels and land use, as well as the “sinks” that take it up: the ocean, the land and the atmosphere.
Over 2016-25, the ocean took up around 27% of total emissions, or 11.1GtCO2 per year, whereas the land around 22%, or 9.2GtCO2 per year. The remaining 48% accumulated in the atmosphere.
The figure below shows the sources of emissions (above zero) and where they end up (below zero) each year. The sum of the sinks is shown as a dashed line for comparison with total emissions.
The Global Carbon Project estimates that the land sink in 2025 was the highest on record, at around 13.3GtCO2 – 50% larger than in 2024.
This reflects a strong recovery in the tropics after the 2023-24 El Niño had suppressed the land sink, along with gradual growth of the sink associated with higher atmospheric CO2 concentrations.

The carbon budget does not always balance. In 2024, the estimated sinks exceeded the estimated sources by 6.7GtCO2, the largest “imbalance” on record. This partly offset an imbalance in the opposite direction in 2023 of 3.3GtCO2.

The report attributes much of the 2023-24 discrepancy to the timing of the atmospheric CO2 growth rate. The changes to the land carbon sink in the tropics driven by the El Niño of that year occurred late in the calendar year, so they straddle the 1 January boundary used to calculate annual growth.

A strong El Niño began in June 2026, but its effects on the carbon cycle are not yet visible, as changes in the carbon cycle lag several months behind changes in the climate. Consequently, the global carbon budget researchers expect the effect of the current El Niño to show up predominantly in 2027.

While natural sinks continue to absorb around half of human emissions, climate change is weakening them. The report estimates that the land and ocean sinks were 19% and 8% smaller, respectively, over 2016-25 than they would have been without the effects of climate change and natural fluctuations to the Earth’s climate.

Atmospheric CO2 is projected to rise by 2.2ppm in 2026, similar to the 2.1ppm rise in 2025 and well below the record 3.8ppm rise in 2024 during the last El Niño. CO2 concentrations are set to average 427.7ppm in 2026, roughly 54% above pre-industrial levels.
With global fossil emissions projected to fall in 2026, a natural follow-up question is whether they have now peaked.
The Nature Climate Change research suggests that the answer is not yet.
In the study, the researchers estimate the emissions “avoided” by solar and wind power and EVs, assuming that in their absence the same energy services would have been supplied by fossil fuels.

They then compare these “avoided emissions” with the emissions growth expected from rising economic activity and trends in the carbon intensity of the economy. The latter are described as “demand-driven emissions”.

This is illustrated in the figure below, which shows how increasing demand-driven emissions – which overwhelmingly come from rising energy demand – would have added around 0.78GtCO2 in 2026. However, growth in solar, wind and EVs offset 0.54GtCO2 – or about 69% – of this.
The rest of the decline in global fossil fuel emissions between 2025 and 2026 is attributed by the researchers mostly to high energy prices and supply constraints.

In other words, clean energy alone was not enough to cut emissions in 2026. The researchers’ central estimate suggests global emissions would have continued to rise had it not been for the energy shock from the Iran war.

The scale of avoided emissions is nonetheless large and growing quickly. The authors estimate that solar and wind avoided around 4.1GtCO2 in 2025 and project that they could avoid 4.6GtCO2 in 2026, up from 0.28GtCO2 in 2010. China accounts for around half of this.

Most of these avoided emissions are attributable to solar and wind. EVs avoided 0.19GtCO2 in 2025. The existing vehicle stock takes time to turn over. Currently, just 10% of the global car fleet has been electrified – a figure that drops to 6% if non-plug-in hybrid cars are excluded.
Without solar, wind and EVs, the study estimates that global fossil emissions would have grown by around 1.9% per year over 2019-25 – more than double the actual rate of 0.8% per year.
It also finds that the growth in data centres, driven largely by AI, added around 0.03GtCO2 in 2025, or about 2% of the “demand-driven” increase.
Looking ahead, the researchers explore how EV, solar, and wind might affect emissions in 2028 under two scenarios.
In the first, EV sales and solar and wind additions stay at 2026 levels. In the second, they continue to accelerate along recent trends.
As the figure below shows, rising demand for energy would add around 2.6GtCO2 between 2025 and 2028.
Clean technologies offset 63% of this in the current deployment scenario and 79% in the accelerated scenario. In both cases, overall emissions would still be higher in 2028 than in 2025.

There are important caveats to this approach. The authors note that the avoided-emissions method is a simplified counterfactual approach. It assumes that each unit of clean energy displaces fossil fuels one-for-one without incorporating potential rebound effects, such as the impact of falling clean energy costs on energy demand and fossil fuel costs.
The researchers conclude that the 2026 decline is “not a sign that emissions have peaked from the transition to cleaner energy”, but more likely a short-term response to higher oil prices.
However, the authors add that “if further acceleration of clean technology deployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away”.

Even then, a peak is only a first step. Limiting warming to well below 2C – let alone 1.5C, with a remaining budget of just three and a half years of current emissions – requires emissions to fall rapidly towards net-zero, not just stop rising.
Friedlingstein, P. et al. (2026) Global Carbon Budget 2026, Earth System Science Data, essd-2026-895.
Le Quéré, C. et al. (2026) A further acceleration of clean energy is needed for global CO2 emissions to peak and decline, Nature Climate Change, doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02821-8.

Un nuevo análisis de Carbon Tracker concluye que una adopción más rápida de vehículos eléctricos podría reducir la dependencia de Chile de las importaciones de petróleo y los costos de transporte, en momentos en que el país debate la siguiente fase de sus estándares de eficiencia vehicular.

Santiago, 10 de noviembre – Chile podría ahorrar aproximadamente US$27 mil millones en costos acumulados de importación de combustible hasta 2050 si acelera su transición desde vehículos a bencina y diésel hacia vehículos eléctricos a batería (BEV), según un nuevo informe del think tank financiero Carbon Tracker, publicado en asociación con el Centro de Movilidad Sostenible (CMS).

El informe, El salto a la electricidad: Los beneficios económicos de una política de promoción de vehículos eléctricos en Chile, concluye que seguir dependiendo de los vehículos con motor de combustión interna (ICE) encerraría al país en décadas adicionales de demanda de combustible y de exposición a la volatilidad de los precios internacionales del petróleo. Chile importa casi la totalidad de su petróleo crudo, y el transporte representa el 57% del consumo nacional de petróleo.

En un escenario sin cambios de políticas (business-as-usual), los costos acumulados de importación de combustible para el transporte terrestre podrían alcanzar casi US120 mil millones hasta 2050. Una transición acelerada hacia los vehículos eléctricos permitiría a Chile ahorrarse más de 27 mil millones en el mismo período. Hacia 2050, los costos anuales de importación de combustible para el transporte de Chile podrían reducirse hasta en un 56% mediante una transición acelerada hacia el transporte eléctrico terrestre, en comparación con un escenario sin cambios de políticas.

Los hallazgos se dan en momentos en que Chile implementa su Estrategia Nacional de Electromovilidad, actualizada en junio de 2026, que introdujo una meta de 20% de ventas de cero emisiones para vehículos livianos y medianos al año 2030. En la próxima sesión del Consejo de Ministros por la Sustentabilidad y el Cambio Climático, los ministros decidirán, antes de fin de año, sobre la Fase 2 de la Ley de Eficiencia Energética (Ley N° 21.305).

El informe pide mantener la Fase 2 de los estándares de eficiencia vehicular establecidos en la Ley de Eficiencia Energética de Chile, que debe entrar en vigencia en 2027. La siguiente fase eleva el rendimiento promedio exigido para los vehículos livianos nuevos de 18,8 a 22,8 kilómetros por litro de gasolina equivalente para el período 2027-2029.

La recomendación surge en medio de las inquietudes planteadas por representantes de la industria automotriz sobre el posible impacto de los estándares más estrictos en los precios y las ventas de vehículos. Carbon Tracker sostiene que mantener el calendario ayudaría a evitar que vehículos de combustión interna menos eficientes sean desviados hacia Chile a medida que otros mercados endurecen sus regulaciones, a la vez que incentivaría a los fabricantes a ofrecer más modelos eficientes y eléctricos.

A pesar de los avances de Chile en la electrificación del transporte público, en particular en Santiago, los vehículos eléctricos representaron solo alrededor del 3,5% de las ventas de vehículos livianos y medianos nuevos en los primeros siete meses de 2026.

Chile cuenta con importantes ventajas para acelerar la adopción. Casi dos tercios de su electricidad proviene de fuentes renovables, y su posición como uno de los principales productores de cobre y litio le otorga un papel estratégico en las cadenas de suministro globales de vehículos eléctricos.

El informe también concluye que, según sus supuestos de precios de combustible y de carga, operar un vehículo eléctrico cuesta aproximadamente un 50% menos por kilómetro que un auto a bencina y un 20% menos que uno a diésel. Una transición acelerada también podría generar cerca de US$493 millones en beneficios económicos acumulados asociados a la salud hasta 2050, gracias a la reducción de la contaminación del aire.
Ben Scott, autor del informe y Jefe de Demanda de Energía de Carbon Tracker, declaró:

“Cada vehículo nuevo a bencina o diésel que se vende hoy fija por años una demanda de combustible importado, dejando a Chile expuesto a los precios internacionales del petróleo. Mantener la Fase 2 de los estándares de eficiencia ayudaría a mejorar la eficiencia de los vehículos que ingresan al mercado chileno. La idea de que los estándares de eficiencia de la flota encarecen automáticamente todos los autos malinterpreta cómo funcionan estas regulaciones. A los fabricantes se les evalúa según la eficiencia promedio de los vehículos que venden, lo que les da flexibilidad para cumplir la meta ofreciendo modelos más eficientes y eléctricos, en lugar de exigir que todos los vehículos cumplan el mismo estándar.”

A partir de las experiencias de electrificación vehicular en economías emergentes como Etiopía, Nepal y Vietnam, el informe recomienda mantener la Fase 2 de los estándares de eficiencia vehicular vigentes en Chile, junto con regulaciones vinculantes del lado de la oferta para reducir progresivamente la venta de vehículos de combustión interna, incentivos fiscales focalizados para mejorar la asequibilidad de los BEV e inversión coordinada en infraestructura de carga, especialmente fuera de Santiago y a lo largo de los principales corredores de carga.

En conjunto, estas medidas podrían respaldar la transición de Chile hacia sus metas de ventas de vehículos de cero emisiones para 2035 y 2045, al tiempo que reducirían los costos futuros de importación de combustible y entregarían mayor certidumbre a inversionistas y proveedores de vehículos.
Leapfrog to Electric: Chile – Los beneficios económicos de las políticas a favor de los vehículos eléctricos en Chile ( partir del 10 de noviembre)
• El informe fue elaborado por Carbon Tracker en asociación con el Centro de Movilidad Sostenible (CMS).

• La cifra de US$27 mil millones representa el ahorro acumulado en importaciones de combustible hasta 2050 bajo el escenario de Transición Acelerada a BEV de Carbon Tracker, en comparación con un escenario sin cambios de políticas basado en las políticas existentes.
• El análisis abarca automóviles de pasajeros, buses y vehículos de carga medianos y pesados.

• El informe es el tercero de la serie Leapfrog to Electric de Carbon Tracker, que examina los beneficios económicos y financieros de acelerar la adopción de vehículos eléctricos en economías emergentes. Los informes anteriores se centraron en Brasil y Colombia, y estimaron ahorros acumulados potenciales en importaciones de combustible hasta 2050 de hasta US250 mil millones y aproximadamente US40 mil millones, respectivamente. En conjunto, los tres estudios muestran cómo los países de América Latina podrían reducir los costos económicos de la dependencia de combustibles importados para el transporte, y el papel que puede desempeñar la política pública para acelerar la electrificación.

• La Fase 2 de los estándares de eficiencia de vehículos livianos de Chile abarca el período 2027-2029, con una meta promedio de flota de 22,8 km/Lge, frente a 18,8 km/Lge durante 2024-2026. Estos estándares evalúan la eficiencia promedio de los vehículos en las ventas de un importador, en lugar de aplicar el mismo mínimo a cada modelo individual.

Despite progress in electrifying public transport, private EV adoption remains low, even as electric vehicles offer lower running costs and Chile’s electricity supply becomes increasingly renewable.

London, 10 November – Chile could save approximately US$27 billion in cumulative fuel import costs by 2050 through an accelerated transition to battery electric vehicles (BEVs), according to a new report from Carbon Tracker.

The research finds that continued reliance on petrol and diesel vehicles would leave Chile exposed to decades of additional fuel demand and international oil-price volatility. Chile imports almost all its crude oil, while transport accounts for 57% of national oil consumption.

Under a business-as-usual scenario, cumulative road transport fuel import costs could reach almost US$120 billion by 2050. An accelerated transition to BEV could also reduce Chile’s annual transport fuel import costs by as much as 56% in 2050, compared with business as usual, while avoiding approximately 600 million barrels of oil equivalent in cumulative fossil-fuel consumption.

The report, Leapfrog to Electric: Chile, also finds that BEVs cost approximately 50% less per kilometre to operate than petrol cars and 20% less than diesel cars, based on its fuel-price and charging assumptions. Reducing vehicle-related air pollution could generate a further US$493 million in cumulative health-related economic benefits by 2050.

Chile has several advantages that could support faster adoption. Almost two-thirds of its electricity comes from renewable sources, while its position as the world’s largest copper producer and second-largest lithium producer gives it an important role in global EV supply chains.

The country has also made considerable progress in electrifying public transport, particularly in Santiago. Yet BEVs accounted for only around 3.5% of new light- and medium-duty vehicle sales in the first seven months of 2026.
Ben Scott, report author and Head of Energy Demand at Carbon Tracker, said:

“Much of the discussion around electric vehicles focuses on their upfront cost. But governments also need to consider the long-term economic costs of every additional petrol or diesel vehicle sold, from imported fuel demand to the wider health and climate impacts. Chile has the renewable electricity resources and industrial advantages to move faster. The challenge is to create the market conditions that will allow more households and businesses to benefit from electrification.”

Chile’s National Electromobility Strategy, updated in June 2026, introduced an interim target of 20% zero-emission sales for light- and medium-duty vehicles by 2030, alongside its ambition to reach 100% by 2035. The Council of Ministers for Sustainability and Climate Change is expected to decide on Phase 2 of Chile’s vehicle efficiency standards before the end of 2026.

The report identifies maintaining Phase 2 of Chile’s Energy Efficiency Law as an immediate policy priority. Scheduled for 2027-2029, the next phase increases the average fuel efficiency standard for new light-duty vehicles from 18.8 to 22.8 kilometres per litre of gasoline equivalent.

Unlike a standard applied uniformly to individual vehicle models, the regulation assesses fleet-wide averages, giving manufacturers flexibility to meet the target through a mix of more efficient petrol, hybrid and electric vehicles. Automotive industry representatives have raised concerns about the potential impact of the tighter standards on vehicle prices and sales. Carbon Tracker argues that maintaining the timetable would help prevent less efficient ICE vehicles from being redirected to Chile as other markets strengthen their regulations, while encouraging manufacturers to supply more efficient and electric models.

Beyond maintaining existing standards, the report argues that achieving these targets will require stronger measures to accelerate adoption and encourage investment. Drawing on experiences in Ethiopia, Nepal and Vietnam, it recommends binding supply-side regulations to progressively phase down internal combustion engine vehicle sales, targeted fiscal incentives to improve BEV affordability, and coordinated investment in charging infrastructure, particularly outside Santiago and along major freight corridors.
These measures could help Chile reduce future fuel-import costs while supporting its energy security and climate objectives.
The Chile study is the third in Carbon Tracker’s Leapfrog to Electric series, which assesses the economic and financial benefits of accelerating vehicle electrification in emerging economies.
Earlier reports found that Brazil [LINK] could avoid up to US$250 billion in cumulative fuel import costs by 2050, while Colombia [LINK] could save approximately US$40 billion.

Together, the three studies point to a broader economic case for transport electrification across Latin America. Although Brazil, Colombia and Chile have different automotive markets and policy frameworks, reducing dependence on imported fuels and accelerating EV adoption through targeted government policies should be priorities across the region.
Leapfrog to Electric: Chile was published in association with Centro de Movilidad Sostenible (CMS).
Chile: Leapfrog to Electric: Chile – The Economic Benefits of Pro-Electric Vehicle Policy

The US$27 billion figure represents cumulative modelled fuel import savings to 2050 under Carbon Tracker’s Accelerated BEV Transition scenario, compared with a business-as-usual scenario based on existing policies.
The analysis covers passenger cars, buses, and medium- and heavy-duty vehicles.
Spokesperson: Ben Scott, Head of Energy Demand, Carbon Tracker.
