articles.title: Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?
articles.standfirst:
One of the key expected outcomes from the upcoming COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is the launch of a…
The post Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’?  appeared first on Carbon Brief.
paragraphs: One of the key expected outcomes from the upcoming COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is the launch of a “just transition mechanism”.
This follows years of calls from civil society to support a “just transition” as countries shift towards low-emissions energy systems and away from fossil fuels.
At the COP30 UN climate talks last year in the Brazilian city of Belém parties agreed to establish a “mechanism” to support this goal, called the “Belém-Antalya mechanism” (BAM).
Groups that have championed the BAM want it to act as a central hub on just transitions, providing support for workers and communities around the world.
However, the details of exactly what the much-touted BAM will consist of remain vague, with developed and developing countries disagreeing about its functions and purpose.
Disagreements continued at the UN climate talks in Bonn in June 2026, including on the crucial question of how the BAM will be financed.
Here, Carbon Brief looks at where the idea for the BAM came from, how it could support just transitions and what to expect from COP31.
A “just transition” is the idea that workers and communities should be supported in the shift to a low-carbon economy. It is a central principle behind the idea of climate justice.
Often, the term refers to those linked to the fossil-fuel industry, but it can also refer to transitions taking place in agriculture, heavy industry and various other sectors.
The concept originated in the 1980s, when US labour unions forged alliances with environmental justice groups. It has since become a key part of international climate discussions.

The preamble to the 2015 Paris Agreement includes a commitment to “tak[e] into account the imperatives of a just transition of the workforce and the creation of decent work and quality jobs in accordance with nationally defined development priorities”.
Bert De Wel, policy officer at the International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC), tells Carbon Brief:

“The labour movement is very happy with the wide audience and broad political support that the concept has received since its inception in the 1980s. The inclusion in the Paris Agreement, with the reference to the creation of decent work and quality jobs was a milestone for the movement. While other demands have been added…we continue to stress the labour dimension as being central to the concept.”
Three years after the creation of the Paris Agreement, at COP24 in the former coal-mining city of Katowice, the Polish presidency highlighted the issue of just transitions.

The need for carbon-cutting policies to ensure “a just transition of the workforce” that creates “decent work and quality jobs” was included in the “Silesia declaration”, issued by the presidency during the first week of COP24.
While the declaration was only signed by 50 countries – roughly a quarter of the parties at the summit – it was still “noted” in the final COP text.
This helped to drive momentum behind the idea, culminating in formal agreement at COP27 in Egypt to launch a “work programme on just transition” (JTWP).
De Wel says the establishment of the JTWP was a “major step forward” that allowed parties to “speak about just transition in more concrete terms”.
In the years since, negotiators have worked to flesh out the JTWP, with disagreements between parties about what its purpose should be.
Broadly, developed countries would like it to focus on domestic workforces, while some nations want a more global outlook, including support for transitions in developing countries.
The JTWP has proved a challenging negotiating space, with talks at the COP29 summit in 2024 closing without an agreement, in what one observer dubbed a “betrayal”.

However, despite these frustrations, parties at COP30 in Brazil agreed to establish a new institutional mechanism on just transitions, which has become widely known as the BAM. The move was hailed as a “victory” by civil society.
In the run-up to COP30, civil society began to push for the establishment of an “institutional arrangement” that would move work under the JTWP from talk into action.

(This was originally called the “Belém action mechanism” by civil society groups, who subsequently updated this to the “Belém-Antalya mechanism” following the outcome at COP30. However, in the JTWP text agreed at COP30 it is only described as a “mechanism”, sometimes also referred to as the “just transition mechanism”.)
Anabella Rosemberg, senior advisor on just transition at NGO umbrella group Climate Action Network (CAN) International, tells Carbon Brief:
“The idea of the mechanism emerged from the collaboration of civil society, trade unions, feminist groups, youth and Indigenous peoples in the UNFCCC.

“It was clear that the kind of activities being run under the JTWP – two dialogues a year and one ministerial – would not support the delivery of just-transition strategies on the ground, so a new approach was developed to get words into action.”
Following the inception of the idea, civil society did “tonnes of stuff to boost it up the agenda”, Dr Leon Sealey-Huggins, a senior campaigner at the charity War on Want, tells Carbon Brief.

This ranged from presenting demands and proposals to different constituents, organising joint letters and writing policy papers, all the way through to designing logos, creating memes and even a song.

These efforts ultimately paid off: during the Bonn climate negotiations in June 2025, one draft text included the idea for a new institutional arrangement. One of the options in the draft text was for a “toolbox, guidance framework, global platform, technical assistance network [or] mechanism”.
This inclusion was broadly welcomed as a “big win” for civil society groups, although parties acknowledged that more needed to be done to flesh out the idea.
Going into COP30, civil society groups continued to push the idea of creating a BAM, with protests, banners and badges visible around the venue.

Early in negotiations, the G77 and China – a large coalition of developing countries at UN climate talks – put forward their own proposal for a just transition “mechanism”. This, they suggested, could provide technical assistance, support international cooperation and help to foster partnerships in an effort to address implementation gaps.

Their proposal faced initial pushback from developed-country parties including Norway, the UK and others, who opposed it due to concerns that it would duplicate existing systems and require additional funding.

Developed countries also opposed the use of the term “mechanism”, with the EU suggesting an “action plan” as a potential alternative. Nevertheless, the creation of a “mechanism” was included in the final draft text on the JTWP.
This text was formally approved during the COP30 closing plenary to extended applause from many in the hall.
In a statement at the time, Chiara Martinelli, director at CAN Europe, welcomed the decision:
“Delivering BAM was a major civil society win. It creates a coordinated institutional home to drive forward progress on the just transition.”
The decision to develop the mechanism included a request for parties to work over the subsequent year – through to COP31 – on a plan to get things started.
According to civil society, the BAM could help tackle the fractured just-transition landscape by centralising resources and helping to overcome a number of barriers.
Speaking to Carbon Brief, Rosemberg says the just-transition space “lacks coordination and the right kind of support and is quite disconnected from climate action imperatives”. She adds:
“The BAM can play a role in bringing those [people] trying to make just transition happen together, identify gaps and barriers, foster cooperation and accelerate support.”

Civil society has put forward a number of proposals likely to inform the structure of the BAM. Most consist of a mechanism with three parts, which would encompass and expand upon the work that is currently being carried out under the JTWP.
One proposal by a coalition of five NGOs suggests the mechanism is formed of a steering body, a “knowledge arm” and an “implementation arm”.

The steering body would coordinate the work of the two arms of the BAM, including deciding the topics that should be discussed under the ongoing JTWP, which will continue to feature in climate negotiations. They suggest the body would recommend topics that require negotiation when “gaps that require political guidance are identified”.
Their proposal is illustrated in the infographic below, showing the steering body acting as a central hub for work within the BAM.
The final part of the BAM, the “implementation arm”, would act as a hub to enable and coordinate technical, financial and knowledge-based assistance for those pursuing a just transition.

Rosemberg says the vision of civil society is for work to go “beyond negotiators’ dialogues”. She says the BAM could enable the organisation of a “matchmaking platform” to provide support faster, as well as dedicated groups to identify and mobilise financial resources. She adds:

“Finally, through bottom-up identification of barriers, the BAM can also allow a discussion on enabling just transition that is informed by practitioners. The BAM can show that implementation does not necessarily mean taking issues outside of the UNFCCC.”

A separate proposal for the structure of the BAM from the Global Campaign to Demand Climate Justice (DCJ) – a separate coalition of NGOs – similarly proposes three elements. These would be: coordination and coherence; knowledge generation; and international cooperation and support.

“If it works in practice, what we’ll see is a cascade of just-transition policies implemented across countries, across sectors in a unifying, transformational moment for justice-centered climate action, and that will be the key to unlocking the transition that’s been missing so far.”

Another proposal for the BAM comes from the Grantham Institute at the London School of Economics. It suggests the three functions of the mechanism should be capacity-building, technical assistance and knowledge-sharing, but it recommends a dual-arm structure comprising a policy arm and an operational arm.
De Wel tells Carbon Brief that while there is “rather broad consensus on the functions”, parties are pushing in “very different directions” on how the BAM will be set up.
Within UN climate negotiations, some parties have raised concerns about the potential cost of the mechanism.

The push to launch the BAM comes at a time when the UNFCCC itself is facing a funding gap, following the US withdrawal. Several other parties have also delayed or reduced their contributions, in response to changes in domestic priorities.
This has led to the UNFCCC cancelling events and not filling vacated positions, as the organisation struggles to carry out its existing functions.

As such, some parties have expressed hesitancy about creating another mechanism under the remit of the UNFCCC, which also requires funding. However, proponents of the BAM argue that the costs of running it would be minimal.
Rosemberg tells Carbon Brief that the BAM represents “an opportunity to streamline and make efficient use of public resources”. She adds:
“The mechanism does not necessarily require the creation of a costly new institution. Instead, it can leverage existing climate-finance channels and philanthropy.”

She adds that a “similar body” to the potential mechanism, the Climate Technology Centre and Network, costs less than $10m a year. Rosemberg notes that this is “not an impossible amount to be found if there is political will to make just transition happen”.

De Wel notes that the mechanism will build on existing work inside the UNFCCC and out, including the International Labour Organization’s “just transition policy gateway”. He further emphasises that “we’re clearly not asking for a new [just-transition] fund, we want all climate finance to be just-transition proof”.

Alongside highlighting the potential efficiencies of the BAM design, many have argued that the potential benefits are well worth the cost of the new mechanism, with Sealey-Huggins telling Carbon Brief:
“The cost to the [BAM] secretariat pales in comparison to the potential benefit of the action.”
Despite the “victory” in Belém of agreeing to set up the new just-transition mechanism, climate negotiations in Bonn in June 2026 quickly hit sticking points.
While Bonn did ultimately agree on a “skeleton” draft text to send forward for further negotiations at COP31, many details still need to be agreed in Antalya for the BAM to start functioning.
De Wel cautions that a “swift approval of the agenda of COP31 allowing parties to start the negotiations” is “crucial”. He adds:

“We can’t lose any time, there is so much work that needs to be done on [just transition]. Then we need a constructive approach by the major country blocs. If one of them starts playing tactical games, then it will be lost.”

In a submission to the UNFCCC earlier this year, CAN called for a series of measures to get the BAM up and running. This includes calling for a decision to be made on a first face-to-face meeting of a “just-transition committee” – a core part of the mechanism in the group’s proposal – to be held in April 2027.

Ahead of COP31, negotiating groups such as the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the least developed countries (LDCs) and the African group expressed support for the mechanism and called for it to be focused on implementation.
The EU also supported the launch of the mechanism, but along with other parties cautioned that it should be complementary to the JTWP.

While no submissions opposed the creation of the mechanism, groups such as LDCs called for a focus on “means of implementation” – commonly understood as finance – highlighting it is likely to continue to be a key point of discussion in the upcoming summit.
Sealey-Huggins tells Carbon Brief what his “pie in the sky best-case scenario vision” for the outcome at COP31 would look like. He continues:

“G77 and China make the case again that the mechanism must be equally resourced. It must be well-designed. It must include people’s participation. It must address the barriers to implementation of just transition. It must facilitate the means of implementation. It must ensure justice at the very heart of climate action.
“And then it’s agreed and it’s implemented immediately. So this work begins straight after Antalya to start forming committees and other bodies that can undertake the implementation.”

However, Rosemberg cautions that there is still a “question mark [remaining over] the level of ambition of the [COP31] presidencies, who need to move from simply talking about establishing any [just-transition] mechanism to engaging parties, so that we get a mechanism that is fit for purpose”.

After Chairing Energy UK’s October Breakfast Briefing on heat networks, Lorenzo Wong of event partner Engage Consulting reflects on the sector’s recent progress, the economic challenges that remain, and why new funding models could be key to unlocking investment at scale. The post Heat networks: a landmark year, but a hard road ahead  appeared first on Energy UK.
paragraphs: After Chairing Energy UK’s October Breakfast Briefing on heat networks, Lorenzo Wong of event partner Engage Consulting reflects on the sector’s recent progress, the economic challenges that remain, and why new funding models could be key to unlocking investment at scale.
This article contains the views of our member organisation and does not necessarily reflect those of Energy UK.

It has been a landmark year or so for heat networks. The introduction of consumer regulation in January 2026 represented a major step towards providing heat network consumers with similar protections to other regulated utilities, a crucial intervention for winning back consumer confidence in light of recent, and ongoing, gas-induced price spikes. Meanwhile, the heat network zoning framework in England is moving towards implementation, with Scotland expected to follow. Zoning will be crucial for enabling large-scale projects to achieve the demand certainty needed to attract investment.

These policies are starting to translate into real-world progress. The Advanced Zoning Programme is moving some of the first prospective zones towards commercial delivery. At Energy UK’s recent Breakfast Briefing on heat networks (29 October 2026), HermeticaBlack highlighted signs of market maturity through increasing segmentation. Different organisations are beginning to specialise in the risks and activities best suited to their capabilities, from early-stage zone development through to “final-mile” heat provision for new developments, suggesting the sector will become easier to finance. Regulation is also supporting interest from institutional investors, indicating that a well-designed regulatory framework can strengthen investor confidence rather than undermine it through fear about pricing rules and restrictions on returns.
Whether policy intent translates into desired outcomes will soon be tested, with much hinging on how requirements to connect and exemptions operate in practice.

However, the picture is far from rosy. Revenue uncertainty and high capital and operational costs continue to hold back investment. Energy UK and the Heat Networks Industry Council (HeatNIC) have estimated that £5 billion of investment could be unlocked by 2030, but projects are unable to reach Final Investment Decision due to the lack of revenue certainty, part driven by the high cost of low-carbon heat. Energy UK and HeatNIC estimate that incumbent gas boilers remain around 50% cheaper for building managers to own and operate than connecting to a new low-carbon heat network.

This led to calls for an additional £1 billion of public investment to unlock private capital which was not committed to in the Autumn Budget. Overall cuts to Warm Homes Plan funding reduce future spending options, with clarity needed on possible cuts to the Green Heat Network Fund. Other announcements were more promising, including no- and low-interest loans of up to £7,500 for a heat network connection through the Warm Homes Loan Scheme.

These commercial challenges can create a “chicken and egg” problem for large heat networks. Prospective customers and owners of recoverable heat sources want confidence that a heat network developer has the required investment before committing to connect. Investors, meanwhile, want developers to demonstrate demand certainty and access to low-cost recoverable heat to provide confidence of healthy returns.

Engage Consulting believes that heat network zoning should help to break this cycle through requiring certain buildings to connect and increasing demand certainty. Whether policy intent translates into desired outcomes will soon be tested, with much hinging on how requirements to connect and exemptions operate in practice. If exemptions create too much scope to delay or avoid connections, demand certainty could be weakened. It is easy to imagine considerable pushback from customers if faced with significant connection charges and behind-the-meter investment costs, while being offered heat at a higher cost than their existing systems.

Amid these challenges, it was telling that nearly all panellists at the Energy UK Breakfast Briefing mentioned a Regulated Asset Base (RAB) model, a subject of growing debate in the sector. RAB models are already well established for electricity and gas networks, with more recent adoption for nuclear. At this year’s International District Energy Association conference in Canada, several attendees from British Columbia argued that their RAB model has been key to heat network growth in Vancouver (with attendees from other Canadian provinces arguing that unregulated models are better!).

The attraction for heat networks is revenue certainty. A regulated return can reduce risk for investors, lowering the cost of capital, which in turn reduces the cost of heat ultimately borne by customers.

The UK Government has committed to exploring a RAB model for heat networks. At this early stage, big policy questions remain unanswered, including who should pay. There is a case for factoring in the benefits heat networks provide to the wider energy system. The Government’s Warm Homes Plan estimates that the flexible capacity provided by heat networks with large thermal stores could avoid between £5 billion and £7 billion of electricity distribution network upgrades by 2035.

Where heat networks deliver sufficient system savings by reducing electricity network reinforcement costs, RAB funding could be shared across all customers who benefit from the resulting net bill savings.

Engage Consulting can see the foundations for growing the heat network market coming together through regulation and zoning. But the conditions needed to grow at the pace required to achieve 7% of heat demand by 2035 and 20% by 2050 are not yet in place.

Industry has a key role to play in bringing capital and operational costs down through innovation, standardisation and scale. Regulation should help create the right incentives to turn to cost reductions rather than price increases.

Government has a key role across several areas: reducing the cost of non-domestic electricity, implementing zoning, introducing the installation and maintenance license regime to enable developers to access statutory powers that will reduce capital costs, and, crucially, exploring a RAB or equivalent revenue-support model.

If the market is to grow quickly, the road ahead will need to be defined not simply by further policy development, but by finding an economic model that allows heat networks to reach investment decisions and then scale.

Lorenzo Wong chaired Energy UK’s October Breakfast Briefing on heat networks. He is a Senior Consultant at Engage Consulting and leads work on heat networks, advising clients on the emerging regulatory framework and its implications for the sector. Engage Consulting is a specialist consultancy, combining energy market expertise with the capability to deliver complex change.

articles.title: ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December
articles.standfirst:
The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to…
The post ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December appeared first on Carbon Brief.
paragraphs: The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.

That is according to Carbon Brief’s latest “state of the climate” update, which analyses El Niño forecasts from more than a dozen climate models, as well as six global temperature datasets.Dr Zeke Hausfather, Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor, described this year’s El Niño as “simply staggering” when answering questions from CB+ members during a CB Connect “ask me anything” session.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.

This year’s El Niño event – which has been underway since June – has already broken a number of records and reshaped the world’s weather, fuelling fires in Indonesia and “super typhoons” in the west Pacific.
The strength of an El Niño is tracked using the “Niño3.4 anomaly”, which is a measure of how much warmer sea surface temperatures are than average in a section of the central Pacific.

Analysis of more than 600 forecasts from 14 different climate models by Hausfather for Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” update shows how models project this year’s El Niño will peak with an anomaly of around 4C. This would be more than a degree above the previous record in 2015-16.

“This El Niño event is developing so quickly and is reaching sea surface temperatures so warm that it’s simply staggering. We haven’t seen anything like this in the historical record and it may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium.”
This year’s El Niño has already chalked up a number of milestones.
On 18 September, the daily anomaly in the Niño3.4 region broke the satellite-era record set in 2015 when it reached 3.11C.
Meanwhile, September as a whole recorded the highest monthly Niño3.4 region temperature anomaly – 2.84C – since sea surface temperature records began in the mid-1800s.
Hausfather wrote on CB Connect that this year’s El Niño had been “running well above any prior El Niño event since June, at times by a full degree [Celsius]”.

Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” analysis indicates that El Niño is set to continue to intensify into December, with 10 out of 14 models expecting temperatures in the Niño3.4 region to peak in the final month of this year. The remainder anticipate a November peak.
While human emissions of greenhouse gases are responsible for almost all of long-term global warming, temperatures in specific years are strongly influenced by El Niño events.

The “state of the climate” analysis explains that this year’s El Niño event will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027. This is because global temperatures typically lag warming in the tropical Pacific by around three months.
Carbon Brief projects that the 2027 average global temperature will reach around 1.74C above pre-industrial levels. It calculates a 96% chance that next year will be the warmest on record.

This projection is based on the historical relationship between year-on-year temperature changes and El Niño conditions the preceding autumn. It also factors in uncertainty around how global temperatures will develop across the remainder of 2026.

articles.title: Analysis: China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid
articles.standfirst:
China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to…
The post Analysis: China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid appeared first on Carbon Brief.
paragraphs: China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.
Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air
This was the largest quarterly reduction since the 2022 Covid lockdowns and means that China’s CO2 emissions have now fallen by an estimated 0.5% in the year to date.
The new analysis for Carbon Brief, based on official figures and commercial data, shows that coal use fell by 3% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, while oil was down 4%.
The main drivers were a fall in power-sector coal consumption, a continued sharp reduction in transport oil consumption and slowing growth in the coal-to-chemical industry.
The sharp decline in China’s CO2 emissions extends a “flat or falling” trend that began in March 2024 and has now lasted more than two years, as shown in the figure below.
The outlook for China’s CO2 emissions depends on the balance between rising energy demand, clean-energy growth and the government response to a GDP slowdown.
Key drivers of the fall in CO2 in the third quarter of 2026 included a 3.3% drop in coal-power generation, after demand growth slowed and the amount of “wasted” wind and solar fell.

Power generation from solar, wind and nuclear increased by 110 terawatt hours (TWh) year-on-year, more than twice as much as the growth in total electricity demand. This added clean-power generation equal to Germany’s total power output in the same time period.

The fall in coal-power output and CO2 emissions came despite the fact that China continues to build new coal-power capacity at near-record rates. This means that average running hours for coal plants are falling even faster than total generation, eroding their profits.

Meanwhile, transport oil consumption continued to fall sharply, down 9% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026. Electric vehicles (EVs) continued to gain market share, hitting a record 67% of passenger car sales and 50% of heavy trucks in September.
The amount of electricity used by EVs grew by 53%, much faster than the number of EVs on the road, showing increased usage of the existing fleet in preference to fuelled vehicles.

Elsewhere, growth in the coal-to-chemical industry continued to slow down in the third quarter of 2026. The sector has been a key source of emissions growth, but high coal prices have weakened profitability and higher output prices hurt downstream demand.
Finally, CO2 emissions from cement and steel production continued to fall in the third quarter, as the contraction in construction volumes accelerated.
Energy consumption growth has been falling after a period of exceptionally high growth during Covid, while clean-power growth has been robust.
This makes it likely that the growth in clean-power generation will exceed total energy demand growth this year, maintaining the structural fall in fossil-fuel use.
Looking ahead, this balance also relies on progress in removing barriers to new solar and wind power being added to the grid, which result in some clean electricity being “wasted”.
The recent slowdown in energy demand growth is partly – but not fully – explained by exceptionally mild weather in the third quarter.
Another key factor is weaker GDP growth. Since reported GDP growth remains within target, however, there is reduced pressure for further stimulus policies.
The focus of the economic stimulus announced to date is “six networks”, which includes the power grid and the transportation network.
These networks are highly relevant for energy and emissions – and they are already covered by policies that emphasise “green” and zero-carbon solutions.

Carbon Tracker will be attending COP31 in Antalya, with a particular focus on the economic and financial implications of transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF). As the second global stocktake (GST2) begins, we expect the practical challenges of delivering that transition to feature prominently in discussions beyond the formal negotiations.

Our programme includes an official UNFCCC side event on transport electrification, alongside speaking engagements on methane, stranded assets and physical climate risk, and discussions with policymakers, financial institutions and research partners.
Carbon Tracker | Status of global climate action and the role of transport electrification in meeting climate goals
Transport electrification has a central role to play in reducing emissions, but progress varies considerably across markets.

This session will examine the economic and financial benefits of accelerating the transition to electric transport, alongside the policy and infrastructure barriers to wider adoption. Speakers will also consider the limitations of biofuels and the measures needed to advance transport decarbonisation in line with global climate goals.
Co-organisers: European Federation for Transport and Environment (T&E), Carbon Tracker Initiative, Climatepolicy.net e.V. (NewClimate Institute) and Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR).

Speakers: Kadi Riskok, Transport & Environment; Fabby Tumiwa, Institute for Essential Services Reform; Nadia Hadad, Madani Berkelanjutan; Ben Scott, Carbon Tracker; Ana Missirliu, NewClimate Institute.
Carbon Tracker representatives will also contribute to the following discussions:
Hosted by Green Transition Denmark. The panel will explore how regulation, investment and corporate action can help deliver measurable reductions in methane emissions from fossil fuel production.

Building on the Global Methane Pledge, which aims to reduce global methane emissions by at least 30% by 2030 compared with 2020 levels, the discussion will examine how effective policy frameworks, financial incentives and corporate accountability can translate commitments into measurable action across the fossil fuel value chain.
11 November | Roundtable on stranded assets and physical climate risk

Hosted by Japan Climate Leaders’ Partnership (JCLP). The discussion will cover Carbon Tracker’s work on stranded assets, the underpricing of climate risk in financial markets and how investors and companies can prepare for these risks.

articles.title: Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit
articles.standfirst:
The centrepiece of every UN climate summit is for countries to negotiate the wording of a large number of legal…
The post Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit appeared first on Carbon Brief.
paragraphs: The centrepiece of every UN climate summit is for countries to negotiate the wording of a large number of legal agreements – and COP31 in the Turkish city of Antalya is no different.
These texts are hashed out behind closed doors in the “blue zone” at the COP, where diplomats from nearly 200 nations – not including the US – will be haggling over each individual verb.
Over the course of the two-week summit, negotiators will be trying to reach consensus on more than 100 separate agreements – but, first, they must agree which issues are on the agenda.
The complexity of this process can make it challenging to keep track of what countries are fighting about and how negotiations are progressing.
Carbon Brief’s real-time text tracker, below, offers a helping hand by decoding the agenda and keeping a searchable record of every document for each part of the negotiations.
The first column of the interactive tracker lists the topic of each agenda item, with further columns including dates, page counts and links to the original PDFs.
The table is searchable via the interactive text box and can be sorted using the arrow icons.
This year’s talks come with a twist: Turkey holds the presidency and is hosting COP31, but Australia is jointly running the show as “president of negotiations”.
The pair have already announced their intention to produce a “cover text” – an overarching political document summarising key negotiated outcomes, along with issues not on the official agenda.

This could include a recognition that warming is set to “overshoot” the 1.5C limit and the impacts this is already causing. It may also include potential solutions, such as the Turkish presidency’s “electrification” target, for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035.
While the summit is not seen as a banner year for the negotiations, falling half-way between two “global stocktakes” of progress, there are still plenty of major topics up for discussion.
These include efforts to finalise the “global goal on adaptation” and whether to continue a contested process on how to cut emissions, known as the “mitigation work programme”.
Negotiators will also be trying to agree on the details of a new “just transition mechanism”, also referred to as the “Belém-Antalya mechanism for global just transitions” (BAM).
While most of the items on the agenda are agreed in advance, parties can suggest late additions. These must be signed off before negotiations can begin, often resulting in an “agenda fight”.
COP30 agreed to put two new items on the agenda for future summits.
These are the provision of climate finance by developed countries, under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, and making global “finance flows” consistent with the treaty, under Article 2.1c.
Ahead of COP31, the African group of nations filed a request to add climate-related trade tariffs to the agenda. COP30 had agreed to annual “dialogues” on this matter at the Bonn climate talks.
The African group also wants further items added, on tripling adaptation finance and on funding for the Green Climate Fund, a flagship UN body designed to support climate action.
Ahead of the opening of the summit, Carbon Brief’s text tracker counts 102 substantive items on the agenda, not including procedural matters, such as the election of COP officials.
The figure below illustrates the status of the COP31 negotiations overall, in a traffic-light format. Each agenda item is colour-coded according to its current status.
For topics shown in red, negotiators have not yet managed to put anything down on paper, perhaps because parties have fundamentally different views on how they should proceed.
For items in orange, negotiators are working on an “informal text”, which is an early draft setting out the views of different parties, but not yet expressed in formal legal language.
Once a draft legal agreement becomes available, topics will be colour-coded yellow. At this point, areas of remaining disagreement will be denoted in the text with [square brackets] and “options”.

As such, texts with many square brackets or options tend to be an indicator of a high level of disagreement between parties. For this reason, the tracker table above counts and displays the number of outstanding brackets and options in each document.

During the course of the summit, negotiators may work through many iterations of texts on each agenda item. These documents may include “bridging text”, designed to resolve differences of opinion and to find a “landing zone” that all groups can agree on.
Agreement is reached on a given topic once all brackets and options have been resolved, at which point the item will be coloured green in Carbon Brief’s traffic-light chart.
Where agreement cannot be reached, discussions may be subject to “rule 16”, meaning negotiations are postponed until the next session. These topics are colour-coded grey.
The figure below gives an at-a-glance overview of the status of the main topics up for negotiation.

As parties narrow down the options and brackets towards the end of each summit, they start to generate “clean” texts, which contain no areas of disagreement and can be converted into “draft decisions” that are ready for formal adoption at the closing plenary of the meeting.
Finally, at the closing plenary, each draft decision must be gavelled through by the COP president, signifying its formal adoption as a legal agreement and outcome of the summit.
This last step is usually a formality, but dramatic exceptions are possible.
During the closing plenary at COP29, the president of the meeting failed to adopt a deal relating to the “global stocktake” from 2023, which had called for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels.
Carbon Brief also ran text trackers for COP28, COP29 and COP30.

articles.title: Investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) mechanisms are threatening economic, energy and security priorities
articles.standfirst:
Investor–state dispute settlement (ISDS) provisions are creating growing tensions between investors’ rights and governments’ ability to act in the public interest. Increasingly they are being used in ways that could constrain governments’ ability to pursue industrial policy, strengthen national security and support domestic economic priorities during the clean energy transition. The post Investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) mechanisms are threatening economic, energy and security priorities appeared first on E3G.
paragraphs: Investor–state dispute settlement (ISDS) provisions are creating growing tensions between investors’ rights and governments’ ability to act in the public interest. Increasingly they are being used in ways that could constrain governments’ ability to pursue industrial policy, strengthen national security and support domestic economic priorities during the clean energy transition.

With claims related to fossil fuel projects rising, and priorities across a range of climate-related policy areas under threat, countries should take the opportunity at COP31 to build the foundations for coordinated investment treaty reform.

ISDS provisions, included in most investment treaties, allow companies to challenge domestic policy and regulatory decisions. Mining, oil and gas companies are prominent users of ISDS. The proportion of claims coming from this sector has increased three years in a row, reaching nearly half of claims in 2025.

Recent claims have targeted decisions relating to fossil fuel projects refused on climate and environmental grounds. For example, Singapore-based investors launched a challenge after the UK High Court quashed the Cumbria coalmine’s approval. The case remains pending, with the potential cost to the UK government some £300 million. Similarly, an Australian billionaire is suing the Canadian government in relation to a coalmine project refusal, despite Canada’s domestic courts upholding local authorities’ decision.

The Irish government is also facing a claim under the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT) for refusal to issue a lease undertaking for an oil and gas field in the North Celtic Sea. The decision was based on financial capacity of British company Lansdowne, who has now found third-party finance to fund their claim. Notably, Lansdowne initiated arbitration just weeks after the Irish government notified its withdrawal from the ECT.
Beyond individual projects, ISDS exposes climate-related industrial policy to legal challenges too. This fundamentally interferes with government autonomy in policymaking.

For example, ExxonMobil recently filed a notice of dispute under the ECT, challenging the EU’s Net Zero Industry Act. The act obliges certain oil and gas producers to contribute to CO₂ storage capacity, a technology which Exxon has previously been publicly supportive of. This illustrates the threat to government deployment of targeted regulation aimed at stimulating specific sectors.

Other recent claims show how ISDS can frustrate states’ ability to respond to perceived economic and national security risks. In June 2026, Chinese company Jingye Group began the process to seek compensation from the UK government in response to the nationalisation of British Steel. The nationalisation was intended to strengthen national security and infrastructure by protecting the future of steel production in the UK – including thousands of jobs.

Similarly, Wingtech – the partially state-owned Chinese parent company of Dutch semiconductor manufacturer Nexperia – is pursuing up to $8 billion in damages after the Dutch government took control of Nexperia due to national security concerns.

As governments increasingly adopt proactive climate and industrial policies, and as precarious economic conditions necessitate strategic interventions, the chilling effect of ISDS risks undermining policy ambition.

The growing interest in ISDS reform was reflected in its position on the official agenda at this year’s First International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF). Several government participants raised concerns about ISDS, and the issue will be taken forward by an informal ISDS Working Group joined by Colombia, Ghana, Tanzania and Vanuatu.

At the UN intersessional meetings in Bonn this year (SB64), the need to address ISDS was also raised repeatedly across several discussions, including the TAFF Roadmap Session, the Trade & Climate Dialogue, and the Veredas Dialogue on climate finance. However, the concerns raised came primarily from civil society organisations and experts. Governments are yet to fully recognise ISDS as a legal and financial barrier to ambitious climate action.

There is fertile ground at COP31 to nourish this momentum: green industrialisation a key part of Türkiye’s COP31 Action Agenda, and Australia is at the forefront of investment treaty reform. Proper recognition of ISDS as a barrier to ambitious climate action – from fossil fuel phase-out and strategic state intervention to industrial policy – would look like including ISDS in the COP31 cover decision, and establishing investment treaty reform as a key component of TAFF roadmaps.

Pursuing investment treaty reform through UNFCCC processes is important for building coordinated action among states, given concerns that unilateral action against ISDS could undermine investor confidence. The discussions at COP can also play a role in catalysing the technical reform discussions at the national, plurilateral, and multilateral levels needed to address the inherently international nature of investment treaties.

Responding to the Energy Independence Bill published today, Dhara Vyas, Chief Executive, Energy UK, said: “The Energy Independence Bill comes at a critical moment for the sector. The post Energy UK responds to the Energy Independence Bill appeared first on Energy UK.
paragraphs: Responding to the Energy Independence Bill published today, Dhara Vyas, Chief Executive, Energy UK, said:

“The Energy Independence Bill comes at a critical moment for the sector. As we navigate a second energy crisis in just five years, the importance of energy security, affordability and resilience has never been clearer.

“Delivering market reform that ensures continued investment in clean power, delivers a more efficient energy system and has a focus on delivering electrification will strengthen energy security, support economic growth and help deliver more stable bills.

“Energy bills are still too high, and it’s right that Government is putting in place the powers to deliver more targeted support, helping more of the people who need it most. Businesses will also benefit from a crackdown on rogue brokers, giving them confidence that the advice they get from intermediaries can be trusted.

“Businesses in the energy sector are rooted in the communities that host them and have a legacy of investing in the people and places they serve. We look forward to seeing the proposals in the Bill to expand the opportunities for community benefits and ownership.
“Energy UK and its members look forward to working with Government and Parliament to ensure the Bill delivers for customers, communities and the wider economy.”

articles.title: The UK’s 2026 Autumn Budget has laid the ground for cleaner and cheaper electricity. The 2027 Spending Review must build on it
articles.standfirst:
Chancellor John Healey’s first Budget accepts that policy costs belong off electricity bills and that the electricity market needs deep reform. That gives the government a platform to cut bills for good, deliver a clean power system and boost growth. UK household energy bills could increase by as much as a quarter, or by £470 […]
The post The UK’s 2026 Autumn Budget has laid the ground for cleaner and cheaper electricity. The 2027 Spending Review must build on it  appeared first on E3G.
paragraphs: Chancellor John Healey’s first Budget accepts that policy costs belong off electricity bills and that the electricity market needs deep reform. That gives the government a platform to cut bills for good, deliver a clean power system and boost growth.

UK household energy bills could increase by as much as a quarter, or by £470 a year, in January 2027 due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the resulting surge in global gas prices. This will hurt for households who are already struggling with a cost-of-living crisis. It is also a stark reminder of the UK’s continued dependence on international gas markets and the urgent need to move to a cleaner more-resilient energy system.

The Chancellor’s response has been to provide a £100 payment to 20 million households. While this support will offer some short-term relief, it is a one-off measure that does little to reduce long-term dependence on gas or encourage the switch from gas boilers to heat pumps. Reliance on gas means the UK will remain vulnerable to economic shocks and military threats.
But the Chancellor did offer some hope, setting out a clear goal: “to get UK energy costs down in line with Europe”, and he recognised that this would take “deep reform” of our energy system.

The Budget makes a start. A new Cost Control Framework will govern what can be charged to energy bills, and no new policy costs will be added until it is in place. The government are offering fixed-price contracts to legacy renewables to lower their windfall profits – though to get a good price for consumers, the government needs to increase the windfall tax on these generators. VAT stays off household electricity until July 2027, the gas standard charge will be abolished, and, as previously announced, 10,000 industrial energy users can apply for energy bill discounts worth a quarter of their current costs.

This falls far short of a package which will get UK electricity costs in line with Europe’s. We recently outlined how the UK could lower its electricity prices by 20% by 2030. The government now needs to release a similar strategy as to how it will achieve this aim.

The measures announced at the budget accept a principle that E3G, industry and energy experts have long argued for: the cost of public policy should be met by the taxpayer, not loaded onto electricity bills, where it falls hardest on lower-income households and inflates the cost of clean electricity. Before the budget, more than 120 businesses and civil society organisations called for the remaining levies on electricity to be moved into general taxation. This would save households around £100 a year and cut business electricity prices by up to 20% in every postcode.

Last year’s Budget moved 75% of Renewables Obligation costs off household bills. This year the government has stopped new levies being added to energy bills. The next step at the 2027 Spending Review is to move all the remaining levies off all electricity bills.

Cheaper electricity only pays off if people can use more of it. To do that it is essential that households can overcome the upfront costs of buying heat pumps. In this respect, the Budget takes steps backwards.

To help fund the Defence Investment Plan, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has cut £2.5bn from the Warm Homes Plan, cutting funding from the heat pump budget by £1bn and cutting £1.5bn of funding to support green loans intended for social housing, innovative businesses and community energy.

These cuts weaken national and economic security. Electric energy systems with rooftop solar, domestic batteries, and electric heating are more difficult for hostile actors to attack compared to gas pipelines and terminals. Every home that moves from a gas boiler to a heat pump reduces the UK economy’s exposure to volatile international gas markets, the source of the price shocks households have faced since 2021 and which have cost the UK £183 billion.
System reform committed to at this budget is a platform to make electricity more affordable, and over the next year the government should take the next steps:

The Chancellor was right to make affordability the north star for energy policy and right to point out that clean power is the way to get there. Over the next year and at the 2027 Spending Review the UK government must deliver the radical changes to the electricity system to ensure all households at last fully benefit from cheaper renewable power in their bills.

articles.title: AI can cut costs and strengthen the energy system – but barriers risk holding back adoption
articles.standfirst:
Coordinated action on skills, regulation and improving access to reliable data will be essential to delivering the benefits of artificial intelligence (AI) across the energy system, according to a new report from Energy UK. Smarter Thinking: Harnessing AI for a cleaner, fairer energy system outlines how AI is already being used across the energy industry…  Read more 
The post AI can cut costs and strengthen the energy system – but barriers risk holding back adoption appeared first on Energy UK.
paragraphs: Coordinated action on skills, regulation and improving access to reliable data will be essential to delivering the benefits of artificial intelligence (AI) across the energy system, according to a new report from Energy UK.

Smarter Thinking: Harnessing AI for a cleaner, fairer energy system outlines how AI is already being used across the energy industry to optimise networks, improve maintenance, manage demand and accelerate innovation. But wider adoption is being held back by gaps in capability, a lack of data-sharing and the need for longer term regulatory direction.

Energy UK is calling on Government and the regulator Ofgem to work with the industry on an economy-wide approach to AI that unlocks even greater value from advanced applications while guarding against potential risks.
The report splits its recommendations across three key themes:
The report also pays particular attention to the potential risks of AI adoption that apply to the energy sector but should be addressed through regulation fit for the whole economy.

These risks include challenges around accountability and oversight as AI systems become more autonomous, threats to privacy and cyber security, and overreliance on a concentrated group of AI providers or overseas infrastructure. The report also warns against accepting AI outputs without scrutiny and highlights the need to manage AI’s environmental footprint.
Proportionate, economy-wide regulation with stronger assurance and personal data protections should be adopted to support investment in the UK’s AI capabilities.
Energy UK will discuss the report’s recommendations directly with government at a roundtable with officials and industry stakeholders on 2 November.
“AI has huge potential to help us build a more efficient energy system that cuts bills and strengthens our energy security, and now is the time we make the most of that opportunity.
“We are continuing work on collaborating with industry to make the best use of AI in the energy system, with our AI for the Energy System Strategy set to take this work even further.”

“AI is already helping many households, communities and businesses benefit from a smarter and more flexible energy system, delivering better outcomes and helping to make the most of today’s technologies. But we need to go further to turn these early successes into lower costs, stronger energy security and a faster transition to a cleaner, more stable system.

“Scaling successful pilots will require the right foundations. Government, regulators and industry must work together to develop the skills, data frameworks and proportionate governance to support innovation while maintaining trust and managing risks responsibly.
“Getting this right will help ensure the UK remains at the forefront of developing and deploying AI in ways that support customers, strengthen the energy system and drive economic growth.”
For full details of Energy UK’s proposals for the development of AI, read Smarter Thinking: Harnessing AI for a cleaner, fairer energy system.

articles.title: How AI is helping build a smarter, more efficient energy system
articles.standfirst:
November 2026 The role of artificial intelligence (AI) is under increasing scrutiny, as concerns over its development have led to important conversations over how the technology should be used. In energy, AI is often viewed as a problem to solve, rather than as a tool to help tackle the problems of the energy system –…  Read more 
The post How AI is helping build a smarter, more efficient energy system appeared first on Energy UK.
paragraphs: The role of artificial intelligence (AI) is under increasing scrutiny, as concerns over its development have led to important conversations over how the technology should be used.

In energy, AI is often viewed as a problem to solve, rather than as a tool to help tackle the problems of the energy system – both today and in the future. Daisy Cross, Head of Future Retail Markets at Energy UK, said in a recent article: “AI could in fact transform the energy system for the better, making us less reliant on fossil fuels and lowering our bills.”[1]

Government is increasingly interested in how AI can be used in energy and has recently published an independent review of AI deployment in the electricity networks alongside its vision for an AI-enabled clean energy system.[2] [3]

In fact, AI is already being used across the industry to deliver against many of the elements of this vision – from helping businesses make better use of infrastructure and operate a more flexible and dynamic energy system, to improving services for customers. This is an increasingly valuable set of benefits within the transition to a cleaner energy system that manages more renewable generation, millions of individual pieces of energy infrastructure and new patterns of supply and demand.

Energy UK members including Centrica, EDF, E.ON, Equinor, GE Vernova, Mesh-AI, National Grid, Octopus Energy, ScottishPower, SSE and Optima Partners have already seized this opportunity by putting the capabilities of AI into practice across a range of use cases.

A flexible energy system can shift consumption to times when electricity is cheaper and more abundant, reducing pressure on networks and limiting the need for costly additional infrastructure. AI can support this activity by matching prices and incentives to individual patterns of demand, while also coordinating large energy users with the needs of the grid.

National Grid took part in a UK-first demonstration of high-performance AI infrastructure acting as a flexible, grid-responsive asset. The trial demonstrated the ability of data centres to adjust their power needs in response to signals from the electricity system.[4]

This capability could provide an answer to concerns over the impact of new demand from data centres on the electricity system by helping to reduce peaks, support renewable generation and ultimately ease pressure on the network.
The same benefits are also being translated onto household flexibility, which is becoming increasingly important as more solar panels, batteries, heat pumps and electric vehicles are adopted.

Traditional tariff structures do not always reflect the new and exciting ways customers use and generate electricity, but Optima Partners is using AI to gain insights from smart meter data and develop new solutions. By combining machine learning, household-level forecasting and scenario modelling, Optima Partners has helped a UK energy provider understand customer behaviours, segment households and test the commercial impact of new tariff options. This has allowed pricing strategies, including subscription-style tariffs, to be designed and assessed before launch with greater confidence around customer value as well as commercial performance.

In addition to helping homes and businesses flex their energy use to suit the needs of the grid, AI has a positive role to play in forecasting the many variables that impact how the system is operated. This capability sits at the heart of a future electricity system that is increasingly powered by intermittent generation, helping grid operators balance supply and demand and deliver secure, stable energy supplies.

National Energy System Operator (NESO) began work with the Alan Turing Institute in 2017 to explore how machine learning can improve solar forecasting. It found that combining several AI models produced forecasts that were 33% more accurate than traditional methods.[5]

As solar continues to break records, and Britain is powered with increasingly higher levels of zero-carbon generation, more accurate forecasts make it easier to balance the national electricity system, reduce uncertainty and use this clean generation more efficiently.[6]

SSE is also using AI to improve how physical infrastructure is used to move electricity around the grid more effectively. As part of the North of Beauly Dynamic Line Rating (DLR) project, it installed sensors across the high-voltage network in northern Scotland to track temperature, wind and other environmental conditions.

The data collected is fed into a digital system in which machine learning is used to forecast how much power lines can safely carry in real time. This allows operators at SSEN Transmission to safely push around 15% more power on average, revealing hidden capacity and reducing the need for costly upgrades.[7]

The same forecasting power can be utilised by suppliers by using AI to respond faster to price changes caused by increased market volatility in wholesale energy prices. EDF, for example, has worked with Mesh-AI to improve the accuracy and efficiency of its wholesale market forecasting. This was found to reduce the risk of human error in its energy trading, mitigating the frequency and financial impact of incidents, and reduced the validation time of energy trades from 150 minutes to under 30 minutes.[8]
As well as keeping track of the flows of electricity across the energy system, AI is also being used to look after the physical infrastructure that makes up the grid itself.

The technology has been used by SSEN to assess the condition of wooden electricity poles on its network. Between 2020 and 2024, the Smart Hammer project used a Bluetooth-connected device to collect soundwave data from a hammer strike to detect signs of internal decay or structural weakness. The insights gained from replacing manual inspections with objective, science-based assessments were used to plan predictive maintenance strategies that help avoid unnecessary pole replacements, improve safety and ensure maintenance is targeted where it’s needed most.[9]

Predictive maintenance is a key application for AI across many energy technologies. SSE has worked with GE Vernova on early power plant failure detection using an AI-driven digital solution; improved operations at an EV charging hub through AI analysis of video footage; and used AI to examine high-resolution images of wind-turbine blades taken by autonomous drones to classify damage, allowing engineers to track deterioration over time.[10] [11] [12]

Equinor also uses AI tools to undertake predictive maintenance of machinery across its facilities, achieving $330 million in savings since 2020 – with $130 million in 2025 alone. This has had a huge impact not only in improving safety and ensuring more stable operations but also reducing the risk of sudden shutdown.[13]

These applications are at the forefront of innovation for the energy industry, with the future workforce developing solutions that can be applied for years to come. Engineering degree apprentices at E.ON are able to work with drones, AI and virtual reality technologies to better understand performance, maintenance needs and safety requirements to help future-proof the company’s renewable energy plants.[14]

The value of many of these applications is being felt in control rooms across the industry, but a wide range of AI capabilities is also being used to improve the experiences of retail energy customers.

Improving customer service through improved use of data has been a key feature of Energy UK’s Vulnerability Commitment, a voluntary industry initiative with 15 signatories supplying energy to more than 95% of UK homes. These suppliers have pledged to continue improving how they identify and support vulnerable customers, over and above existing licence requirements.

In 2024, ScottishPower and EDF highlighted how they are using AI to support a deeper understanding of the underlying reasons for customer contact and to help identify customers experiencing vulnerability.[15]

Since then, EDF has added to its customer-centric AI initiatives with the launch of the Bill Explainer digital tool in May 2026. In an effort to demystify energy bills, the solution uses AI to present an interactive, step-by-step breakdown of customer charges and usage, highlighting key information and offering tailored explanations based on the individual account.[16]

During the pilot phase, the tool was made available to more than 58,000 customers with early results demonstrating a 5.6% reduction in billing-related telephone inquiries, indicating a positive shift in digital engagement. Since launch, Bill Explainer has supported approximately 349,500 customer sessions, with more than 132,500 bill summaries generated through self-service.

Centrica has also launched an AI-powered solution to help with early identification of customers who may need additional support. Its credit risk tool recognises signals of potential financial hardship, allowing its support team to intervene earlier and provide more personalised support before challenges escalate.[17]

The success of an AI-driven approach has also been highlighted by Octopus Energy. The Arlo customer support chatbot achieved a 76% customer satisfaction score during early trials, narrowly beating comparable responses from human advisors.[18]

These examples show that AI is not a single product or a distant prospect. It is already being used across the energy system in control rooms, contact centres and trading floors, at charging stations and on wind farms.

The Government’s vision for an AI-enabled clean energy system recognises that this adoption is already under way. The priority now should be on the system-level changes that allow AI to create value across the energy system, rather than a focus on a few high-value use cases.Unnecessary barriers need to be removed to turn successful pilots into operational deployment and capture greater value from existing use cases, supporting the system-wide transformation required to unlock more advanced applications in the future.

With responsible innovation and collaboration between industry and government that manages risks while unlocking future potential, AI can help deliver an energy system that is cleaner, more flexible, more resilient and better for customers.
For more on Energy UK’s proposals for the development of AI, read Smarter Thinking: Harnessing AI for a cleaner, fairer energy system.
