articles.title: Smarter Thinking: Harnessing AI for a cleaner, fairer energy system
articles.standfirst:
November 2026 Artificial intelligence is already helping transform the way energy is generated, managed and used across the UK, and supporting better outcomes for customers and the wider economy. From improving network planning and forecasting demand to supporting customer service and accelerating the transition to clean power, AI has the potential to make the energy…  Read more 
The post Smarter Thinking: Harnessing AI for a cleaner, fairer energy system appeared first on Energy UK.
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence is already helping transform the way energy is generated, managed and used across the UK, and supporting better outcomes for customers and the wider economy. From improving network planning and forecasting demand to supporting customer service and accelerating the transition to clean power, AI has the potential to make the energy system more affordable, resilient and clean.

In ‘Smarter Thinking’, Energy UK explores how AI is being used across the energy sector today, the opportunities it presents for delivering energy ambitions, and the barriers and risks that could slow progress.

Drawing on real-world case studies from Energy UK members, the report sets out recommendations for Government, regulators and industry to support responsible adoption while maintaining public trust, security and consumer protections.
To request this report in an alternative format, email [email protected].

There are many examples of AI already being used across the Government’s four priority areas – system optimisation and operation; asset planning, operation and maintenance; end-use efficiency and demand management; and energy innovation and R&D – from supporting management of the grid to planning maintenance schedules and smart electric-vehicle charging.

Education and training pathways need to be updated to embed baseline AI literacy across all roles, while good practice on workforce engagement, change management and trust should be shared from key industrial sectors through the AI Adoption Coalition.

A risk-based, whole-of-economy approach to AI regulation should be developed, with consideration of how this could align with the EU AI Act, with further development of assurance practices to build trust.

Government and industry should accelerate energy-system digitalisation through a shared approach to data sharing alongside cross-sector standards and APIs for high-value datasets. Stronger validation and certification of synthetic data also needs to be brought forward, particularly when used in safety-critical settings.

Risk management efforts need to be improved as AI becomes more autonomous. Agentic systems, for example, can make and execute decisions independently while adapting their behaviour over time to interact with multiple systems at scale. This creates new risks that need to be addressed, alongside improving cyber security and privacy controls. Stronger supply chains and domestic AI capability also need to be built up with environmental impacts carefully considered.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as an important tool for addressing affordability, resilience and decarbonisation challenges across the UK energy system.

AI technologies can optimise the use of energy assets and improve the responsiveness and predictability of energy systems, helping lower costs, enhance resilience and reduce emissions. As capabilities develop, advanced applications could also reshape how energy services and systems operate, transforming jobs and industries to support long-term economic growth.

The UK Government has set out its ambition for the UK to lead on AI adoption across key industrial sectors and ensure the benefits are felt across public services, businesses and the wider economy.[1] The UK has the third-largest AI market globally (and the largest in Europe), with strong capabilities in commercial activity, policy leadership and research.

This report sets out the energy industry’s view on AI adoption. It explains where AI can create value, identifies the barriers to wider adoption, and examines how the sector can manage potential risks responsibly.

Further case studies showcasing where AI technologies are already being used successfully within the sector can be found in ‘Energy in Action: How AI is building a smarter, more efficient energy system’.

Energy UK welcomes the measured, pro-innovation approach the Government and Ofgem have taken with industry to support and regulate AI technologies. This work must continue alongside industry to develop a clear, practical strategy for an AI-enabled clean energy system that can create value and manage risks effectively.

This report focuses on the energy sector’s adoption of AI technologies rather than the infrastructure that supports and powers them. A separate report, ‘Powering the Cloud: How data centres can deliver sustainable growth’, examines the challenges and opportunities created by the expansion of data centres.[2]
Understanding where AI already creates value in the energy system can help the sector unlock more of that value in the near term.
In its ‘Vision for an AI-Enabled Clean Energy System’, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has already identified four broad areas where AI could play a role today:[3]
AI can be used to improve real-time network management, optimise and forecast supply and demand, support the integration of renewables, and strengthen system reliability.

Frazer-Nash Consultancy has applied deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to energy-system planning and developed a model that supports long-term capacity investment decisions across a broad range of generation technologies.[4]

The AI model analyses millions of scenarios to 2050, reflecting variations in demand, weather and technology performance. For any given demand scenario, it can identify the investment choices that best balance cost, emissions and security of supply, producing an optimal power mix in under a second.

National Grid secured alpha-phase funding from the Strategic Innovation Fund in June 2026 to develop Foundational Shared Model Operations (FoSMo), the UK’s first collaborative AI system for managing assets across the electricity network.[5]

FoSMo is a shared AI model that standardises how electricity network operators collect, analyse and act on visual data from their physical assets. If adopted across all participating operators, the shared approach could save the industry around £22.6 million over five years from 2027.

AI can be used to support the planning, operations and maintenance of generation, network and industrial assets to reduce downtime and premature replacement while improving reliability and security of supply.

E.ON’s Evailable platform used AI technology to make charging stations more reliable, cost efficient and user-friendly.[6] Evailable’s algorithms analysed each individual charging station’s usage patterns to identify abnormal operations and potential maintenance issues. This reduced the need for technicians to spend time travelling to sites and diagnosing problems, slashing maintenance costs for operators while ensuring a seamless experience for drivers.

EDF has developed AI-optimisation tools that can enhance maintenance planning at offshore wind farms by automatically producing annual and daily maintenance schedules and vessel routes that account for weather, technicians, spare parts and vessel availability.[7] By testing against historical wind-farm data, this approach was found to offer the potential to reduce maintenance-related costs and revenue losses by up to 50% across a year.
AI can be used to optimise energy use and automate flexibility and demand-side response, shifting consumption to cheaper and cleaner periods.
In partnership with Octopus Energy, the Centre for Net Zero ran a randomised controlled trial involving more than 13,000 customers to evaluate an AI-managed EV charging tariff.

The tariff-controlled charging in response to real-time wholesale electricity prices and ancillary markets, while respecting customers’ preferred charge level and departure time. The trial showed that AI-managed EV charging can reshape electricity demand at scale, creating significant benefits for customers and the grid.[8]

Optima Partners has developed AI-driven hardware identification for an energy provider to deliver customer asset intelligence. It developed a machine learning solution able to use smart meter and customer data to identify ownership of energy assets such as solar, battery storage and electric vehicles.

Without this understanding, the business working with Optima faced challenges forecasting demand, designing targeted tariffs, and identifying customers most likely to engage with new products and services. The AI solution provided a new and trusted intelligence layer to overcome these challenges and support business decisions.

AI can be used to accelerate discovery, design and scale-up of new technologies, materials and processes including in renewables, energy storage, industrial decarbonisation and nuclear fusion. We note that many promising use cases today could also be considered under this theme, given the innovative nature of AI technologies generally.

Alongside several other partners, Smart DCC (Data Communications Company) has worked with Urban Tide to develop an AI tool that can help identify properties at risk of, or already in, fuel poverty.[9]

The ‘uZero’ software uses AI and anonymised smart meter data from Smart DCC to identify areas in fuel poverty, provide better targeted support, identify priority areas for retrofitting, improve uptake of efficiency schemes and create brand new insights.

Centrica has established an ‘Energised Futures’ programme, combining AI expertise with engineers and academic partners to conduct research into intelligent heat-pump control, consumer-led flexibility, and bidirectional charging systems.[10] It aims to combine AI and behavioural research to accelerate energy system transformation.

Energy UK believes government policy should focus on the system-level changes that allow AI to create value across the energy system, rather than accelerating individual high-value use cases. This is in line with ‘The Grid We Need Now: Independent Review of AI Deployment in the Electricity Networks’ (Lucy Yu Review), an independent report commissioned by DESNZ.[11]
We broadly support government focus on four high-impact areas:
1. Reforming the underpinning rules for operating the grid to make the most effective use of AI to run it more effectively.
2. Ensuring AI applications deliver tangible benefits for domestic and business customers.
3. Preparing the grid and wider system to make responsible use of future opportunities for increased autonomy.
4. Streamlining testing and deployment so that AI solutions can make a positive impact for the grid more quickly.

While AI is already delivering benefits across the energy system today, its potential is far from fully realised. More fundamental barriers across the sector are constraining wider adoption, limiting the transition from pilot projects to operational deployment at scale. Addressing these barriers is critical not only for enabling organisations to capture greater value from existing AI use cases, but also for supporting the system-wide transformation required to unlock more advanced applications in the future.

While AI technologies are often treated as a siloed, technical solution in organisations, success in practice is dependent on human capabilities, organisational readiness and public trust. However, people working in the energy industry today are largely not equipped with the necessary capabilities or trust in AI technologies.[12] Ultimately, this may be the greatest barrier for AI’s widespread adoption across the sector, given the complexity of cultural change.

We welcome the Interim Government response from the former Department for Science, Innovation and Technology’s (DSIT), now the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST), to the AI Champions’ AI Adoption Plans.[13] This includes a new package of support for workers and opportunities for young people, in addition to establishing an AI Economics Institute to track how AI is affecting jobs and growth. We also note the recent introduction of three AI Leadership apprenticeship units, which provide short, flexible training courses that support upskilling in the workplace.[14] Government needs to go further in giving businesses the confidence to invest in AI capabilities.

Clear, proportionate and risk-based expectations for AI adoption are critical as regulatory uncertainty can hold back innovation, even when technologies are technically mature. We welcome the measured and collaborative approach taken by the Government and Ofgem to date. This includes guidance from Ofgem and the former DSIT, now DBIST.[15]

Some businesses may find it difficult to ensure robust data governance for use in auditing their AI operations. Unlike traditional approaches, AI technologies require businesses to integrate diverse and expanding datasets while managing dynamic data flows and feedback loops. This makes transparency and explanation more complex, but both remain essential to prevent faulty outputs due to AI drift, bias or hallucinations. Organisations without AI expertise across the business may find these safeguards particularly difficult to design and oversee.

Successful AI solutions depend on access to high-quality, timely, and interoperable datasets. This has been a problem across the industry to date, as many datasets are siloed or incomplete due to commercial and confidentiality constraints, or use different standards. This can affect the quality or scale of the outputs and prevent systems-level AI technologies from being deployed.

Where real-world data is inaccessible or incomplete, synthetic data – generated to replicate the statistical properties and characteristics of real datasets – offers a promising alternative. For example, synthetic smart meter or grid topology datasets can support AI development and testing while reducing data-sharing and privacy constraints.[19]
However, there remains a lack of clear frameworks and standards governing the generation, validation and use of synthetic data, which may limit confidence in when and how it can be used.[20]

As previously discussed, most risks of AI adoption are not unique to the energy sector and should be addressed at a whole-of-economy level. It is therefore important to interrogate potential risks both for the energy industry and more broadly to determine how these should be managed responsibly.

As more autonomous types of AI technologies emerge, including agentic AI, current risk management frameworks may prove insufficient in capturing novel problems. Existing frameworks have generally been designed for systems with predictable behaviour and clear human oversight. Agentic systems can make and execute decisions independently, adapting their behaviour over time to interact with multiple systems at scale, and this can create challenges around accountability, explainability, cybersecurity and risk assurance.

Agentic AI contrasts with many AI technologies in the energy sector today (for example, predictive machine-learning and generative AI models), which largely focus on optimising existing operations rather than transforming them completely. To date, organisations have been able to leverage current frameworks with confidence, with the addition of AI-specific policies such as ensuring a ‘human in the loop’.

We note that international standards and guidance do exist for enhanced controls when deploying agentic models, including ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management systems) and ISO/IEC 23894 (AI risk management).[22], [23] Ofgem’s AI guidance also provides cross-cutting principles that can inform AI assurance, but further thinking is needed to determine if these are sufficient in adequately managing emerging risks.

AI technologies can extract granular information from multiple datasets, and agentic models may use this information in unpredictable ways. This can make it difficult to tell people which insights from their data have been used. It also creates privacy and security risks, particularly if personal data is used inappropriately or exposed in a breach.

As the energy sector becomes more digital and uses more AI technologies, cyber security risks will grow, particularly for critical national infrastructure. We welcome the Government’s Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which will bring more organisations within the regulatory framework and enhances cyber security standards across the energy [24] This should be viewed as the start, rather than the end of efforts to strengthen protections across the sector.

The prevalence of third-party AI tools raises potential risks around data location and sovereignty, as UK organisations’ data may be stored or processed outside of national borders. This may limit regulatory oversight, create complexity if there are conflicting data governance regimes, or expose critical systems to foreign access.

The Lucy Yu Review recommended the Government invests in resilient, UK-based AI computing infrastructure to support the AI systems that may be needed to operate future electricity grids. This approach could also be applied to other critical parts of the energy system.

There is also a systemic risk of supply chain concentration if most organisations rely on the same AI models. The economy and energy sector may become more vulnerable to shared assumptions or errors, cascading failures or exploitation by malicious actors that identify common weaknesses.

Passive reliance on AI may weaken people’s intellectual resilience. This can occur when people outsource critical thinking to AI tools and incorporate its outputs with limited scrutiny. Energy suppliers are beginning to observe this trend among customers who use AI to write or interpret correspondence rather than engaging directly, which may reduce their understanding of the issues at hand. Research also finds that customers are using AI large language models to inform their energy decisions, with the majority saying it affected what they understood or decided.[26]

A recent study found that when interacting with an AI chatbot programmed to deliver 50% of responses incorrectly, participants accepted flawed reasoning in 73% of occurrences and overruled it only 20% of the time.[27] These effects were not uniform across all test subjects, with those viewing AI as authoritative being more likely to accept faulty answers.

We welcome the government-industry initiative ‘AI Skills Boost’, as a promising first step in addressing this risk.[28] It leverages training of government and industry partners to support the UK workforce to adapt and thrive in a workplace where AI tools are increasingly widespread.

AI technologies are being used to decarbonise the energy sector and the broader economy.[29] Analysis by the International Energy Agency finds that if there is widespread adoption of AI for decarbonisation globally, emissions reductions could be three to five times larger than total data centre emissions.[30]

Nevertheless, it is important to recognise the potential energy consumption and emissions impact of using AI technologies, alongside other dimensions of its potential environmental footprint including water consumption, hardware and e-waste.[31]

The Government has rightly recognised these challenges, and there is ongoing work to ensure the physical infrastructure for AI is strategically planned in the UK. The Government’s recently published ‘Data Centre Covenant’ will offer strategic benefits to data centres that can support security, lower electricity bills, and offer benefits for local communities.[32] While this is a positive step from the Government, significant further detail is required to ensure that the sustainable benefits can be delivered, with determination of how standards will be enforced and whether they will only apply voluntarily for data centres not deemed to be strategically important.

articles.standfirst:
Responding to the energy debt ‘circuit breaker’ strategy launched by the Government and Ofgem, Energy UK’s Deputy Director of Policy (Customers) Ned Hammond said: “Energy UK has been raising the alarm around energy debt for some time so it’s great to finally see a joint debt strategy launched by Government and the regulator Ofgem. “Our…  Read more 
The post Energy UK responds to joint debt strategy from Government and Ofgem appeared first on Energy UK.
paragraphs: Responding to the energy debt ‘circuit breaker’ strategy launched by the Government and Ofgem, Energy UK’s Deputy Director of Policy (Customers) Ned Hammond said:
“Energy UK has been raising the alarm around energy debt for some time so it’s great to finally see a joint debt strategy launched by Government and the regulator Ofgem.

“Our report in February called for action on many of the areas set out today, from promoting the positive role of smart Pay-as-you-Go meters and tackling the debt that builds up when people move home to reducing the number of customers on standard credit – the most expensive way to pay energy bills.

“The update on the Debt Relief Scheme, with the possibility of more households being supported, is also welcome. We appreciate the relief will be targeted at customers most in need of support, but this must be delivered in collaboration with suppliers to ensure it reaches them effectively.

“With debt heading towards a staggering £7 billion by the end of 2026 and potentially reaching £8 billion in the first half of 2028 without action, it is vital all these measures are delivered at pace alongside industry to get the debt burden down for customers and the suppliers they owe.”
The report Energy debt: Everyone pays outlines Energy UK’s proposals for a comprehensive energy debt mitigation strategy.
In August Energy UK figures revealed domestic customer energy debt is likely to have hit a record £6 billion in the first half of 2026.

The report Improved Energy Bill Support: The case for a social discount outlines Energy UK’s proposals for a social discount scheme that is better targeted, provides adequate support, and is flexible enough to reflect differing levels of need and respond to changing prices.
Energy UK is the trade association for the energy industry, representing companies investing billions of pounds to secure our country’s energy needs, today and in the future.

From growing start-ups to major electricity generators, grid and infrastructure developers, and energy suppliers, our members are driving change across power, heat, transport and flexibility, while working to serve customers, citizens and communities.

We provide a collective voice for the sector working with governments, regulators, charities and other organisations to provide crucial insight that shapes policy, offers solutions and promotes best practice.

Our broad view across the whole system supports evidence-based positions which are not tied to particular technologies, and are focused on delivering strategic benefits for people, businesses and the economy.

We champion initiatives such as our Vulnerability Commitment, which pushes suppliers to go beyond regulation to support customers with additional needs, and TIDE, the industry’s drive for greater inclusion and diversity. Through our Young Energy Professionals Forum, we support the development of future leaders. We are equally committed to our team and are proud to be recognised as a ‘Platinum’ Investors in People employer.

articles.title: Breathing Space, Not a Strategy
articles.standfirst: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council...
paragraphs: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council taxes. Against an already difficult domestic and international macroeconomic backdrop, which has created a strain on the public finances, the net effect of today’s measures has been a reduction in the Chancellor’s buffer against his fiscal rules from £23.6 billion in March to £14.5 billion now. Market reaction to the Budget was subsequently muted. Ten-year gilt yields fell by only a few basis points on Wednesday afternoon, while sterling hardly budged.

Therefore, while today’s Budget appears to have not resulted in a backlash from the markets, maintaining a backloaded path for tax rises and deferring major fiscal decisions on defence and other spending until the 2027 Spending Review to buy time is not a credible fiscal strategy.

The ten-year gilt yield has risen by around 100 basis points since February, to around 5.3 per cent. As explained in this blog, some of that rise can be traced to the war in the Middle East and would presumably unwind if there were a resolution. But over half of it likely reflects other factors, including heavy government borrowing worldwide and the AI investment boom, which have pushed up global long-term real interest rates. These are forces that could exert a persistent effect on gilt yields.

The DMO’s financing remit for 2026-27 has been modestly revised up today by £7.4 billion, taking planned gilt issuance to £250.6 billion. This means taking on additional debt at what could prove to be a persistently higher cost of borrowing.
Successive economic shocks this century have ratcheted up the debt-to-GDP ratio. After both the global financial crisis and the pandemic, debt stabilised at a higher level.

But for fiscal policy to act as a shock absorber, the government needs to have adequate capacity to step in and act when the next shock hits the economy. A consistently high debt ratio limits this ability. Therefore, the minimal test of credibility of for today’s budget was whether the Chancellor was willing to stop the debt rising even further.

The OBR forecasts that policies announced in this budget will lead to increased borrowing over the next three years of £12.4 billion, which will then be followed by a reduction of £7 billion on average in the years after. Based on the forecast paths laid out by the OBR today we can see that our minimal test of credibility was not met with Public Sector Net Debt peaking at around 97 per cent of GDP in 2028-29 before falling only slightly to 96 per cent of GDP in 2031-32, higher than the ratio in August this year of 94 per cent.
Today’s Budget comes against a fragile global backdrop as the risk of adverse shocks appears to have increased over the past year. Bond markets are jittery and looking for the next shoe to drop

UK ten-year gilt yields remain the highest in the G7, leaving the public finances exposed to shifts in market sentiment. In our judgement, this strengthens the case for building fiscal buffers. The Chancellor’s decision to reduce headroom by £9 billion therefore leaves the government vulnerable to future shocks.

This is underscored by the path for debt interest now being higher than was set out in March 2026. By the end of the decade UK debt interest is expected to rise to around £150 billion annually – more than the government currently spends on education.

A credible fiscal strategy could help to reduce debt interest. Even modest fiscal restraint could deliver a credibility dividend of 10-20 basis points off gilt rates (worth around £1-2 billion a year by the end of the parliament).

Today’s Budget measures do not attempt to place the debt-to-GDP ratio on a sustained downward path in the medium term. Difficult decisions have, once again, been deferred, leaving the integrity of public finances contingent on good fortune. But hoping for the best is not a credible basis for managing the public finances. This approach leaves the UK government more exposed to renewed market scrutiny in the months ahead.
The longer the Chancellor delays the necessary adjustment, the larger, and more difficult, these adjustments will be.

articles.title: Why the UK needs a fossil fuel transition roadmap
articles.standfirst:
How can the UK reduce its reliance on fossil fuels while protecting jobs, strengthening energy security and growing the economy?
The post Why the UK needs a fossil fuel transition roadmap appeared first on E3G.
paragraphs: With soaring oil and gas prices relentlessly pushing up energy bills, it’s never been clearer that the UK, like all countries, must urgently pivot away from economic reliance on fossil fuels. Recent debates around the approval of the Jackdaw gas field have highlighted a broader domestic challenge – how can the UK reduce its reliance on fossil fuels while protecting jobs, strengthening energy security and growing the economy?

The good news is that Britain is already much further along than many countries. The UK has established ambitious, legally binding plans for boosting clean power, electric vehicles, industrial decarbonisation, energy efficiency and low-carbon heating, including through one of the most comprehensive legally-binding emissions reductions plans in the world, the Climate Change Committee (CCC)’s seventh carbon budget (CB7).

Policies and plans for managing UK oil and gas production do exist, but lack the equivalent quantitative targets and detailed implementation plans to those in CB7. The UK’s North Sea field is entering a period of sharp structural decline, with around 90% of the basin having already been drained, production falling, and oil and gas revenues projected to drop by 98% in the next five years. The challenge is therefore no longer how to maximise dependence on fossil fuels, but how to manage a successful transition beyond them, and crucially, how to maximise and fairly distribute the benefits of the transition.

What is missing is a coherent single framework which brings policies to wean the UK off fossil fuel demand together with plans for reducing fossil fuel production in the North Sea into a politically credible, long-term pathway. This document – a roadmap on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) – would not only provide a clear, long-term domestic policy signal, but allow the UK to demonstrate its continued international leadership on climate change and the energy transition.

Many countries have been exploring or are already in the process of developing roadmaps (including France, Germany and the Netherlands, and the Pacific) since the concept emerged at COP30 in Brazil, with more likely to be announced at COP31, kicking off in Antalya, Türkiye, next week. To be credible and lead to genuine impact, however, roadmaps must be sufficiently detailed, ambitious and financeable, and be backed by the whole of government. This takes time, resources, and political capital – but a strong, slower-produced roadmap is better than a quick, weak one. So while the UK shouldn’t be expected to present a fully-fledged roadmap in Antalya, COP31 does provide a clear opportunity to clearly signal intent to develop one.
Every TAFF roadmap will look different, but our assessment is that a credible UK roadmap will need to include the following core pillars:

Elevating explicit messaging from CB7 and key sectoral policies and financing plans into a TAFF roadmap, to clarify how fossil fuel demand is expected to fall across power, transport, buildings and industry over time, would create a transparent political signal of future demand and help policymakers, industry and investors assess implications for fossil fuel production. This modelling exists, but must be actively reframed around fossil fuel demand as a principle element of economic planning.

Climate action is often pitted against domestic fossil fuel production, but the more important question is how already declining oil and gas demand affects future production needs. On this basis, a UK TAFF roadmap should set out:

This would anchor individual project decisions in a national transition strategy, but it would also clarify the long-term public costs and liabilities associated with fossil fuel production. As production declines, decommissioning, clean-up responsibilities and taxpayer exposure become increasingly important – if any of the North Sea oil and gas companies goes bust, it will be the UK taxpayer that picks up a decommissioning tab which could run into the billions. A strategic TAFF framework would support early planning rather than reactive management.

The energy crisis exposed the risks of dependence on volatile international fossil fuel markets, and it’s now impossible to ignore the fact that both climate security and energy security are national security issues, as UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a recent speech in New York.

E3G-commissioned research has shown that the Russian invasion of Ukraine cost the UK economy £183 billion – triple the UK’s annual defence budget. Energy bills are surging again following the war in Iran. Long-term energy security requires clean power, electrification and energy efficiency to reduce that exposure.

A TAFF roadmap should show how reducing fossil fuel demand and managing the decline of domestic production during the transition can strengthen security, aligning with the government’s aim to reduce reliance on foreign fossil fuels and support economic resilience.

Energy security is not delivered through new fossil fuel supply. Debates over fields such as Rosebank show that new production is unlikely to lower bills or even substantially reduce import dependence. Reducing demand through clean technologies remains the most durable long-term route to greater security.
Transition planning is not just about building new infrastructure. It is also about managing the retirement or repurposing of existing systems.

The UK has world-leading expertise in decommissioning and is well placed to develop a practical approach to managing this change. Given the scale of North Sea infrastructure approaching the end of its productive life, planning for decommissioning is not simply an environmental requirement; it is becoming a major economic and fiscal priority and opportunity. Effective management can reduce risks to taxpayers while supporting the growth of a globally competitive decommissioning industry.
As UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has emphasised, the transition will only succeed if it supports workers and communities and contributes to economic renewal.
A successful roadmap should therefore show how the transition can:

The transition should be seen not only as an environmental necessity, but as a major industrial opportunity. As activity in the North Sea evolves, workers and businesses possess valuable expertise that can be deployed across offshore wind, decommissioning, and other growth sectors. A TAFF roadmap can help provide the certainty needed to accelerate this shift and ensure communities benefit from emerging industries.

At COP31, the UK can send a clear and timely signal on how it will manage the transition by committing to develop a comprehensive, credible TAFF roadmap. Such a roadmap would demonstrate implementation-focused leadership – not new targets, but a demonstration of how to transition a whole economy away from fossil fuels while supporting workers, strengthening security and building long-term prosperity.

As countries turn climate commitments into economic strategies, the UK can show that transition planning need not mean choosing between climate action and economic growth, rather than a wealthy, diversified economy can responsibly manage fossil fuel decline, keep bills down, protect the public interest, give workers confidence and foster industries that drive future growth. It can take this message into its forthcoming G20 Presidency leadership too, showcasing its own plans for transition planning as a model for other major economies looking to manage their exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets and macroeconomic risks.

Finally, the UK should champion TAFF roadmaps as practical tools for cross-government planning, working to support countries from around the world, and work with vulnerable and new fossil fuel producing countries to support and facilitate their transitions.

The UN officially noted in September 2026 that “exceedance of the 1.5°C global warming target is unavoidable” and we are now in era of overshoot and managing its consequences.
In some ways this was inevitable, as we had no detailed plan to achieve the target.
So let’s back up ten years to COP 21 in Paris 2015, where the warming target was agreed amongst almost all the countries in the world.

Now, any serious multi-billion-dollar project normally has an objective, design, costs and schedules and controls. Even a house extension has these basics in place before a brick is laid, or money spent.

So Paris gave us the objective. But the rest could not yet be specified – no formal “design”, no working overall cost and schedule toward the objective, and little in the way of formal project controls.
But ten years of execution have now produced enough evidence to construct a working integrated plan, even if the original 1.5°C stretch pathway without material overshoot has been lost

By a baseline I mean the current working project plan against which actual progress is measured: the objective, design, major milestones, cost estimates and critical dependencies such as technology developments.
What it is not – It is not a prediction of what might happen in various scenarios, and it is not a model to get us to a temperature destination eg 2 or 2.7°C.
What it is is the baseline plan we manage against until evidence requires a controlled change.
For the climate project, the objective baseline remains Paris.

The climate effort had fragmented baseline elements — the Paris goals, country plans (Nationally Determined Contributions, NDCs), analytical pathways, scenarios, milestones,— but no single integrated delivery baseline.
So a key act now is to simultaneously reconcile those original commitments and attempt the first integrated working baseline.
The objective baseline — held (Paris, < 2°C) The delivery baseline — developing and needing project controls
The Paris Agreement has in effect created a climate mega-project, but an odd one.
Take the climate “mega-project” compared to conventional project delivery systems:
→ Began executing thousands of uncoordinated work packages (solar, wind, CCS, nuclear, hydrogen, batteries, EVs, geo-thermal, low-carbon fuels…)
→ Discover the effective / ineffective design through deployment
→ And now – perhaps – gather enough information to contemplate an integrated design basis.

Most project plans would start with a clear design, and then the detailed engineering plans first and work to execute and construct them: this one executes various engineering concepts and then discovers the grand design and plan in retrospect.
This is not unknown – large IT projects, even the internet can be described this way.
But so far this activity still does not offer a design concept for the climate project, and how well we are doing in delivering it.

No agreed answer yet to how the temperature control outcome is produced: is it through solar and wind, through nuclear, through carbon capture, through behaviour change and efficiency, through some combination of these or a technology X not yet specified?
And it still has no explicit cost and schedule, beyond various estimates, scenarios and outlooks.
It also has no project organisation with the authority to own project progress, costs and milestones, check against them and hold anyone to account.
In project terms, Paris set an objective without constituting an integrated plan.
This is not a criticism of the early diplomatic and analytical efforts.
But it is a description of the climate project delivery problem.

When the key project objective requires cooperation between nearly two hundred sovereign states, each with its own politics, its own capital constraints and its own veto, you do not get a project schedule.
But an accord is not a plan: the problem is though, by having an explicit project objective that is well publicised, we have spent a decade treating it as one.
We have almost certainly breached the stretch target of 1.5°C.
Emissions are not falling fast enough, if at all, although it is likely a high-level plateau has been achieved. And this acts also as a major project signal, as it links closely to the objective.

There is a robust near-linear relationship between cumulative CO₂ emissions and warming, allowing a solid carbon budget to be estimated: in 2018 we calculated we had about 580 billion tonnes of CO2 we could emit and stay below 1.5degC, with a 50% chance.

In project terms that is known as a contingency – in normal projects this is usually expressed as the amount of money or time we have added to the plan estimate – as a buffer against events and errors. We used carbon emitted as a best alternative measure.

By early 2026 we had used up all but around170 billion tonnes of this carbon contingency, meaning that at our current rate of emissions, 42 billion tonnes per year (5 tonnes per human), we have about four years left before it is all gone, end 2029.
In that sense the temperature violation is a lagging project indicator – it confirms what we expected.
Emissions are more a current variable – telling us today what the status is.
And deployment of technologies or policies against a plan to reduce them are leading indicators – suggesting what should now be prioritised or reprioritised.
In sum – we need to re-baseline the project – we need to create a new plan.

In lock-step with the climate objectives is an underlying energy transition: staying with fossil fuel combustion which creates CO2 as waste and pollution, would leave us fully exposed to the volatilities of unchecked global temperature rise.
Hence the pivot over the past few decades to alternatives: zero or low-carbon energy sources as a substitute, to lower climate risk as fast as possible.

And here there is a better story – the energy transition on several major fronts is accelerating, some even ahead of “plan” or expectations at least — solar power, wind power, large scale storage batteries, electric vehicles and other electrification industries are becoming an economically preferred system, not merely an environmentally desirable one.

In project parlance, whilst the emissions / temperature levels are a negative variance to plan (ie behind expectations) wind, solar, batteries and electrotech such as EVs, are a positive variance to plan (ie doing better than imagined).
Both things (temperature target breached with emissions at a high plateau, but new technologies arriving more quickly) can be true at once.
It is what happens when a project runs without an integrated project plan or dedicated programme control function.

The red signal of emissions persisting should have caused a resultant activity in the plan to address the negative variation: a shift in capital allocation, or a prioritisation of effective technologies the key examples.
The useful move now is not to abandon the target climate objective, but also not to pretend it is still on schedule.
It is to do what any competent project does when reality overtakes the original plan:
– change the execution plan using new knowledge gained in the project
But a re-baseline is legitimate only if it records rather than conceals the original variance.
The original objective remains visible; assumptions are changed because reality has changed.
A re-baseline is not an admission of failure. It is a normal, disciplined project act.
The original baseline has moved. 1.5°C is no longer the planning case; the new planning case is overshoot.
And overshoot is no longer a scenario, it is the observed trajectory.
Recognition means writing down what has actually happened, not what we hoped would happen.

Much climate reporting still measures progress against the old plan as though nothing has changed — announcing record solar additions in the same breath as record emissions, without reconciling the two.
Many scenarios still record emissions targets for 1.5degC that involve almost impossible technical deployments aligned with a sudden collective policy consensus.
Second, preserve the objective. This is where a re-baseline differs from abandonment.
The goal — limiting warming, minimising peak temperature, shortening the duration of overshoot — remains and is expressed in the UN report.
Every tenth of a degree still matters, and every single year spent above 1.5°C still adds major long-term risk.
What changes is the route and the pace required to reach it.
Third, change the execution plan and unearth the critical path. This is the part almost nobody is doing.
Without an integrated plan, the climate project has no “critical path”.
The critical path of any major project is a sequence of critical tasks – if any task on this path is delayed by even one day, the final completion date of the whole project slips by one day too.
An integrated plan needs to make that critical path clear and transparent.
While we have likely missed the original stretch target, we have still learned an enormous amount via the active pursuit of it.
If the old plan assumed a certain mix of technologies would deploy at a certain speed, and they have not, then the plan should be rewritten — not the target.
If solar and batteries have outperformed while grids and permitting have underperformed, then capital, policy attention and institutional effort must move accordingly.

That is what a re-baseline does: it learns from project actions – and then reallocates scarce resources against the actual critical path such as electric grids – not the one assumed previously such as renewable supply capacity.
In that example – if we are ahead on renewable capacity an integrated plan reallocates spare capital to the grid.

Conversely, with no integrated plan the climate project cannot see its critical path – it is guessing what is on it. Perhaps spending excess capital on solar deployment when grid capacity would better retain the cost and schedule.

And it is rare that an integrated plan retains “all of the above” for energy technologies and policies and generates multiple often contradictory scenarios. It is forced to select among them to keep to cost and schedule.
But we know the Climate Project is an odd one – so as we analyse it we should expect no single stable critical path: it is likely to move round at global and country level,
China may have a very different critical path eg less EV / electrotech investment vs more coal retirement compared to the path for the EU or US – where investment in electrotech remains behind plan.
If the climate project can never have a project manager, it can still have project controls.
Absent a project manager it can still determine a baseline, a critical path (or paths) and a cost and schedule to monitor progress.
But – project controls hold the baseline, measure variance, and report what is actually happening — without owning the work.
In a normal project programme the two – Project Manager and Projects Control Lead – sit together.
In the not-so-normal climate project, only the second, integrated project controls function, is available. But it may be enough.
The project control function asks fundamental questions, constantly:
It communicates the answers against the original and new baseline — for example the NDCs, the 2030 and 2035 milestones, the Net Zero dates — and lets the gaps speak for themselves.
It does not advocate for solar over nuclear, or mitigation over adaptation, or ambition over realism.
It also has to deal with the fact that a single “design concept” is likely only going to be delivered or conceived in retrospect – eg “we achieved the climate target via the combination of ….”
It simply holds the best overall plan we have against reality and reports the delta.
Climate debate under a target missed, under stress, seems to bifurcate into two positions (this is a rough summary, but it does condense a lot of latest commentary):
Either way – both are more political, not project-based positions.
A project controls function dissolves the binary by refusing to take either side, and instead produces a more objective assessment: here is where the project actually stands against its baseline.
Independence — it cannot sit inside a negotiating body, or it becomes a party.
Evidence — it works from hard data, not relying on scenarios, and reports against physical progress measures: gigawatts connected, gigawatts approved – not gigawatts in a given scenario.

Consistency — it uses the same baseline every time, so that variance is measurable across time. Without that consistency, re-baselining becomes a habit of moving the goalposts. With it, it becomes a discipline.
None of this requires global governance reform, a new treaty, or anyone’s permission.
It requires a competent institution or globally agreed framework willing to hold the baseline and publish the differences —in public, and without advocating for anyone’s preferred outcome.
We set the climate objective before we knew the design to deliver it; but pursuing the objective helped us discover it.
In 2015, the plan could not have been written. Not by diplomats, not by engineers, likely not by anyone.
The learning rates did not exist yet, because the deployment had not yet happened.
Asking the world to produce a design concept, a cost estimate and a schedule for “avoiding dangerous warming” was asking for something no institution on earth could have delivered.
It was not a failure of will. It was a condition then of the world.
A decade later, the condition of the world has changed. Its knowledge and its climate situation have altered.
A design concept has started to emerge – and now we can perhaps create a continuing design that we can better define, allowing better execution.
The design was not declared at a conference, or frozen via internal expert analysis.
It was selected somewhat in the wild by cost curves and manufacturing scale.

Solar, wind, batteries, electric vehicles, electrification – not because anyone declared them the winner, but because repeated deployment has increasingly demonstrated their efficiency, economics and scalability
That is not the standard concept selection process. But it is likely the climate project will never look like a standard phased project from concept to operation.
These are climate plan milestones whether anyone calls them that.
They sit in the data, in the global technical reviews, in the observed trend lines.
A schedule is simply a sequence of dates against which progress can be measured.
Ten years of deployment bought us the numbers that ten years of negotiation could not. The cost we could not devise in 2015 is more priceable now.
It was a de facto networked programme in which the design is still being discovered during execution rather than fixed before sanction.
It is not that the world failed to plan. It is that the plan could only be written after the attempt had started.
Which means the first task of project control is not to impose a plan.
It is to notice the one that has quietly begun assembling itself, so now hold it against the original objective, and write it down.
Deriving the climate project concept, cost and schedule retrospectively after creating its ultimate target is not just tidying up.
It is the act that converts a target into something that can be delivered, measured, and corrected.
The megaproject disciplines reveal what the climate effort is missing.
The analogy does not tell us that climate can be managed like a project.
In Part 2 we change gears and propose a practical Action Plan.
And our plan will not start with primary energy consumed, but with the useful energy services delivered, and work backwards.

articles.title: The Return of the Energy Shock
articles.standfirst: In this blog we present updated forecasts from our Multi-Recurrent Neural Network (MRN) model, extending the outlook from September 2026 to August 2027.1 This is our fourth MRN update of...
paragraphs: In this blog we present updated forecasts from our Multi-Recurrent Neural Network (MRN) model, extending the outlook from September 2026 to August 2027.1 This is our fourth MRN update of the year, following the February, May and July 2026 blogs. Three things have changed since July:

The July blog made a testable claim: our recommended Intermediate Energy MRN projected 3.0 per cent for June 2026, easing to 2.7 per cent by August, before rising to a 4.5 per cent peak in February 2027. The outturns were 2.6 per cent in June and 3.1 per cent in August. The model was 0.4 percentage points too high in June and 0.4 points too low in August, and the sign of the error flipped exactly as the geopolitics did. In June the peace announcement was pulling energy prices down faster than the model’s training data allowed for; by August the collapse of that deal was pushing them up faster. We flagged the first possibility explicitly in July (“a June print materially below this range would suggest the peace-deal energy price fall is passing through faster than the model anticipates”). We did not anticipate the second, and nor, on the evidence of its July Report, did the Bank of England, whose central projection assumed oil prices would drift from $76 to $71, and inflation would peak at 3.2 per cent in the fourth quarter of 2026. Two lessons follow. The first is that the MRN carries no oil price assumption at all; it extrapolates from the energy history it has seen. So its twelve-month path is best read as an unconditional projection of where the data were pointing at end-August. The Bank’s and NIESR’s forecasts are conditional on an assumed path for oil prices. Part of the gap between us is therefore a difference in what is being forecast, not only in how; the fair test is whether the unconditional path keeps moving the right way when the world moves, as it did between June and August. The second is that readers of our May blog will recall that the then-current MRN had inflation “well beyond 5 per cent in early 2027”; the July update, trained during the brief peace, pulled that back to 4.5 per cent. The present round returns to the May reading.

Figure 1 shows the current forecast of two classes of MRN model: the Simple Energy + MPC MRN, which uses CPI level and month-on-month change, ONS UK energy CPI, the monthly Brent average and, new in this round, Bank Rate; and the Intermediate Energy MRN, which adds real GDP, PPI, the 10-year gilt yield and the sterling effective exchange rate to that set. The Intermediate Energy MRN projects annual CPI inflation of 3.7 per cent in September 2026, 4.1 per cent in November, 4.4 per cent in December, and then a step up to 5.4 per cent in January 2027, holding at 5.4 per cent in February and March before easing to 4.3–4.4 per cent in April–May and drifting back up to 4.9 per cent by July and August 2027. The Simple Energy + MPC MRN follows a similar path but peaks later and higher, at 5.7 per cent in June 2027. The Average MRN peaks at 5.3 per cent in February and does not fall below 4.5 per cent at any point in the forecast window. The quarterly averages are 3.9, 5.2 and 4.8 per cent for the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first two quarters of 2027, respectively.

We must state two things about this path clearly. The first is that the peak has moved up by almost a full percentage point since July, from 4.5 per cent to 5.4 per cent, while its timing has stayed put in the first quarter of 2027. That revision is almost entirely the energy channel doing what it is designed to do: the price of Brent crude oil is 50 per cent higher than when the July models were trained, UK wholesale gas prices have risen 78 per cent since the Bank’s July Report, and the Ofgem energy price cap has gone from £1,477 in Q2 to £1,663 in Q3 and £1,723 for October–December, with Cornwall Insight now forecasting £1,999, a 16 per cent rise, for January 2027. The second is that part of the January step is arithmetic rather than economics. The CPI fell by 0.5 per cent month-on-month in January 2026; so, roughly half a point of the first quarter peak is that base effect. It is real, in the sense that the headline rate will print it, but it does not imply a fresh burst of price pressure in that month.

This is the first round in which we forecast the policy rate, and the two classes disagree in a way we think is informative rather than embarrassing. The Simple Energy + MPC MRN, which sees inflation, energy and the rate itself, but nothing of the real economy, has Bank Rate rising from 3.75 per cent to 4.0 per cent by February 2027 and 4.5 per cent by June. The Intermediate Energy MRN, which also sees GDP, producer prices, gilt yields and sterling, has it falling to 3.5 per cent by November, 3.25 per cent by January and 3.0 per cent by March, before settling at 3.25 per cent. The average of the two dips to 3.5 per cent through the winter, touches 3.25 per cent in March, and is back at 3.75 per cent by June 2027.

Read the two classes as the two sides of the Monetary Policy Committee’s own argument. At its 17 September meeting the Committee held at 3.75 per cent by six votes to three, with Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill voting for an immediate quarter-point increase on the grounds that slack “may have already peaked” and that raising rates is “a better risk-management strategy when faced with uncertainty about inflation dynamics and second-round effects”. The six who held pointed to “very limited evidence of emerging second-round effects” and to slack “still evident in a range of indicators”, with Alan Taylor arguing that policy “should respond to evidence of propagation rather than mechanically to volatile ticks in headline energy prices”. The Simple class, which has no measure of slack and reacts to headline energy, is the hawkish minority’s direction of travel. The Intermediate class, which can see weak activity and the restrictiveness of financial conditions, is the majority’s. We do not claim the network understands this debate; we claim that the two feature sets encode the two positions, and that is exactly why we report both rather than only the average.

The September 2026 inflation number from the ONS is due on 21 October and is the first direct test of these forecasts. The Intermediate Energy MRN projects 3.7 per cent, the Simple Energy + MPC MRN 3.9 per cent and the Average 3.8 per cent, all well above August’s 3.1 per cent, reflecting the motor-fuel surge the Bank has already documented. A September number in the 3.6–3.9 per cent range would validate the near-term path; something nearer 3.3 per cent would suggest the VAT cut and the G7 reserve release are biting faster than the model allows. The second test is the 6 November MPC decision: the Simple MRN class implies the hawks gain ground, the Intermediate MRN class implies the first cut arrives by November, and the two cannot both be right. The third is the Ofgem announcement for January 2027, due in late November, which will fix the single biggest input into our peak in the first quarter of 2027. The IMF’s October World Economic Outlook and the NIESR Autumn Economic Outlook both appear before our next update, and we will report how the MRN stands against their revised paths.

1 The modelling approach is described in Binner, J. M., Kelly, L. J. and Tepper, J. A. (2025) ‘Professional Forecasters vs. Shallow Neural Network Ensembles: Assessing Inflation Prediction Accuracy’, Journal of Risk and Financial Management, 18(4), 173 (MRN methodology). https://doi.org/10.3390/jrfm18040173.

Recent months have reinforced the case for accelerating action on the energy transition and climate, particularly from a European perspective.

On the face of it, the case for accelerating the transition has never been stronger. But despite this, the state of multilateral action on climate change can probably be summed up by the collective shrug in response to the Climate Summit convened by the outgoing UN Secretary-General in New York on 23 September. In his final UNGA week, Antonio Guterres again argued that fossil fuel expansion “defies science, economics and common sense”. In language reflecting an increasing sense of alarm and urgency, he talked about this being the last generation “who can avert climate catastrophe”.

The weakened state of climate multilateralism is often attributed to a geopolitical environment in which political consensus has fractured and climate science is more openly challenged. This is evident not only in North America but in several European countries. But are there still opportunities this autumn for the pendulum to swing back towards concerted policy action that reflects the favourable platform that science, technology and economics are providing?

All roads on climate tend to lead to the COP, which this year will meet in Antalya, Turkey, from 9-20 November. COP31 will feature an unusual co-hosting arrangement between Turkey and Australia, alongside a pre-COP meeting hosted by Fiji and Tuvalu from 5-8 October. Crucially, the Pacific gathering will give small island states a platform to highlight the existential threat posed by climate change.

As for COP31 itself, the co-hosts face the challenge of providing a central focus for a COP where no single major negotiated decision is expected and which is being described as an “implementation COP”. But two key themes are emerging:

Serious discussion of both issues will be welcome. Yet many increasingly view the COP process, and the wider UN system, as unable to move beyond being a talking shop. Which is why, perhaps even more than is usual at a COP, some of the more consequential action in Antalya may take place in the margins outside the formal negotiations.

This would be consistent with the most significant outcomes from COP30 in Belém, with the emergence of two separate “coalitions of the willing” to work on international roadmaps: to transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF); and to halt and reverse global deforestation.

This TAFF initiative in particular will be put to the test of COP politics, even if it’s not on the formal agenda. Twelve months on from its birth in Belém, and seven months since the coalition of nearly 60 countries met in Santa Marta, Colombia, to kickstart work on a global TAFF process, there will be pressure to start turning high-level ambitions into concrete plans. This will mean attention on the Netherlands, which co-hosted Santa Marta with a Colombian government that has since been replaced by a new administration not committed to the initiative, and Ireland and Tuvalu, which will host a “Santa Marta 2.0” in the Pacific next July. These governments will want to show whether their initiative can work alongside the COP process and even restore some faith in the value of international cooperation to tackle global challenges. Other members of the coalition may also face questions about whether their domestic policies match their claims to international leadership: from the UK Government, which will also take on the G20 presidency in 2027, to Canadian and Australia governments, where fossil fuel production policy is moving in a different direction.

Looking beyond COP31, there are still grounds for optimism, whether through existing institutions or coalitions such as TAFF. The possibility, if recent reports are to be believed, that China could host COP33 in 2029 could be a game-changer, another Paris moment for the UNFCCC and multilateralism to demonstrate that it can deliver more than rhetoric. But back in the present, the science is making clear that delaying meaningful action, even now, will only do further harm. As the Belém Declaration on a TAFF spelled out nearly 12 months ago, action needs to be accelerated.
As progressives gather in Antalya, they may therefore do well to keep two overarching priorities at top of mind.

First, revisit the Belém Declaration as a constant reminder that limiting global temperature rises requires a “shared determination to work collectively towards a just, orderly and equitable transition away from fossil fuels”. This work will require, as the Declaration detailed, a focus on economic diversification, reducing structural dependence on fossil fuel revenues and phasing out inefficient fossil fuel subsidies. Progressive policymakers will also need to consider how to support a step-change in finance for the Global South, given the vulnerability of many emerging and developing economies to both the transition and the physical impacts of climate change. The work that has begun since the Santa Marta conference – both in the Santa Marta workplan and the separate but closely linked Brazilian COP Presidency TAFF exercise – will give policymakers the tools to start implementing TAFF in practice. That collective effort can begin in the discussions in and around COP31, even if not yet in the formal negotiations.

Second, one of the most positive developments this year has been the reframing of climate around energy security, risk and resilience. The statement by the UK Prime Minister at the same UNGA week where the UN Secretary-General’s Climate Summit yielded little tangible progress, that “the climate crisis is now a national security threat for countries around the world”, is a sign of an evolving narrative. As is this line from the recent Green Central Banking newsletter: “maybe resilience, for lack of a better word, is a new, pragmatic way to ensure climate action and collaboration still take place in an ever more geopolitically fragmented world.”
COP delegates will also be mindful that they are convening just after the US mid-terms on 3 November.

Many of the underlying conditions (economic, technological and scientific) are in place for governments to make this autumn one of significant progress on climate ambition. The case for framing the transition around economic opportunity and 21st-century energy security is clear. Policymakers may remain cautious in the current geopolitical environment; but this is time to seize the moment.
